Description: Candidate conjoint: 311 MTurk respondents each compared up to 6 pairs of hypothetical U.S. presidential candidates varying on 8 attributes (military service, religion, college, profession, income, race/ethnicity, age, gender); forced choice plus a 7-point rating of each candidate.
Reference: Hainmueller, J., Hopkins, D. J., & Yamamoto, T. (2014). Causal inference in conjoint analysis: Understanding multidimensional choices via stated preference experiments. Political Analysis, 22(1), 1-30.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/hainmueller_2014.R. Task and profile inferred from row order; MTurk IDs dropped.

Description: COVID-19 vaccine conjoint: 1,971 U.S. adults (Lucid, July 2020) each saw 5 pairs of hypothetical vaccines varying on 7 attributes (efficacy, duration, major and minor side effects, FDA approval, origin, endorsement); choice of vaccine A, B or neither, plus a 7-point likelihood of taking each.
Reference: Kreps, S., Prasad, S., Brownstein, J. S., Hswen, Y., Garibaldi, B. T., Zhang, B., & Kriner, D. L. (2020). Factors associated with US adults' likelihood of accepting COVID-19 vaccination. JAMA Network Open, 3(10), e2025594.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/kreps_2020.R. Opt-out tasks have choice = 0 on both profiles. Published AMCEs reproduce exactly.

Description: US adults (n=1,154) chose between and rated (0-100) pairs of hypothetical school energy-saving programs varying in who makes decisions, who gets implementation information, CO2 reduction and cost savings, after a randomized low-trust prime. Forced choice plus a rating of each program.
Reference: Liu, Y., Lee, H., & Berry, F. (2023). How and when democratic values matter: Challenging the effectiveness-centric framework in program evaluation. Public Performance & Management Review, 46(4), 820-845.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/liu_2023.R. All 1,154 respondents kept; the authors analyse the 885 passing manipulation and attention checks (cov_manip_check_pass, cov_attention_pass).

Description: Finnish adults (n=2,005, Qualtrics panel, 2021-22) chose between pairs of hypothetical citizens' forums varying on 9 design features (issue, convenor, recruitment, size, composition, aim, consensus, output, authorization). Forced choice; no rating was collected in Finland.
Reference: Goldberg, S., Lindell, M., & Bächtiger, A. (2025). Empowered minipublics for democratic renewal? Evidence from three conjoint experiments in the United States, Ireland, and Finland. American Political Science Review, 119(3), 1393-1410.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/goldberg_2025.R. attr_output: level text confirmed by the survey document, but which code is 'in favor' is inferred (codes unlabelled in the deposit; see script header).

Description: Irish adults (n=2,007, Psyma panel, 2022) chose between and rated (1-7) pairs of hypothetical citizens' forums varying on 9 design features (issue, convenor, recruitment, size, composition, aim, consensus, output, authorization). Forced choice plus a support rating of each forum.
Reference: Goldberg, S., Lindell, M., & Bächtiger, A. (2025). Empowered minipublics for democratic renewal? Evidence from three conjoint experiments in the United States, Ireland, and Finland. American Political Science Review, 119(3), 1393-1410.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/goldberg_2025.R. attr_output: level text confirmed by the survey document, but which code is 'in favor' is inferred (codes unlabelled in the deposit; see script header).

Description: US adults (n=2,045, Psyma panel, 2022) chose between and rated (1-7) pairs of hypothetical citizens' forums varying on 9 design features (issue, convenor, recruitment, size, composition, aim, consensus, output, authorization). Forced choice plus a support rating of each forum.
Reference: Goldberg, S., Lindell, M., & Bächtiger, A. (2025). Empowered minipublics for democratic renewal? Evidence from three conjoint experiments in the United States, Ireland, and Finland. American Political Science Review, 119(3), 1393-1410.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/goldberg_2025.R. attr_output: level text confirmed by the survey document, but which code is 'in favor' is inferred (codes unlabelled in the deposit; see script header).

Description: Paraguayan adults (n=2,058, online panel 2021) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical municipal candidates varying in anti-corruption platform, bribery and embezzlement record, gender, ideology, party, competence, age and education. Two choices per pair: which to vote for (with an option not to vote) and which would most reduce corruption.
Reference: Vera, S. (2025). Cleaning up politics: Anti-corruption appeals in electoral campaigns. British Journal of Political Science, 55, e108.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/vera_2025.R. Task/profile inferred from row order. 2 respondents with corrupted attribute cells dropped (paper n=2,060). Spanish text for 3 attributes, author English labels for 6.

Description: 2,042 white US-born Prolific respondents each chose between 6 pairs of hypothetical candidates varying in party and in campaign statements on six issues, after a status-threat vignette. Outcomes are forced choice and a 1-7 likelihood of voting for each candidate.
Reference: Ferrari, D., & Smith, B. (2025). Status threat, partisanship, and voters' conservative shift toward right-wing candidates. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 12(3), 324-338.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/ferrari_2025.R. Issue attributes hold the displayed statement text. Paper reports 2,080 collected vs 2,042 in the deposit (the authors' analysis sample).

Description: 778 market vendors, motorcycle-taxi drivers and shopkeepers in 18 Ugandan towns, interviewed face to face, compared 4 pairs of hypothetical officials accused of embezzlement. Outcomes are which official they would rather see punished and a 1-5 rating of how serious each official's corruption was.
Reference: Martin, L. (2021). All sins are not created equal: The factors that drive perceptions of corruption severity. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 8(1), 15-25.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/martin_2021.R. rating: higher = MORE severe corruption, kept as in the source. attr_ text is the English captions of picture icons explained verbally. GPS, enumerator IDs and town dropped.

Description: 18,021 eligible voters in 15 European countries (about 1,200 per country, online, 2016) each compared 5 pairs of hypothetical asylum-seeker profiles varying on 9 attributes. Outcomes are forced choice and a 1-7 rating of support for granting asylum.
Reference: Bansak, K., Hainmueller, J., & Hangartner, D. (2016). How economic, humanitarian, and religious concerns shape European attitudes toward asylum-seekers. Science, 354(6309), 217-222.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/bansak_2016.R. One table across 15 countries (one translated design; deposit stores English master labels only); country in cov_country. cov_survey_weight raw (authors top-code at 6).

Description: UK respondents compared pairs of hypothetical international missions (peacekeeping, diplomatic or humanitarian) varying in personnel, size, lead organisation and location; 646 respondents, 6 pairs each. Outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-5 perceived-effectiveness rating of each mission.
Reference: Pickering, S. (2025). Replication data for: Peacekeeping by any other name: A conjoint experiment evaluating support for peacekeeping, diplomatic and humanitarian missions in Japan and the UK [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/pickering_2025.R. The deposit's file names are swapped (replication_data_jp.csv is the UK sample). No published article found; question wording not deposited; level labels are the authors' English labels.

Description: Japanese respondents compared pairs of hypothetical international missions (peacekeeping, diplomatic or humanitarian) varying in personnel, size, lead organisation and location; 1,509 respondents, 4 pairs each. Outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-5 perceived-effectiveness rating of each mission.
Reference: Pickering, S. (2025). Replication data for: Peacekeeping by any other name: A conjoint experiment evaluating support for peacekeeping, diplomatic and humanitarian missions in Japan and the UK [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/pickering_2025.R. The deposit's file names are swapped (replication_data_jp.csv is the UK sample). No published article found; question wording not deposited; level labels are the authors' English labels.

Description: German online-panel respondents chose between pairs of hypothetical Brexit withdrawal agreements varying on seven negotiation issues (exit bill, citizens' rights, free movement, EU law, trade, services, EU programmes); 2,388 respondents, 6 pairs each, two survey waves pooled. Outcome is a forced choice.
Reference: Jurado, I., León, S., & Walter, S. (2022). Brexit dilemmas: Shaping postwithdrawal relations with a leaving state. International Organization, 76(2), 273-304.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/jurado_2022.R. Two cross-sectional waves pooled (trial_wave), as in the paper. Respondents saw German; English author labels used. Profile A/B mapping from the source's undocumented ab column assumed.

Description: Spanish online-panel respondents chose between pairs of hypothetical Brexit withdrawal agreements varying on seven negotiation issues (exit bill, citizens' rights, free movement, EU law, trade, services, EU programmes); 2,408 respondents, 6 pairs each, two survey waves pooled. Outcome is a forced choice.
Reference: Jurado, I., León, S., & Walter, S. (2022). Brexit dilemmas: Shaping postwithdrawal relations with a leaving state. International Organization, 76(2), 273-304.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/jurado_2022.R. Two cross-sectional waves pooled (trial_wave), as in the paper. Respondents saw Spanish; English author labels used. Profile A/B mapping from the source's undocumented ab column assumed.

Description: A race-balanced US Qualtrics panel judged pairs of hypothetical neighborhoods described only by racial composition; 1,999 respondents (1,803 after excluding 196 straightliners), 4 pairs each. Outcomes are a forced choice of the more racially diverse neighborhood and a 1-7 diversity rating of each.
Reference: Abascal, M., Xu, J., & Baldassarri, D. (2021). People use both heterogeneity and minority representation to evaluate diversity. Science Advances, 7(11), eabf2507.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/abascal_2021.R. Includes 196 Qualtrics-flagged straightliners (cov_straightliner = 1) that the paper's N = 1,803 excludes. Rating measures perceived diversity, not preference.

Description: Turkish online-panel respondents (n=2,362) rated and chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical Syrian refugee profiles varying on nine attributes (gender, age, ethnicity, religion, education, Turkish friends, Turkish language, civil-war involvement, torture), for three questions: as a neighbor, for a work permit, and for citizenship.
Reference: Getmansky, A., Matakos, K., & Sinmazdemir, T. (2024). Diversity without adversity? Ethnic bias toward refugees in a co-religious society. International Studies Quarterly, 68(2), sqae031.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/getmansky_2024.R. Three outcomes as choice_/rating_ neighbor, work_permit, citizenship. Task/profile inferred from row order (verified). Level text from the authors' pre-analysis-plan instrument; respondents saw Turkish.

Description: YouGov respondents in eight US metro areas (Jan 2018, n = 7,800) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical local development plans varying in education, higher-education, investment/tax, governance, worker/entrepreneur and local-service policies; forced choice.
Reference: Jensen, A., Marble, W., Scheve, K., & Slaughter, M. J. (2021). City limits to partisan polarization in the American public. Political Science Research and Methods, 9(2), 223-241.
Notes: data/conjoint/jensen_2021.R. Eight cities pooled (cov_city) as in the paper; $msaname/$statename placeholders in three levels filled with the respondent's city/state, so those levels are city-specific; attribute order randomized within respondent but not recorded; YouGov weight kept; county/ZIP dropped.

Description: Face-to-face sample in low-to-middle-income Santiago neighbourhoods (2017, control arm, n = 290) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical presidential candidates varying in ideology (left/right), profession and age; choice with a volunteered 'neither' option.
Reference: Visconti, G. (2021). Reevaluating the role of ideology in Chile. Latin American Politics and Society, 63(2), 1-25.
Notes: data/conjoint/visconti_2021.R. Undocumented outcome code 3 (222 tasks) treated as opt-out 'neither' as the authors code it; DK/DA tasks dropped (300 -> 290 respondents); levels are the Spanish card words; authors' balance script mislabels gender (b6==1 as female), 2 = female used here.

Description: US Democrats and Republicans (online panel, July 2016) chose between 7 pairs of hypothetical candidates varying in party, gender, race and stances on Obamacare, Muslim immigration, corporate taxes, birth-control coverage and illegal immigration; 3,015 respondents, forced choice.
Reference: Mummolo, J., Peterson, E., & Westwood, S. (2021). The limits of partisan loyalty. Political Behavior, 43, 949-972.
Notes: data/conjoint/mummolo_2021.R. Study 1 only; Study 2 held (conjoint_divisive.csv not deposited). Repeat survey takers (same panel id) reduced to first response (3,073 -> 3,015). Outcome wording from data, paper not accessed.

Description: Face-to-face national sample of Costa Ricans aged 18-64 (Dec 2013-Feb 2014) compared pairs of hypothetical trade agreements on 11 attributes (partner country, number of countries, prices, sectoral jobs, environmental/labour standards, work permits for foreign workers); 821 respondents, preferred-agreement choice and 1-7 support rating.
Reference: Spilker, G., Bernauer, T., & Umaña, V. (2018). What kinds of trade liberalization agreements do people in developing countries want? International Interactions, 44(3), 510-536.
Notes: data/conjoint/spilker_2018.R. Task 4 dropped: its profile-1 outcomes are a copy of task 1's in the deposit. Task/profile inferred from row blocks. Level text = English rendering from article Table 2.

Description: Face-to-face national sample of Nicaraguans aged 18-64 (Dec 2013-Feb 2014) compared pairs of hypothetical trade agreements on 11 attributes (partner country, number of countries, prices, sectoral jobs, environmental/labour standards, work permits for foreign workers); 800 respondents, preferred-agreement choice and 1-7 support rating.
Reference: Spilker, G., Bernauer, T., & Umaña, V. (2018). What kinds of trade liberalization agreements do people in developing countries want? International Interactions, 44(3), 510-536.
Notes: data/conjoint/spilker_2018.R. Task 4 dropped: its profile-1 outcomes are a copy of task 1's in the deposit. Task/profile inferred from row blocks. Level text = English rendering from article Table 2.

Description: Face-to-face sample of adults aged 18-64 in the Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City areas (Dec 2013-Feb 2014) compared pairs of hypothetical trade agreements on 11 attributes (partner country, number of countries, prices, sectoral jobs, environmental/labour standards, work permits for foreign workers); 700 respondents, preferred-agreement choice and 1-7 support rating.
Reference: Spilker, G., Bernauer, T., & Umaña, V. (2018). What kinds of trade liberalization agreements do people in developing countries want? International Interactions, 44(3), 510-536.
Notes: data/conjoint/spilker_2018.R. Task 5 dropped: its second profile's attributes are corrupt in the deposit (one missing per row, dummies inconsistent). Task/profile inferred from row blocks. Level text from article Table 2.

Description: UK YouGov respondents (Jan 2025, n = 2,231 answering the conjoint) chose between 4 pairs of hypothetical parliamentary candidates varying in name (sex, Turkish vs majority ethnicity), age, years in profession, occupation and stated task priority; forced vote choice.
Reference: Pedersen, H. H. (2025). Legislator or representative? Politicians' tasks according to voters. British Journal of Political Science.
Notes: data/conjoint/pedersen_2025.R. Levels = the deposit's English master value labels (UK wording). Young age restricted to 1-3 years' experience. Non-consenters (no conjoint) dropped. Danish and German samples held: localized names/text not deposited.

Description: US YouGov respondents (Jan 2025, n = 2,185 answering the conjoint) chose between 4 pairs of hypothetical legislative candidates varying in name (sex, Turkish vs majority ethnicity), age, years in profession, occupation and stated task priority; forced vote choice.
Reference: Pedersen, H. H. (2025). Legislator or representative? Politicians' tasks according to voters. British Journal of Political Science.
Notes: data/conjoint/pedersen_2025.R. Levels = English master labels, which say 'Parliament'; US screens probably said House/Congress (not verifiable). Young age restricted to 1-3 years' experience. Non-consenters dropped.

Description: Respondents chose between, and rated 1-7, two hypothetical arms deliveries from their own country, with nine attributes (recipient regime, human rights, conflict, security partnership, trade, economic value, jobs, weapon type, other suppliers). Quota samples from Kantar's online panel in Germany and France (n = 6,617; 6 pairs each); outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-7 approval rating.
Reference: Rudolph, L., Freitag, M., & Thurner, P. W. (2024). Deontological and consequentialist preferences towards arms exports: A comparative conjoint experiment in France and Germany. European Journal of Political Research, 63(2), 705-728.
Notes: data/conjoint/rudolph_2024.R. One table pooling Germany and France (cov_country), English master labels; other-suppliers country placeholder resolved per respondent. Attribute order randomized but not deposited; cov_war_1..5 item mapping inferred from questionnaire order; timers dropped (CJ_3 = CJ_4 in every row); vignette and party split experiments dropped; no survey weight.

Description: US adults (Bovitz panel, wave 2, June 2020; n=996) chose between two versions of the same consumer product varying in country of origin, customer rating and price, 10 tasks each; forced choice.
Reference: Bankert, A., Powers, R., & Sheagley, G. (2023). Trade politics at the checkout lane: Ethnocentrism and consumer preferences. Political Science Research and Methods, 11(3), 605-612.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bankert_2023.R. Price text rebuilt from markup x appendix Table A3 base prices; profile position not recorded (profile = file row order); Lucid replication not built (no product column).

Description: Block Development Officers in Telangana, India (elite sample, n=221) chose which of two hypothetical village heads (sarpanches) they would help get work done, varying gender, seat reservation, education and family background; up to 4 tasks.
Reference: Purohit, B. (2026). Bureaucratic discretion against female politicians. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/purohit_2026.R. Attribute text is the author's short labels; exact outcome wording not in deposit; only respondent gender kept (elite sample).

Description: Adults in Austria, Italy, the Netherlands, Slovakia, Spain and Sweden (2025, n=9,045) compared pairs of national migration-policy packages on six dimensions (asylum, labour shortages, welfare, regularization, borders, returns), 5 tasks; forced choice plus a 1-7 support rating per policy.
Reference: Jeannet, A.-M., & Rubio, M. G. (2026). PACES public opinion dataset [Data set]. DANS Data Station Social Sciences and Humanities.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/jeannet_2026.R. Six countries pooled with cov_country; attr text is the English master with [pipe: COUNTRY]; 80-char truncated values matched to codebook; dimension order randomized but not recorded; survey weight included.

Description: British adults (YouGov, May 2023, n=2,001) chose between two fictional candidates varying in social traits, policy positions and working-class group appeals, 2 tasks; forced vote choice plus 1-7 ratings of representation and left-right placement.
Reference: Finseraas, H., Heath, O., Langsæther, P. E., & Smets, K. (2026). How group appeals shape group-party linkages in two political systems. The Journal of Politics, 88(3), 1264-1269.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/finseraas_2026.R. Occupation collapsed to class in deposit (6 job titles shown); rating_leftright is placement, not favourability.

Description: Norwegian adults (Kantar, Jan-Feb 2022, n=3,171) chose between two fictional candidates varying in social traits, policy positions and working-class group appeals, 2 tasks; forced vote choice plus 1-7 ratings of representation and left-right placement.
Reference: Finseraas, H., Heath, O., Langsæther, P. E., & Smets, K. (2026). How group appeals shape group-party linkages in two political systems. The Journal of Politics, 88(3), 1264-1269.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/finseraas_2026.R. English translation of Norwegian text; occupation collapsed to class; paper reports 2,931 analysed vs 3,171 here (unreconciled); 228 tasks lack a choice.

Description: US MTurk respondents (n=1,500) chose which of two hypothetical school board candidates they would vote for, varying occupation, party, incumbency, race and gender, 3 tasks; forced choice.
Reference: Atkeson, L. R., & Hamel, B. T. (2020). Fit for the job: Candidate qualifications and vote choice in low information elections. Political Behavior, 42(1), 59-82.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/atkeson_2020.R. Level text as in deposit; screen wording undocumented; derived shared-party variables dropped.

Description: Spanish mayors (elite sample, 2018-19, n=913) chose which of two hypothetical party leaders they would form a coalition with, varying gender, age, education, council terms, ideology and seats, 2 tasks; forced choice plus four 1-5 agreement ratings on the second task.
Reference: Huidobro, A. (2026). Partners in government: Politicians' gender preferences in coalition formation. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/huidobro_2026.R. Task/profile inferred from row order (verified); paper reports 979 mayors/3,324 obs, author's log 905/3,526 (reproduced); grouped covariates only.

Description: Japanese adults (Rakuten Insight, Aug 2021, n=2,511) chose which of two prospective immigrants they would support admitting, varying gender, age, nationality, education, previous job, purpose and duration, 5 tasks, after a randomized framing vignette; forced choice.
Reference: Song, J., & Woo, Y. (2026). Replication data for: "Public support for migration policies in new immigration countries: Evidence from framing and conjoint experiments in East Asia" [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/song_2026.R. English level text from authors' appendix (shown in Japanese); trial_framing arm; survey weight; article DOI not found.

Description: South Korean adults (Dynata, Oct 2020, n=1,991) chose which of two prospective immigrants they would support admitting, varying gender, age, nationality, education, previous job, purpose and duration, 5 tasks, after a randomized framing vignette; forced choice.
Reference: Song, J., & Woo, Y. (2026). Replication data for: "Public support for migration policies in new immigration countries: Evidence from framing and conjoint experiments in East Asia" [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/song_2026.R. English level text from authors' appendix (shown in Korean); trial_framing arm; survey weight; article DOI not found.

Description: US adults (Prolific, June 2022; n=997) compared 10 pairs of hypothetical state supreme court candidates described by prior political experience, law school, gender, occupation and newspaper endorsement; outcomes are a forced choice of preferred candidate and a 4-point rating of each candidate's qualification.
Reference: Kennedy, M., Nelson, M. J., & Heidt-Forsythe, E. (2025). Gender stereotypes and candidate qualifications in judicial elections. Political Research Quarterly, 78(1).
Notes: data/conjoint/kennedy_2025.R. Raw Qualtrics wide export. Rating reversed from source (1 = most qualified) to 4 = most qualified, as in authors' code; anchor wording not in deposit. 15 tasks (2 respondents) lack a choice. Covariates are unlabelled Qualtrics codes. 2 Prolific IDs appear twice (kept). Article N not checked (unreachable).

Description: Colombian adults (Netquest online panel, Feb-Mar 2024; n=1,642, 1,572 completing all tasks) compared 6 pairs of hypothetical Colombians abroad wishing to return, described by intended employment, savings, political ambition and country of return; outcomes are a forced choice and a 0-10 favourability rating of each.
Reference: Scholten, M. (2025). The prodigal child returns? Attitudes towards return migration in a developing economy. International Studies Quarterly, 69(2), sqaf041.
Notes: data/conjoint/scholten_2025.R. Raw Qualtrics export inside isq_replication.zip (experimental/conjoint.csv). Spanish level text as displayed. Keeps all respondents with any outcome, including partials (authors use the 1,572 with all 6 choices). Rating anchors not in deposit. Article N not checked (closed access).

Description: Colombian adults in a face-to-face Ipsos survey compared two hypothetical migrants (Venezuelan or Peruvian, varying on skills, age, gender, family, ideology, Colombian relatives and reason for migrating) in one paired task; 1,429 respondents. Outcomes: which migrant is preferred (choice) and a 1-7 support rating.
Reference: Argote, P., & Daly, S. Z. (2024). The formation of attitudes toward immigration in Colombia. International Interactions, 50(2), 370-384.
Notes: data/conjoint/argote_2024.R. Level text = authors' English labels (Spanish shown not in deposit); outcome wording undocumented; rating direction inferred (7 = most support). Source respondent_serial contains PII in some rows and is dropped; ids re-keyed. Reproduces Table D1 AMCEs exactly.

Description: US adults compared pairs of hypothetical migrant applicants (gender, language fluency, occupation, origin, reason for migration incl. climate reasons, religion, vulnerability) over 9 tasks; 1,085 respondents. Outcomes: 1-7 rating of whether their state should admit each migrant, and a forced choice of which one may stay.
Reference: Arias, S. B., & Blair, C. W. (2022). Changing tides: Public attitudes on climate migration. The Journal of Politics, 84(1), 560-567.
Notes: data/conjoint/arias_2022.R. Attribute order re-randomized per task (attrpos_*). Intended restriction (no 'None' fluency for internal migrants) was not enforced in the US fielding. Article N 2,160 across US+Germany vs 2,157 here.

Description: German adults compared pairs of hypothetical migrant applicants (gender, language fluency, occupation, origin, reason for migration incl. climate reasons, religion, vulnerability; German text) over 9 tasks; 1,072 respondents. Outcomes: 1-7 rating of whether Germany should admit each migrant, and a forced choice of which one may stay.
Reference: Arias, S. B., & Blair, C. W. (2022). Changing tides: Public attitudes on climate migration. The Journal of Politics, 84(1), 560-567.
Notes: data/conjoint/arias_2022.R. Level text in German as displayed (religion levels shown in English; 'Atheist' where the US had 'Agnostic'). Attribute order re-randomized per task (attrpos_*). Article N 2,160 across US+Germany vs 2,157 here.

Description: US adults (n=1,999, online panel) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical immigrants described by immigration status, country of origin, education, employment and taxes paid; forced choice of which of the two is most beneficial to the US. Fielded right after an information experiment (Study 1 arm recorded).
Reference: Aviña, M. M. (2026). Perceived economic contributions increase positivity toward undocumented immigrants. Public Opinion Quarterly, 90(3), 591-629.
Notes: data/conjoint/avina_2026.R. Study 2 only. Question wording from the OSF preprint SI (no questionnaire in deposit); renamed from avina_2026_immigrant_admission on 2026-10-08; level text from codebook/factor labels; randomization non-uniform ('Illegal alien' ~50% of profiles); Prolific-type IDs re-keyed; authors' binary splits dropped.

Description: Adults in 15 European countries (n=14,966, Respondi online panels, May-June 2022) evaluated 5 pairs of hypothetical asylum seekers on 9 attributes; forced choice of which to let stay and a 1-7 rating of each.
Reference: Bansak, K., Hainmueller, J., & Hangartner, D. (2023). Europeans' support for refugees of varying background is stable over time. Nature, 620(7975), 849-854.
Notes: data/conjoint/bansak_2023.R. 2022 wave only (2016 wave = bansak_2016_asylum). Pooled with cov_country, English master labels. 10 respondents with no attribute levels dropped (paper N 14,976); 120 lack weights; attribute order randomized but not recorded; trial_frame = survey-opening frame.

Description: US adults (SSI online panel, January 2014; 1,627 respondents) compared 7 or 10 pairs of hypothetical immigrants on six attributes including religion and religious attendance, choosing which to admit and rating each 1-7 on admission.
Reference: Berinsky, A. J., Rizzo, T., Rosenzweig, L. R., & Heaps, E. (2020). Attribute affinity: U.S. natives' attitudes toward immigrants. Political Behavior, 42(3), 745-768.
Notes: data/conjoint/berinsky_2020.R; only the SSI 2014 file is a conjoint (other deposit files are single-vignette experiments, not converted); article reports N=1,571 vs 1,627 respondents answering in the deposit (unexplained); Table 6 reproduces exactly

Description: French adults (Qualtrics online panel, Dec 2017-Jan 2018; 1,500 respondents) chose which of two hypothetical immigrants should be admitted to live in France, over 10 pairs described by nine attributes shown in French.
Reference: Clayton, K., Ferwerda, J., & Horiuchi, Y. (2021). Exposure to immigration and admission preferences: Evidence from France. Political Behavior, 43(1), 175-200.
Notes: data/conjoint/clayton_2021.R; attribute text in French as displayed with three soft-launch spelling variants harmonized; soft-launch tasks with unrestricted education x profession combinations kept (authors drop 332 tasks); N matches article (1,500); AMCEs reproduce within 0.001

Description: British adults in a YouGov omnibus (Oct 2018, n=1,648; 1,597 British citizens analysed in the paper) saw 5 pairs of vignettes of foreign-born naturalisation applicants (gender, residence length, British ancestry, origin, religion, English, occupation, refugee status) and said for each whether they should be granted British citizenship (one, both or neither).
Reference: Donnaloja, V. (2022). British nationals' preferences over who gets to be a citizen according to a choice-based conjoint experiment. European Sociological Review, 38(2), 202-218.
Notes: data/conjoint/donnaloja_2022.R. Per-profile grant/not-grant in rating (0/1). Level text = vignette fragments from Codebook.xlsx; attr_ancestry '(no ancestry clause)' = the paper's 'Neither' level, attr_refugee '(no refugee clause)' = clause not shown (refugee status shown only for Pakistan/Nigeria/Syria/Somalia). Non-citizens kept (cov_citizenship 3); YouGov weight kept.

Description: Italian citizens in a YouGov online panel (n=1,463, December 2021) saw 5 pairs of profiles of children born in Italy to foreign parents (11 parental attributes) and said for each child whether they would grant Italian citizenship at birth (A, B, both or neither).
Reference: Donnaloja, V., & Vink, M. (2023). Like parent, like child: How attitudes towards immigrants spill over to the political inclusion of their children. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 50(14), 3435-3452.
Notes: data/conjoint/donnaloja_2023.R. Per-profile yes/no in rating (both/neither allowed); Italian level text from the YouGov fielding spec; Romania never with undocumented status; attribute order randomized but not recorded; non-citizens dropped as in the paper; YouGov weight kept.

Description: Colombian adults in Cali and Cúcuta (face-to-face, 2019; n=1,003) chose which of two hypothetical migrant profiles (origin, gender, race, skill, employment prospects, reason for leaving, partisanship) they would prefer to stay in their city and receive housing and employment assistance, 5 pairs each.
Reference: Holland, A. C., Peters, M. E., & Zhou, Y.-Y. (2024). Left out: How political ideology affects support for migrants in Colombia. The Journal of Politics, 86(4), 1291-1303.
Notes: data/conjoint/holland_2024.R; attribute text is authors' English labels (Spanish shown); 51 task-3 pairs dropped for a missing attribute level; deposit contains respondent PII, none kept

Description: Venezuelan migrants in Cali and Cúcuta (face-to-face, 2019; n=1,608) chose which of two hypothetical migrant profiles (origin, gender, race, skill, employment prospects, reason for leaving, partisanship) they would prefer to stay in their city and receive housing and employment assistance, 5 pairs each.
Reference: Holland, A. C., Peters, M. E., & Zhou, Y.-Y. (2024). Left out: How political ideology affects support for migrants in Colombia. The Journal of Politics, 86(4), 1291-1303.
Notes: data/conjoint/holland_2024.R; attribute text is authors' English labels (Spanish shown); deposit contains respondent PII, none kept

Description: Taiwanese adults (n=2,075) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical immigrant (New Resident) profiles varying country of origin, ethnicity, occupation/visa status and Mandarin proficiency, choosing one per pair on three questions: admission, national health insurance, and mother-tongue instruction.
Reference: Kao, J. C., & Liu, A. H. (2025). Racial identities, linguistic proficiency, and public attitudes towards immigrants: Evidence from two surveys in Taiwan. Political Research Quarterly, 78(2), 701-719.
Notes: data/conjoint/kao_2025.R; attribute text is authors' English labels (Chinese shown); 'No Info' level kept as text (probably attribute not shown); outcome wording unconfirmed (article not reachable)

Description: Pakistani citizens in the 15 largest Afghan-refugee-hosting districts (face-to-face, Gallup Pakistan, 2024; n = 2,786 who answered at least one round) chose which of two unregistered Afghan refugee profiles they would prefer to stay in Pakistan, over 3 rounds. Attributes: ethnicity, gender, household-head occupation, years in Pakistan.
Reference: Malik, M., Siddiqui, N., & Zhou, Y.-Y. (2025). How does coethnicity with refugees shape their reception? Evidence from Afghan refugees in Pakistan. SocArXiv. Forthcoming in The Journal of Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/malik_2025.R. Skip/DK tasks omitted (714 skipped all rounds). Occupation level can be the respondent's own household-head occupation (piped). English codebook labels; interviews were in Urdu/Pashto. Pashtun-Tajik marginal-mean gap 0.090 vs 0.092 reported.

Description: US Lucid quota sample (Feb 2019, n = 2,247) rated 4 pairs of immigrant profiles (a Hainmueller & Hopkins 2015 replication) on a 1-7 admit/allow-to-stay scale, under one of three randomized framings: visa applicants abroad (flows), resident aliens renewing visas (stocks), or stocks with refusal framed as deportation.
Reference: Margalit, Y., & Solodoch, O. (2022). Against the flow: Differentiating between public opposition to the immigration stock and flow. British Journal of Political Science, 52(3), 1055-1075.
Notes: data/conjoint/margalit_2022.R. Three framing arms in one table (trial_frame). Attribute text is the authors' short labels; full wording is in online Appendix 4. No covariates: the respondent file cannot be linked to the conjoint file.

Description: Qatari citizens (SESRI face-to-face survey, May 2018, n=488) chose which of two 'baskets' of non-citizen groups (each naming two of five groups, e.g. children of Qatari mothers, those with military service) should be prioritised for citizenship, over up to 3 pairs. Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Shockley, B., & Gengler, J. J. (2024). Sharing citizenship: Economic competition, cultural threat, and immigration preferences in the rentier state. Political Science Research and Methods, 12(1), 59-75.
Notes: data/conjoint/shockley_2024.R; level labels are the authors' English analysis labels from their R code (respondents saw Arabic; no codebook deposited); group-position attrpos_ inferred from e1p/e2p codes; no survey weight in this file.

Description: Qatari citizens (SESRI face-to-face survey, May 2018, n=657) chose between pairs of hypothetical candidates for permanent residency varying religion (cued by first name), nationality, occupation, salary, time in Qatar and language, over up to 3 pairs. Outcome: choice with an option to reject both.
Reference: Shockley, B., & Gengler, J. J. (2024). Sharing citizenship: Economic competition, cultural threat, and immigration preferences in the rentier state. Political Science Research and Methods, 12(1), 59-75.
Notes: data/conjoint/shockley_2024.R; level labels are the authors' English analysis labels (Arabic shown; names cueing religion not deposited, level = cued identity); opt-out in 35 tasks; profile order within pair assumed from row order; profile ratings mentioned in the article are not deposited.

Description: Online respondents in 22 countries (Lucid, Feb-Mar 2022, n=45,724) acting as immigration officers chose which of two applicants for permanent residence would be a better fit, over 6 pairs; applicants varied in language proficiency, age, country of origin (rival/ally x racially similar/different), gender, occupation and length of residence. Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Wimmer, A., Bonikowski, B., Crabtree, C., Fu, Z., Golder, M., & Tsutsui, K. (2024). Geo-political rivalry and anti-immigrant sentiment: A conjoint experiment in 22 countries. American Political Science Review, 119(2), 1018-1035.
Notes: data/conjoint/wimmer_2024.R; one pooled table with cov_country (English master labels; respondents saw national languages); task/profile inferred from row order (verified); deposit has 45,740 respondents vs 46,549 in the article; rival/similar classification dropped (mapping in script header); superiority items' wording not deposited.

Description: US Lucid respondents (n=929, December 2019) rated 15 pairs of hypothetical immigrant profiles (age, gender, race/ethnicity, education, English proficiency, prior trips to the U.S.) on an 11-point scale from 0 = definitely not admit to 10 = definitely admit.
Reference: Zhirkov, K. (2022). Estimating and using individual marginal component effects from conjoint experiments. Political Analysis, 30(2), 236-249.
Notes: data/conjoint/zhirkov_2022.R. Ratings only (no choice); attrpos_* from per-respondent randomized attribute order; 7 missing ratings omitted; authors' extra drop of respondents lacking variation on dichotomized attributes not applied; ethnocentrism scale score dropped.

Description: 3,036 respondents in the US (MTurk), UK (Prolific) and Israel (Midgam, in Hebrew) each read 7 single hypothetical cyber-incident scenarios varying in method, target, actor, motivation and outcome (August 2020). Outcome is whether they classified each incident as cyberterrorism (1) or not (0).
Reference: Shandler, R., Kostyuk, N., & Oppenheimer, H. (2023). Public opinion and cyberterrorism. Public Opinion Quarterly, 87(1), 92-119.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/shandler_2023.R. One table with cov_country because the authors pool the three samples; English level text, mapped through level codes for Israel (Hebrew shown). Replaces shandler_2023_cyberterror_us/_uk/_il. Binary judgement in rating (1 = cyberterrorism).

Description: Immigration conjoint: 1,396 U.S. respondents (GfK, 2012) each compared 5 pairs of hypothetical immigrant applicants varying on 9 attributes (education, gender, origin, reason for applying, profession, job experience, job plans, prior trips, language); forced choice of which to admit and a 1-7 rating of each.
Reference: Hainmueller, J., Hopkins, D. J., & Yamamoto, T. (2014). Causal inference in conjoint analysis: Understanding multidimensional choices via stated preference experiments. Political Analysis, 22(1), 1-30.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/hainmueller_2014.R. Restricted randomization (education x job, country x reason). Rating, survey weight and demographics added from the same experiment's fuller deposit, Hainmueller & Hopkins (2015), doi:10.7910/DVN/25505 (CC0), matched row by row. Choice AMCEs match the cjoint package exactly.

Description: 2,653 US respondents (Dynata panel and undergraduates, 2022) each rated 9-10 single profiles (blurred face photo with varied skin tone, self-identified race, parents' race, parents' occupations, religion, English at home, age) on six 1-5 agree statements that the person is White, Black, Latino, Asian, MENA or a person of color.
Reference: Abascal, M., Armenta, A., Halm, W. M., & Hopkins, D. J. (2025). Who polices which boundaries? How racial self-identification affects external classification. American Journal of Sociology, 131(3), 630-683.
Notes: data/conjoint/abascal_2025.R. Two samples pooled (cov_sample) as the authors did. Single-profile tasks (profile = 1). Photo stored as image code + skin tone, with the authors' face gender/ethnicity coding. Qualtrics response IDs re-keyed; free-text write-ins dropped.

Description: Candidate choice conjoint fielded on MTurk in the US: respondents chose between two candidates in 5 tasks, with candidate party shown in one between-subject arm and hidden in the other (1,326 respondents). Outcomes: candidate choice, and in the no-party arm's last task a guess of each candidate's party.
Reference: Andersen, S. C., & Hjortskov, M. (2026). Masking or lexicographic preferences? Using conjoint experiments to distinguish between two fundamental theories of choice. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/andersen_2026.R. Level text from Stata value labels; question wording and display format not deposited. Party arm = the MTurk sample of Hjortskov & Andersen (2024, BJPolS; doi:10.7910/DVN/F53FQ1). Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: Tax-reform conjoint: 921 German adults (Lucid quota sample, 2021 federal election campaign) each compared 5 pairs of reform packages varying personal income, inheritance and corporate taxes, and chose which package contributes more to reducing inequality and which more to economic growth.
Reference: Becker, B., Castanho Silva, B., & Lierse, H. (2025). Taxing your cake and growing it too: Public beliefs on the dual benefits of progressive taxation. Journal of Public Policy, 46, 1-20.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/becker_2025.R. Respondents saw German; attr_ text is the article's English Table 1 level text mapped from the authors' short codes. No overall preference question (outcomes choice_inequality, choice_growth). Deposit has 921 respondents; the article implies about 1,214 analysed (1,360 minus 146 attention-check failures).

Description: 2,382 Senegalese (Dakar) firm respondents each judged 4 pairs of hypothetical business deals varying in contract formality, the partner's political connections and party affiliation, firm size, and the manager's ethnicity and religion; per-deal 0/1 outcomes for which deal they would choose (one, both or neither) and which would end in breach.
Reference: Bhandari, A. (2023). Social, formal, and political determinants of trade under weak rule of law: Experimental evidence from Senegalese firms. Comparative Political Studies, 56(2), 163-192.
Notes: data/conjoint/bhandari_2023.R. Answers allowed Deal 1/Deal 2/Neither/Both, so outcomes are per-profile 0/1 ratings (= authors' preferred_firm, breach_risk). rating_breach higher = worse. Attribute order randomized (4 undocumented schemes, trial_attribute_order). Refusals/don't know blank. ODK uuids re-keyed.

Description: US respondents (n = 2,078 answering; survey-weighted sample) each chose between 12 pairs of hypothetical military strikes varying strike type (nuclear or conventional), chance of success, military casualties, allied approval, civilian casualties and environmental damage; half the pairs used restricted 'realistic' randomization.
Reference: Bowen, T., Goldfien, M. A., & Graham, M. H. (2023). Public opinion and nuclear use: Evidence from factorial experiments. The Journal of Politics, 85(1), 345-350.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bowen_2023.R. Level text = the file's short labels (questionnaire not deposited; outcome wording unknown). trial_randomization: Realistic (restricted: nuclear always Option 1 vs conventional Option 2) or Conjoint (fully randomized). Pilot conjoint not built (display order lost).

Description: Japanese adults (Rakuten Insight online panel, March 2019; n = 1,274 answering) each chose between 2 pairs (a third pair was asked, but its answers in the deposit duplicate the second's) of policy packages varying spending on education, women's employment, childcare and social security, income, sales and corporate taxes, and government debt.
Reference: Brazzill, M., Magara, H., & Yanai, Y. (2020). When voters favour the social investment welfare state. Japanese Journal of Political Science, 21(4), 194-205.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/brazzill_2020.R. Levels kept as the authors' English codes (increase / decrease / sq = status quo; debt noIncrease / gradualDecrease / immediateDecrease); Japanese display text and question wording not deposited. Task 3 dropped: its selections in the deposit copy task 2's.

Description: US adults (Ipsos KnowledgePanel, summer 2021; n=2,777) rated 5 single-profile political-conversation scenarios varying the partner's relationship, party, knowledge, news source, engagement, race and gender and the setting (face-to-face vs social media); the outcome is a 5-point rating of how likely they would be to express their true opinion.
Reference: Carlson, T. N., & Settle, J. E. (2023). Freedom of expression in interpersonal interactions. PS: Political Science & Politics, 56(2), 245-249.
Notes: data/conjoint/carlson_2023.R. Single profile per task (rating only). Level text from the pre-registration in the article supplement; 'mainstream partisan' news names Fox News/MSNBC by partner party, outlet unrecorded for Independent partners; partisan news level ~66% of tasks. 25 respondents with no answered task omitted. Article N not checked (paywalled).

Description: Respondents in Cote d'Ivoire, Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda (n = 4,920 with at least one answer) each rated four hypothetical scenarios about a media outlet accused of an infraction, varying the funding source, the accuser and the infraction, on how harshly the station should be restricted (1 = nothing to 5 = shut down permanently).
Reference: Conroy-Krutz, J. (2025). Muzzling the media? Explaining popular support for media restrictions in Africa. The Journal of Politics, 87(3), 1169-1181.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/conroykrutz_2025.R. One profile per task (profile = 1). Task inferred from row order, verified against the task-numbered wide file. Level text from the codebook/Stata labels (English); vignette wording and interview language not deposited. Higher rating = harsher restriction. Refused/don't know dropped.

Description: US MTurk workers (July 2016; n=2,512) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical trade agreements described by effects on US jobs, US growth and partner growth and by the partner's regime and wealth; two of three randomized arms added the agreement's effect on US global influence or the partner's security relationship to the US.
Reference: DiGiuseppe, M., & Kleinberg, K. B. (2018). Economics, security, and individual-level preferences for trade agreements. International Interactions, 45(2), 289-315.
Notes: data/conjoint/digiuseppe_2018.R. trial_arm = control / global_influence / political_relations; arm-specific attributes blank where not shown. Level text from article Table 1. One respondent with no regime values dropped (2,512 = article N). Control-arm AMCEs reproduce article Table 2. Qualtrics response IDs dropped (re-keyed to deposit's anonymous id).

Description: US Prolific respondents (n=1,996, March 2024) chose between pairs of hypothetical newly elected state legislatures (members' occupational class, session length, staff, salary, party control, bill limits, calendar posting) on three questions: which benefits society, which benefits people like you, and a third whose wording is not deposited.
Reference: Dobson, M. R., Lollis, J. M., Harden, J. J., & Kirkland, J. H. (2026). Legislative professionalism and perceptions of white-collar government. Journal of Political Institutions and Political Economy, 7(2), 145-161.
Notes: data/conjoint/dobson_2026.R. Task 2 dropped (one attribute cell of profile A empty for everyone in the deposit). choice_q3 wording unknown. Attribute names assigned from level text; question wordings from the authors' figure titles. PII (IP, GPS, ResponseId, Prolific IDs, occupation text) dropped.

Description: 962 US MTurk respondents (Nov 2019) each compared 15 pairs of hypothetical congressional candidates differing in party, four issue positions and support for one of five court-curbing proposals (10 general-election, 5 primary pairs); outcomes are the preferred candidate and two 5-point ratings (candidate rating, mobilization).
Reference: Driscoll, A., & Nelson, M. J. (2023). The costs of court curbing: Evidence from the United States. The Journal of Politics, 85(2), 609-624.
Notes: data/conjoint/driscoll_2023.R. Level text is the authors' factor labels from Study2.R (displayed wording is in the article's Appendix B, not deposited). Candidate name attribute dropped (unlabelled codes). Rating recode follows the authors but is not monotone in choice share; exact wording and anchors unknown. Study 1 (vignette) not built.

Description: COVID-19 vaccine prioritisation conjoint: 15,536 adults in 13 countries (late 2020) each chose which of two hypothetical people should get the vaccine immediately in 8 tasks, profiles varying COVID-19 death risk, transmission risk, income, occupation and age; forced choice.
Reference: Duch, R., Roope, L. S. J., Violato, M., Fuentes Becerra, M., Robinson, T. S., Bonnefon, J.-F., Friedman, J., Loewen, P. J., Mamidi, P., Melegaro, A., Blanco, M., Vargas, J., Seither, J., Candio, P., Gibertoni Cruz, A., Hua, X., Barnett, A., & Clarke, P. M. (2021). Citizens from 13 countries share similar preferences for COVID-19 vaccine allocation priorities. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 118(38), e2026382118.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/duch_2021.R. Screened from the re-host in Robinson & Duch (doi:10.7910/DVN/CG9VPE); the file is byte-identical to the original deposit PMV0TG, which is cited. Countries pooled with cov_country as in the paper; English level text, display languages outside the UK not documented. The 1-7 priority ratings in the questionnaire are not in the deposited data.

Description: 942 university students in Chile, China, India and the UK (2018) each chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical employment destinations abroad and rated each 1-7; destinations varied social benefits, GDP growth, service-sector salaries, university rankings and a destination country label (Australia / U.K. or, for U.K. subjects, Canada / U.S.A.). Conjoint 3 of 3 in the study.
Reference: Duch, R. M., Laroze, D., Reinprecht, C., & Robinson, T. S. (2022). Nativist policy: The comparative effects of Trumpian politics on migration decisions. Political Science Research and Methods, 10(1), 171-187.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/duch_2022.R (builds all three conjoints; same respondents/ids). Levels are the authors' English (Chile saw Spanish, China Chinese). Ratings attached from the raw Qualtrics exports by replaying the authors' respondent filter (choices verified). Countries pooled with cov_country.

Description: 942 university students in Chile, China, India and the UK (2018) each chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical employment destinations abroad and rated each 1-7; destinations varied social benefits, GDP growth, service-sector salaries, university rankings and an immigration policy (point system / visa-centre change / deportation of all illegal immigrants). Conjoint 2 of 3 in the study.
Reference: Duch, R. M., Laroze, D., Reinprecht, C., & Robinson, T. S. (2022). Nativist policy: The comparative effects of Trumpian politics on migration decisions. Political Science Research and Methods, 10(1), 171-187.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/duch_2022.R (builds all three conjoints; same respondents/ids). Levels are the authors' English (Chile saw Spanish, China Chinese). Ratings attached from the raw Qualtrics exports by replaying the authors' respondent filter (choices verified). Countries pooled with cov_country.

Description: 942 university students in Chile, China, India and the UK (2018) each chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical employment destinations abroad and rated each 1-7; destinations varied social benefits, GDP growth, service-sector salaries, university rankings and an immigration policy (point system / visa-centre change / restriction on Muslim immigration and tourist visas). Conjoint 1 of 3 in the study.
Reference: Duch, R. M., Laroze, D., Reinprecht, C., & Robinson, T. S. (2022). Nativist policy: The comparative effects of Trumpian politics on migration decisions. Political Science Research and Methods, 10(1), 171-187.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/duch_2022.R (builds all three conjoints; same respondents/ids). Levels are the authors' English (Chile saw Spanish, China Chinese). Ratings attached from the raw Qualtrics exports by replaying the authors' respondent filter (choices verified). Countries pooled with cov_country.

Description: Japanese respondents (n=2,018) chose between 10 pairs of hypothetical House of Councillors candidates described by age, gender, incumbency, education, local ties, prior occupation and political background; forced choice. Attribute text is the authors' English labels (respondents saw Japanese).
Reference: Eshima, S., & Smith, D. M. (2022). Just a number? Voter evaluations of age in candidate-choice experiments. The Journal of Politics, 84(3), 1856-1861.
Notes: data/conjoint/eshima_2022.R. Authors' processed file only (raw not deposited): task/profile inferred from row order; English author labels; question wording and the meaning of treatment arms T1-T4 (trial_treat_group) not in the deposit (appendix paywalled). Qualtrics response IDs re-keyed. Marginal means match the authors' stored subgroup results.

Description: Candidate conjoint on anti-Muslim bias: 3,171 Norwegian adults (Verian panel; 629 first-stage baseline respondents plus 2,542 second-stage respondents randomized to five information arms) each chose between two candidates varying gender, age, occupation, family, experience and religion, plus party, policy or personal attributes by arm, in 6 tasks; forced choice.
Reference: Finseraas, H., & Heim, R. (2026). What drives voter bias against Muslim politicians? An experimental examination. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/finseraas_2026_muslim.R. Two samples pooled as the authors do (trial_stage; trial_arm 0-5); source responseid collides across stages, so ids re-keyed. Display language not documented (presumably Norwegian); attr_ text is the deposit's English value labels (party written out from the authors' Table 1). Task 6 repeats task 1 with profiles swapped. Article DOI not found; year from the deposit.

Description: 1,205 Mexican respondents each saw one pair of photographs of security personnel varying in uniform (police/military), weapon, gender and skin colour; outcomes are a forced choice of who is more effective and four 0-1 ratings (effectiveness, civil liberties, corruption, acceptance in own neighbourhood).
Reference: Flores-Macías, G., & Zarkin, J. (2022). Militarization and perceptions of law enforcement in the developing world: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in Mexico. British Journal of Political Science, 52(3), 1377-1397.
Notes: data/conjoint/floresmacias_2022.R. Attributes shown in photos; level text is the authors' labels. Rating wording, anchors and the direction of rating_corrupt are not in the deposit. Municipality identifiers dropped. Standardized civil-liberties AMCEs reproduce exactly.

Description: 651 political, civil-society and academic elites in ten Latin American countries (2018 online survey) each chose between 2 hypothetical climate-mitigation treaties in up to 7 tasks; treaties varied in who makes the rules, conflict resolution, punishment, penalties for repeat violations, cost sharing and renegotiation interval.
Reference: Freire, D., Mignozzetti, U., & Skarbek, D. (2021). Institutional design and elite support for climate policies: Evidence from Latin American countries. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 8(2), 172-184.
Notes: data/conjoint/freire_2021.R. Countries pooled (cov_country) as in the authors' main models. Level text is the authors' English labels; respondents saw Spanish or Portuguese. One randomization restriction (no None punishment with Less penalty). Duplicate task records for 3 respondents collapsed. Qualtrics GPS coordinates dropped. Marginal means reproduce the supplement.

Description: 805 Malawian respondents each chose between 2 hypothetical candidates in 6 contests; candidates varied in disaster-prevention and relief effort and effectiveness, asking for relief, constituency visits and honesty. Outcome is the supported candidate.
Reference: Hartmann, F. (2026). Do voters value relief over preparedness? Evidence from disaster policies in Malawi. The Journal of Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/hartmann_2026.R. Level text is the author's short English factor labels; displayed wording, language and survey mode are not in the deposit. Gender, education, income codes unlabelled and dropped; village dropped. Main AMCE table reproduces exactly.

Description: Adults in nine European countries (Bilendi panels, Feb-Mar 2023; n=9,125) each saw 4 single hypothetical person profiles varying EU attitude, immigration attitude, class, education and age, and judged whether the person typically lives in a rural or urban area, how sure they were, and rated the person on a 0-100 feeling thermometer.
Reference: Hegewald, S. (2026). The urban-rural divide in people's minds: Stereotypes of urbanites and ruralites in nine European countries. Political Behavior.
Notes: data/conjoint/hegewald_2026.R. Single-profile design (profile = 1); countries pooled with cov_country (EL -> GR). Attribute text is the English master from the author's preprint (doi:10.31219/osf.io/x25ne) with '[country]' placeholder; respondents saw national languages. rating_sureness 1 = very sure (higher = less sure, as stored). Pooled AMCEs reproduce the preprint.

Description: 3,027 US respondents (2022 wave (Lucid)) each chose between two candidates in 10 tasks (House vs city council candidates, party labels shown to a random half (trial_show_party)); each candidate took affirmative or negated positions on 4 policies drawn from 10 national and 9 municipal policies. Outcome is the preferred candidate.
Reference: Holliday, D. E., & Rudkin, A. (2026). DC on my mind: Voter evaluations of nationalized policy positions in state and local elections. The Journal of Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/holliday_2026.R (one script, three tables). Policy attributes blank when not shown (4 per task); row positions not kept. Tasks 1-5 House, 6-10 city council (trial_office). cov_baseline_* = respondent's own stance on each policy. Raked weight in cov_survey_weight. Raw Qualtrics exports in the deposit hold IP/lat-long/Lucid ids (not read).

Description: 1,377 US respondents (2021 pilot wave (Lucid)) each chose between two candidates in 10 tasks (House vs state assembly candidates, no party labels); each candidate took affirmative or negated positions on 4 policies drawn from 10 national and 10 state policies. Outcome is the preferred candidate.
Reference: Holliday, D. E., & Rudkin, A. (2026). DC on my mind: Voter evaluations of nationalized policy positions in state and local elections. The Journal of Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/holliday_2026.R (one script, three tables). Policy attributes blank when not shown (4 per task); row positions not kept. Tasks 1-5 House, 6-10 state assembly (trial_office). cov_baseline_* = respondent's own stance on each policy. Raked weight in cov_survey_weight. Raw Qualtrics exports in the deposit hold IP/lat-long/Lucid ids (not read).

Description: 1,537 US respondents (2022 wave (Lucid)) each chose between two candidates in 10 tasks (House vs state assembly candidates, each with a party label); each candidate took affirmative or negated positions on 4 policies drawn from 10 national and 10 state policies. Outcome is the preferred candidate.
Reference: Holliday, D. E., & Rudkin, A. (2026). DC on my mind: Voter evaluations of nationalized policy positions in state and local elections. The Journal of Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/holliday_2026.R (one script, three tables). Policy attributes blank when not shown (4 per task); row positions not kept. Tasks 1-5 House, 6-10 state assembly (trial_office). cov_baseline_* = respondent's own stance on each policy. Raked weight in cov_survey_weight. Raw Qualtrics exports in the deposit hold IP/lat-long/Lucid ids (not read).

Description: Japanese adults (online panel, November 2015; n=2,200) chose between 10 pairs of hypothetical national legislators described by party, age, gender, terms, experience, hometown, education, prior occupation and parental political background, for one house (lower or upper) and both electoral tiers (district and PR, 5 tasks each); attribute text is the Japanese shown.
Reference: Horiuchi, Y., Smith, D. M., & Yamamoto, T. (2020). Identifying voter preferences for politicians' personal attributes: A conjoint experiment in Japan. Political Science Research and Methods, 8(1), 75-91.
Notes: data/conjoint/horiuchi_2020.R. Raw Qualtrics export; levels in Japanese as displayed (hometown/occupation/parent name the respondent's prefecture). trial_house and trial_tier give the condition of each task. Experience 'never in office' only with terms 'none'. Authors' entropy-balancing weights not deposited. Article N not checked (paywalled).

Description: Tunisian adults (n=1,497) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical foreign investments (company nationality, industry, urban/rural, whether jobs are for men or for women with/without the hijab, skill level, prayer facilities), choosing one and rating support for each on a 7-point scale.
Reference: Jamal, A., & Milner, H. V. (2022). Islam and mass preferences toward foreign direct investment in Tunisia. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 9(3), 314-325.
Notes: data/conjoint/jamal_2022.R. Rating reversed from source (1 = very strongly support) so higher = more support, as the authors do. Blank industry/jobs-for/skill/prayer levels are randomized not-mentioned levels. English text only in the deposit; rating stem wording not deposited. Qualtrics ResponseId dropped.

Description: South Korean National Police frontline investigators (n=1,294) chose which of two assault cases to prioritize (accuser age, accuser gender, accuser occupation, accused age, accused reachability, assault story); 3 pairs each, experiment 1 of 2.
Reference: Kang, I., & Jilke, S. (2024). Mapping out the motivational basis of active representation as intergroup behavior. Public Administration, 102(1), 164-187.
Notes: data/conjoint/kang_2024.R. Task inferred from profile order (pairs 1-2, 3-4, 5-6; one chosen per pair, checked). Attribute text is the authors' English coding labels; Korean displayed text not deposited. Question wording not deposited. Article not read (publisher blocks access).

Description: South Korean National Police frontline investigators (n=631) chose which of two assault cases to prioritize (accuser-and-accused age, accuser occupation, accused occupation, assault severity, intimate-partner relationship, accused's devaluation of women); 3 pairs each, experiment 2 of 2.
Reference: Kang, I., & Jilke, S. (2024). Mapping out the motivational basis of active representation as intergroup behavior. Public Administration, 102(1), 164-187.
Notes: data/conjoint/kang_2024.R. Task inferred from profile order (pairs 1-2, 3-4, 5-6; one chosen per pair, checked). Attribute text is the authors' English coding labels; Korean displayed text not deposited. Question wording not deposited. Article not read (publisher blocks access).

Description: Criminal-opportunity conjoint: 1,000 adults from a national sample (country not stated in the deposit; payouts in dollars) each chose between two hypothetical criminal opportunities in 5 tasks, varying victim, co-offenders, completion time, payout, payout timing, arrest chance and punishment; forced choice.
Reference: Krajewski, A. T., Pickett, J. T., & Jacobs, B. A. (2025). How people choose between criminal opportunities. Criminology, 63(3), 639-660.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/krajewski_2025.R. Task and profile inferred from row order (exactly one chosen per pair). Attribute text from Stata value labels; question wording not deposited. Deposit has 1,000 respondents, article abstract reports 1,023.

Description: US adults (YouGov, 2018; n=1,000) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical Supreme Court nominees described by judicial philosophy, party, ideology, ABA rating, position, law school, demographics and office history; outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-5 rating of each nominee.
Reference: Krewson, C. N., & Owens, R. J. (2021). Public support for judicial philosophies: Evidence from a conjoint experiment. Journal of Law and Courts, 9(1), 89-110.
Notes: data/conjoint/krewson_2021.R. Task/profile inferred from row blocks; authors' short attribute labels; question wording and rating anchors not deposited (5 = favourable inferred). Party-ideology restricted and non-uniform race/law-school weights (cjoint design object in deposit). Sample facts from the companion 2022 JLC paper's appendix. Article N not checked.

Description: Ethnic-Danish YouGov respondents (n=4,368, Feb-Mar 2022) saw 15 hypothetical male public-goods-game participants, three at a time (name: Danish or Middle Eastern, born in Denmark, religiosity, age, plus treatment-dependent information), chose who would contribute most and rated each one's expected contribution 0-10 (DKK 100 units).
Reference: Kruse, M. (2025). The correlates of ethnicity: Why the ethnic majority expects that ethnic minorities contribute less to the collective. British Journal of Political Science, 55, e70.
Notes: data/conjoint/kruse_2025.R. Information treatment (trial_information) decides which attributes are shown; unshown attributes blank. Level text is the English codebook translation (Danish shown); names are the actual names. Question wordings paraphrased from the article (Appendix A not read).

Description: Conjoint experiment in which 1,213 US online respondents compared five pairs of hypothetical US military interventions differing in security and humanitarian outcomes, casualties, costs, durability of peace and target regime. Outcomes: which intervention was more successful, and a 1-4 success rating of each.
Reference: Maxey, S. (2025). Good enough? Public perceptions of success in military interventions. International Studies Quarterly, 69(3), sqaf051.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/maxey_2025.R. Survey one only (surveys two and three are single-scenario vignettes). Task and profile inferred from row order (verified by choice pairing). Level text = Stata value labels, possibly abbreviated from the displayed wording. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: Electoral-reform conjoint (Study 1): 2,177 US adults each compared 3 pairs of hypothetical electoral-rule-change scenarios varying partisan support, number of House parties, ideological distribution (graph), ballot structure and district magnitude; four forced choices per pair (overall pick, voice, governability, responsiveness).
Reference: Mayne, Q., & Singh, S. P. (2026). Attitudes toward electoral system reform and party system change in the U.S. American Political Science Review, 1-24.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mayne_2026.R. Built from the raw Qualtrics export (Study 1 Source.xlsx); Qualtrics ResponseId dropped, ids re-keyed. Ideological representation was shown as a graph; level text = lead sentence + the authors' graph name (Unimodal/Flat/Bipolar). Study 2 (fixed vignettes) not built. 12,842 rows match the Supplementary Material.

Description: Democratic congressional primary candidate conjoint (Lucid study 1): 469 white Democrats (Lucid, 2022) each chose between one Black and one White hypothetical candidate differing in race, age, job, political experience, endorsement and positions on healthcare, fossil fuels and reparations. Outcomes: vote choice plus eight 0-1 ratings of each candidate (favourability, perceived ideology, six trait descriptions).
Reference: Mikkelborg, A. C. (2025). White Democrats' growing support for Black politicians in the era of the "Great Awokening." American Political Science Review.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mikkelborg_2025.R (study1.csv). One task per respondent; deposit holds white respondents only. Candidate race fixed as one Black, one White per pair. Profile A/B recorded. Level text as stored (policy levels may be abbreviated in studies 1-2). Studies 5 and the California voter survey in the same deposit were not built.

Description: Democratic congressional primary candidate conjoint (Lucid study 2): 1,999 white respondents (Lucid, 2023; 1,852 Democrats) each chose between one Black and one White hypothetical candidate differing in race, age, job, political experience, endorsement and either policy positions or self-described ideology (between-subject versions in trial_version). Outcomes: vote choice plus six 0-1 trait ratings of each candidate.
Reference: Mikkelborg, A. C. (2025). White Democrats' growing support for Black politicians in the era of the "Great Awokening." American Political Science Review.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mikkelborg_2025.R (study2.csv). One task per respondent; deposit holds white respondents only. Candidate race fixed as one Black, one White per pair. Profile order inferred from row order. Level text as stored (policy levels may be abbreviated in studies 1-2). Studies 5 and the California voter survey in the same deposit were not built.

Description: Democratic congressional primary candidate conjoint (Lucid study 3): 272 white respondents (Lucid, 2023) each chose between one Black and one White hypothetical candidate differing in race, age, job, political experience, endorsement and self-described ideology. Outcomes: vote choice.
Reference: Mikkelborg, A. C. (2025). White Democrats' growing support for Black politicians in the era of the "Great Awokening." American Political Science Review.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mikkelborg_2025.R (study3.csv). One task per respondent; deposit holds white respondents only. Candidate race fixed as one Black, one White per pair. Profile order inferred from row order. Level text as stored (policy levels may be abbreviated in studies 1-2). Studies 5 and the California voter survey in the same deposit were not built.

Description: Democratic congressional primary candidate conjoint (Lucid study 4): 153 white respondents (Lucid, 2023) each chose between one Black and one White hypothetical candidate differing in race, gender, age, job, political experience, endorsement and positions on fossil fuels, healthcare and reparations. Outcomes: vote choice.
Reference: Mikkelborg, A. C. (2025). White Democrats' growing support for Black politicians in the era of the "Great Awokening." American Political Science Review.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mikkelborg_2025.R (study4.csv). One task per respondent; deposit holds white respondents only. Candidate race fixed as one Black, one White per pair. Profile order inferred from row order. Level text as stored (policy levels may be abbreviated in studies 1-2). Studies 5 and the California voter survey in the same deposit were not built.

Description: 756 respondents in Myanmar (June 2022) each chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical 2023 scenarios varying the COVID-19 situation, vaccine availability, access to medical services, and whether elections are restored.
Reference: Mon, S. O., & Yamada, K. (2024). Do pandemics reduce support for democracy? A survey experiment in Myanmar. Japanese Journal of Political Science, 25(3), 140-161.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mon_2024.R. Levels rebuilt from 0/1 dummies using codebook wording; the codebook swaps the government and medical-services attributes relative to the Stata labels and the authors' analysis, Stata labels used. Vaccine base-level text ('Pfizer/Moderna') is from a variable label, not displayed text. Fixed (non-independent) design.

Description: US MTurk workers (Sept 2019; n=736) compared 15 pairs of hypothetical job offers described by salary, firm size, location type, workplace culture, the state's presidential partisanship and a state democratic-backsliding event; outcomes are a forced choice of offer and a 5-point rating of each.
Reference: Nelson, M. J., & Witko, C. (2022). The economic costs of democratic backsliding? Backsliding and state location preferences of US job seekers. The Journal of Politics, 84(2), 1233-1238.
Notes: data/conjoint/nelson_2022.R. Attribute text is the authors' recode labels, not displayed text (backsliding levels are code names, e.g. VoterID, Unionize; BikeTrails = placebo). Rating 1-5 is the authors' recode of nonmonotone Qualtrics codes; higher = favourable inferred. Wording not deposited. PII in raw export (IP, lat/long, ResponseId) dropped. Authors' code slips (task 5 choice, task 11 partisanship) not reproduced. Article N not checked. Student sample is a separate table (authors analyse samples separately).

Description: Students at a large US public university (Sept 2019; n=337) compared 15 pairs of hypothetical job offers described by salary, firm size, location type, workplace culture, the state's presidential partisanship and a state democratic-backsliding event; outcomes are a forced choice of offer and a 5-point rating of each.
Reference: Nelson, M. J., & Witko, C. (2022). The economic costs of democratic backsliding? Backsliding and state location preferences of US job seekers. The Journal of Politics, 84(2), 1233-1238.
Notes: data/conjoint/nelson_2022.R. Attribute text is the authors' recode labels, not displayed text (backsliding levels are code names, e.g. VoterID, Unionize; BikeTrails = placebo). Rating 1-5 is the authors' recode of nonmonotone Qualtrics codes; higher = favourable inferred. Wording not deposited. PII in raw export (IP, lat/long, ResponseId) dropped. Authors' code slips (task 5 choice, task 11 partisanship) not reproduced. Article N not checked. Separate table from the MTurk sample (authors analyse samples separately).

Description: 1,583 US adults (SSI online panel, March 2016) each chose between 10 pairs of hypothetical candidates (5 for President, 5 for the U.S. House) described by 13 attributes including sex, age, race, family, experience, party, issue positions and poll favorability.
Reference: Ono, Y., & Burden, B. C. (2019). The contingent effects of candidate sex on voter choice. Political Behavior, 41(3), 583-607.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ono_2019.R. Issue-position levels replaced by the displayed text from the working paper's Table 1. trial_office = President/Congress; task numbers put President first for everyone although block order was randomized, so task is not display order. Derived pair flags dropped.

Description: Candidate choice conjoint in the 2022 Cooperative Election Study (University of Georgia module): 1,308 US respondents chose between two candidates in five hypothetical nonpartisan local elections, with candidates varying in name (signalling race and gender), age, career, political experience, endorsements, family and community ties.
Reference: Ornstein, J. T., Heideman, A. J., Moy, B. J., & Schiff, K. J. (2024). Hometown advantage: Voter preferences for community embeddedness in local contests. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 12(3), 267-281.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ornstein_2024.R. Task inferred from row order (five stacked blocks). Candidate race/gender carried only by names; the authors' name codings (B/L/W, Female/Male) are not attributes (gender in crosswalk). Question wording not deposited. cov_survey_weight = CES team weight.

Description: 506 hiring managers in China each judged 3 hypothetical job applicants' resumes, varying an ideological study group (blocked: one of each per respondent), GPA rank, gender, CCP membership, a political statement, major and university, reporting whether they would call each applicant back (0/1).
Reference: Pan, J., & Zhang, T. (2023). Does ideology influence hiring in China? Evidence from two randomized experiments. Political Science Research and Methods, 11(1), 63-79.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/pan_2023.R. Level text and outcome wording are the ReadMe's English variable definitions (Chinese resumes not deposited). One resume per task; task = row order (inferred). Study group blocked within respondent.

Description: 121 respondents (pretest; sample not described) each rated 10 hypothetical job applicants, varying master's major, highlighted courses and extracurricular study group (socialist vs Western), on academic merit, government connections and political conformity (1-10 each).
Reference: Pan, J., & Zhang, T. (2023). Does ideology influence hiring in China? Evidence from two randomized experiments. Political Science Research and Methods, 11(1), 63-79.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/pan_2023.R. Level text and outcome wording from the ReadMe definitions (paraphrase). One profile per task; task = profile letter A-K order (display order undocumented). Sample/country not documented.

Description: Choice-based candidate conjoint (two vignette pairs per respondent, one with and one without party labels) on candidate disability, fielded to online quota samples in the US and UK (5,969 respondents). Outcomes: vote choice, perceived left-right position (0-10) and agreement that the candidate represents under-represented groups (0-4).
Reference: Reher, S. (2025). Voting for disabled candidates. The Journal of Politics, 87(2), 790-794.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/reher_2025.R. Gender and minority ethnic background were conveyed only by candidate names, which are not in the deposit; attr_gender and attr_name_minority are the codebook's codings. Level text from the article SI Table S1. US and UK pooled (cov_country) as in the article.
