Description: 3,413 members of the Swiss Environmental Panel (wave 8, 2022), each randomly assigned a smartphone, TV or washing machine, chose which of two products to buy in 4 rounds; products varied price, functional duration, environmental production impact, energy-efficiency class, recyclability and repairability.
Reference: Brügge, C. (2024). Replication data: Circular products resonate well with diverse consumers. Evidence from a choice experiment in Switzerland [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/brugge_2024.R. Level text is the authors' English recode of the panel's German labels; price and functional duration are resolved to the respondent's own product (trial_product_type), so those levels depend on the product arm. Question wording not deposited (paraphrase). The authors' raking weight and attribute-order variables are not in the deposit. Article not found; reference is the data set.

Description: 1,000 US adults (Verasight panel) chose between two hypothetical flights in 5 tasks; flights varied airline, fuel type (sustainable aviation fuel vs conventional), included baggage, legroom, seat type and price.
Reference: Kriner, D., Goldfarb, J. L., Tester, J., & Bhujle, T. (2026). Replication data for: Comfort or climate? Consumer trade-offs between sustainable aviation fuel and flight amenities [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/goldfarb_2026.R. Attribute text and per-respondent attribute order (attrpos_) from the Qualtrics conjoint export columns; the fuel level 'Sutainable' typo is in the source. Survey weight kept. ZIP codes and Qualtrics IDs dropped; unrelated omnibus items dropped. Article not found; SAF AMCE +0.069 matches the deposit abstract.

Description: 771 Certified Crop Advisors (North America, Feb-Mar 2024) chose among three AI decision-support systems varying cost, accuracy, spatial precision and data ownership, or none of them, in 5 fixed choice sets (discrete choice experiment).
Reference: Zia, A., Gardezi, M., Yu, X., Ryan, B., Merrill, S. C., Clark, E. M., Dadkhah, A., Rizzo, D. M., McMaine, J., & Clay, D. (2026). Harnessing discrete choice experiments to elicit preferred configurations of trustworthy AI augmented decision support systems for certified crop advisors. Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, 9, 1747663.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/zia_2026.R. Fixed design: all respondents saw the same 5 choice sets (15 alternatives, levels strongly collinear, data ownership tied to the alternative's column), so attribute effects are weakly identified. task = choice-set id, not display position (order randomized, not recorded). 'None of these' opt-out: choice 0 on all three profiles (995 of 3,823 tasks). Level text from the questionnaire PDF.

Description: Malawian phone-survey respondents (May 2020) heard one vignette in which Covid-19 prevalence in their area, the authority asking (district hospital head or Traditional Authority) and the requested action (handwashing, no gatherings over 50, stay home) were randomized, then said whether they would comply and judged others' compliance, the authority's right to ask, risk reduction and monitoring. 3,125 respondents (religious-leader arm excluded).
Reference: Kao, K., Lust, E., Dulani, B., Ferree, K. E., Harris, A. S., & Metheney, E. (2021). The ABCs of Covid-19 prevention in Malawi: Authority, benefits, and costs of compliance. World Development, 137, 105167.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kao_2021.R. Single-profile factorial vignette, one per respondent. The religious-leader authority level was piped from the respondent's religion (Pastor/Priest/Sheikh) and not saved, so its 1,510 respondents (a random third) are excluded; the article's authority contrasts with religious leaders cannot be reproduced. Don't know/refuse -> NA. Yes/No outcomes coded 1/0; others-comply coded 1 None .. 4 Most.

Description: 1000 Japanese online (Lucid) respondents each saw 5 pairs of hypothetical House of Representatives candidates (occupation, Diet experience, education, age, gender, party, relatives in politics) and rated each candidate's perceived anti-elitism and people-centrism (1-6); arms with and without party affiliation shown.
Reference: Miwa, H. (2024). Why voters prefer politicians with particular personal attributes: The role of voter demand for populists. Political Studies, 73(2), 725-752.
Notes: data/conjoint/miwa_2024.R. Attribute text in Japanese as displayed; attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Ratings only, no choice.

Description: 3636 Japanese online (Lucid) respondents each saw 2 pairs of hypothetical House of Representatives candidates (occupation, Diet experience, education, age, gender, party, relatives in politics) and rated each candidate's desirability as a member of the House of Representatives (1-6); in one arm each candidate also had a randomly assigned 'special note' on populist or elitist conduct.
Reference: Miwa, H. (2024). Why voters prefer politicians with particular personal attributes: The role of voter demand for populists. Political Studies, 73(2), 725-752.
Notes: data/conjoint/miwa_2024.R. Attribute text in Japanese as displayed; attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Ratings only, no choice.

Description: 406 Japanese online (Lucid) respondents each saw 4 pairs of hypothetical House of Representatives candidates (occupation, Diet experience, education, age, gender, party, relatives in politics) and rated each candidate's perceived anti-elitism and people-centrism (1-6); pilot 1 for Study 2, with a randomly assigned 'special note' per candidate in one arm.
Reference: Miwa, H. (2024). Why voters prefer politicians with particular personal attributes: The role of voter demand for populists. Political Studies, 73(2), 725-752.
Notes: data/conjoint/miwa_2024.R. Attribute text in Japanese as displayed; attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Ratings only, no choice.

Description: 432 Japanese online (Lucid) respondents each saw 4 pairs of hypothetical House of Representatives candidates (occupation, Diet experience, education, age, gender, party, relatives in politics) and rated each candidate's perceived anti-elitism and people-centrism (1-6); pilot 2 for Study 2, with a randomly assigned 'special note' per candidate in one arm.
Reference: Miwa, H. (2024). Why voters prefer politicians with particular personal attributes: The role of voter demand for populists. Political Studies, 73(2), 725-752.
Notes: data/conjoint/miwa_2024.R. Attribute text in Japanese as displayed; attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Ratings only, no choice.

Description: 410 Japanese online (Lucid) respondents each saw 4 pairs of hypothetical House of Representatives candidates (occupation, Diet experience, education, age, gender, party, relatives in politics) and rated each candidate's perceived anti-elitism and people-centrism (1-6); pilot 3 for Study 2, with a randomly assigned 'special note' per candidate in one arm.

Description: 2367 Finnish online respondents each read 6 vignettes about an unfulfilled election pledge of a coalition-government party (randomized: number of government parties, party status, coalition agreement, ministry, other parties' attitude) and rated the acceptability of the non-fulfillment 0-10.
Reference: Ylisalo, J., Matthieß, T., Praprotnik, K., & Ennser-Jedenastik, L. (2025). Election pledges in multiparty governments: When do voters accept non-fulfillment? British Journal of Political Science.
Notes: data/conjoint/ylisalo_2025.R. Factorial vignette experiment; level text is the English codebook labels (survey instrument not deposited). Task = recorded vignette view order; attr_pledge is the fixed pledge topic of the vignette. 2,466 in the file (paper code 2466); 44 never reached the vignettes and 55 more gave no rating, so 2,367 remain; the paper's figures keep Finnish citizens only (cov_citizenship).

Description: 1359 German online respondents each read 6 vignettes about an unfulfilled election pledge of a coalition-government party (randomized: number of government parties, party status, coalition agreement, ministry, other parties' attitude) and rated the acceptability of the non-fulfillment 0-10.
Reference: Ylisalo, J., Matthieß, T., Praprotnik, K., & Ennser-Jedenastik, L. (2025). Election pledges in multiparty governments: When do voters accept non-fulfillment? British Journal of Political Science.
Notes: data/conjoint/ylisalo_2025.R. Factorial vignette experiment; level text is the English codebook labels (survey instrument not deposited). Task = recorded vignette view order; attr_pledge is the fixed pledge topic of the vignette. All 1,359 respondents (paper code 1359).

Description: 2093 German online respondents (a separate sample with a propensity-to-vote outcome) each read 6 vignettes about an unfulfilled election pledge of a coalition-government party (randomized: number of government parties, party status, coalition agreement, ministry, other parties' attitude) and rated their propensity to vote for the pledging party 0-10.
Reference: Ylisalo, J., Matthieß, T., Praprotnik, K., & Ennser-Jedenastik, L. (2025). Election pledges in multiparty governments: When do voters accept non-fulfillment? British Journal of Political Science.
Notes: data/conjoint/ylisalo_2025.R. Factorial vignette experiment; level text is the English codebook labels (survey instrument not deposited). Task = recorded vignette view order; attr_pledge is the fixed pledge topic of the vignette. 4,721 rows in the file; 2,093 respondents with vignettes and ratings remain; attention test kept as cov_attention_pass.

Description: 445 international-relations scholars based in Latin America each chose between two hypothetical journals to submit to in 3 tasks (8 attributes: methods relevance, audience, editorial location, response time, colleagues published, Scimago indexing, language, acceptance rate).
Reference: Montal, F., Yamin, P., & Pauselli, G. (2024). A matter of journal choice: A conjoint experiment on submission choices of Latin American IR scholars. International Studies Perspectives, 25(3), 407-424.
Notes: data/conjoint/montal_2024.R. Attribute text is the deposit's short English level labels; displayed wording, outcome wording and survey questions are not deposited (covariates named by question number). 4 unanswered tasks dropped (paper N 446, table 445).

Description: 2071 German respondents (quota sample plus an Eastern German oversample) each chose between two hypothetical emerging politicians in 8 tasks; profiles are positions on democracy, the economy, welfare, gender roles and ethnic/cultural diversity, shown as statements in German.
Reference: Brehm, N., Zhou, A. H., & Denney, S. (2025). From division to democracy: Integrating post-socialist citizens in Germany and South Korea. Communist and Post-Communist Studies.
Notes: data/conjoint/brehm_2025.R. Dataverse licence field says CC0 1.0 but the deposit's LICENSE/README say CC BY 4.0 (carried here). The Gender attribute is a gender-roles stance, not the politician's gender. Outcome wording not deposited. cov_female is 1 = answered female, 0 = any other answer; authors' age dropped (inherits implausible birth years).

Description: 1994 South Korean online panel respondents each chose between two hypothetical emerging politicians in 7 tasks; profiles are positions on democracy, the economy, welfare, gender roles and ethnic/cultural diversity, shown as statements in Korean.
Reference: Brehm, N., Zhou, A. H., & Denney, S. (2025). From division to democracy: Integrating post-socialist citizens in Germany and South Korea. Communist and Post-Communist Studies.

Description: 893 urban Chinese online respondents (SSI and Qualtrics panels) each compared 4 pairs of hypothetical property tax policies varying citizen input, provincial supervision, payment penalty and exemption, choosing one and rating each 1-5.
Reference: Lü, X., Tsai, L. L., Zheng, P., & Trinh, M. (2025). Do government accountability and responsiveness enhance support for property taxes? Experimental evidence from China. World Development, 194, 107051.
Notes: data/conjoint/lu_2025.R. Level text is the .dta value labels (terse English: Yes/No, 15%/3%); displayed Chinese wording and the rating's wording/anchors are not deposited. Two panels pooled as the authors do (trial_panel).

Description: 277 lab-in-the-field subjects in urban China each compared 6 pairs of hypothetical property tax policies (citizen input, provincial supervision, exemption threshold, tax rate, payment penalty, public-goods spending), choosing one and rating each 1-5.
Reference: Lü, X., Tsai, L. L., Zheng, P., & Trinh, M. (2025). Do government accountability and responsiveness enhance support for property taxes? Experimental evidence from China. World Development, 194, 107051.
Notes: data/conjoint/lu_2025.R. Level text is the .dta value labels (terse English); displayed Chinese wording and the rating's wording/anchors are not deposited. Lab session-subject codes re-keyed.

Description: 2161 a representative online sample of German voters each compared 8 pairs of coal phase-out scenarios (end date, annual costs, lost jobs, new jobs, structural-change measures), choosing one per pair and rating each 1-7. One of three samples from the same experiment.
Reference: Rinscheid, A., & Wüstenhagen, R. (2019). Germany's decision to phase out coal by 2038 lags behind citizens' timing preferences. Nature Energy, 4(10), 856-863.
Notes: data/conjoint/rinscheid_2019.R. Level text is the article's English Table 1 (German questionnaire not deposited). Half the respondents also saw the economy-wide cost next to the household cost; which trial_conjoint_type code is which is undocumented, attr_annual_cost holds the household amount. Attention-check failures kept (cov_attention_pass).

Description: US municipal government officials chose which of two hypothetical collaborative policy programs to adopt (up to 3 pairs; attributes: resource split, jobs created, proposing party, past collaborative experience). 772 officials, forced choice.
Reference: Liu, Y. (2024). Partisan collaboration in policy adoption: An experimental study with local government officials. Policy Studies Journal, 52(4), 955-967.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/liu_2024.R. Attribute levels are the author's short labels as stored (displayed wording not deposited); outcome wording paraphrased from the abstract. City, county, state and city census figures dropped (re-identify officials). Education/tenure/party/gender kept as codes (no labels in deposit).

Description: UK adults (SSI online panel, the week before the 2015 general election) chose between two anonymous parties' policy packages built from the 2015 manifestos (economy, jobs, immigration, EU, education), 4 pairs each. 1,403 respondents, forced choice.
Reference: Matsuo, A., & Lee, S. (2018). Multi-dimensional policy preferences in the 2015 British general election: A conjoint analysis. Electoral Studies, 55, 89-98.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/matsuo_2018.R. Profile (Party A/B) inferred from row order. One respondent ID with two complete answered sessions dropped. 1,403 respondents vs 1,394 in the paper. Attribute order randomized per respondent, not recorded. Post-stratification weight not deposited.

Description: Moroccan adults (face-to-face national survey, 2023) read one vignette about an MP whose gender/mode of election (district vs gender quota) and collaboration (own party vs other parties) were randomized, and rated the MP's competence, pawn-likeness and cooperativeness on 1-10 scales. 914 respondents.
Reference: Barnett, C., Blackman, A., & Shalaby, M. (2025). Competent legislators or mere pawns? Experimental evidence of attitudes toward gender quota politicians. Political Science Research and Methods, 13(4).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/barnett_2025_quota.R. Factorial vignette, one vignette per respondent; politician arm 25/25/50 (no quota-man arm). Levels stored as the article's English vignette text; interview language undocumented. 13 of 927 respondents with no rating dropped. Paper's quota-vs-non-quota-woman pawn difference (0.35) and collaboration difference (0.377) reproduce.

Description: Czech adults (online quota panel, 2019) rated two hypothetical strangers on a 0-100 feeling thermometer and chose which one they would prefer to talk to, 5 pairs each; profiles varied gender, education, values, party, immigration attitude and how often they talk about politics. 1,032 respondents.
Reference: Hrbková, L., Voda, P., & Havlík, V. (2024). Politically motivated interpersonal biases: Polarizing effects of partisanship and immigration attitudes. Party Politics, 30(3), 450-464.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hrbkova_2024.R. Conjoint only (trust-game files not used). Attribute and covariate text in Czech as stored; English level translations in the article's Table 1. Tasks with unsaved attributes (321) or no outcome (14) dropped; N matches the paper (1,032; 10,250 rows). Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed. Paper's +0.18/-0.18 party-match effects reproduce.

Description: Members of Austrian party executives (2021 web survey) saw nine hypothetical aspirant profiles, deselected three, then ranked the remaining six to list positions 1-6 (two-stage conjoint, one task). 324 respondents.
Reference: Jankowski, M., & Rehmert, J. (2024). Selecting and ranking female candidates under PR: Evidence from a two-stage conjoint experiment with party elites. European Journal of Political Research.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/jankowski_2024.R. One task of nine profiles; rating_deselected (3 of 9 ticked) and rating_list_position (1-6, NA if deselected). German level text; one of two dual-candidacy attributes shown per respondent, the other '(not shown)'. Attribute row order recorded (attrpos_). Qualtrics IDs, dates, free text and party-entry/office years dropped; birth year coarsened to decade (cov_birth_decade; small named elite population).

Description: Study 1: a national PureSpectrum sample of Japanese citizens (n=1,002, May 2023) chose which of two hypothetical job applicants should be hired, in two sets of 8 pairs (private-company R&D post and public elementary-school teacher), applicants varying in name (Japanese, Zainichi Korean with Japanese pseudonym, or Korean name; also signals gender), university, experience and screening result.
Reference: Zhou, K., & Horiuchi, Y. (2026). Disclosing invisible attributes leads to discrimination. Journal of Race, Ethnicity, and Politics, 1-26.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/zhou_2026.R. Both job sets show the same 7 pairs (trial_pair); set order randomized and not recorded, so tasks 1-8 (private) and 9-16 (public) give order within set only; tasks 8 and 16 repeat tasks 1 and 9. Attribute text in Japanese.

Description: Study 2: a Kansai-region PureSpectrum sample of Japanese citizens (n=1,001, February 2024) chose which of two hypothetical job applicants should be hired, in two sets of 8 pairs (private-company R&D post and public elementary-school teacher), applicants varying in name (Japanese, Zainichi Korean with Japanese pseudonym, or Korean name; also signals gender), university, experience and screening result.
Reference: Zhou, K., & Horiuchi, Y. (2026). Disclosing invisible attributes leads to discrimination. Journal of Race, Ethnicity, and Politics, 1-26.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/zhou_2026.R. Both job sets show the same 7 pairs (trial_pair); set order randomized and not recorded, so tasks 1-8 (private) and 9-16 (public) give order within set only; tasks 8 and 16 repeat tasks 1 and 9. Attribute text in Japanese.

Description: US Lucid respondents (n=1,008, October 2022) each rated 5 hypothetical AI-enabled technologies varying in domain (cars, armed drones, surgery, content moderation, police surveillance), autonomy, precision and regulator, on 1-5 scales of support for and trust in the use of AI.
Reference: Kreps, S., George, J., Lushenko, P., & Rao, A. (2023). Exploring the artificial intelligence "Trust paradox": Evidence from a survey experiment in the United States. PLOS ONE, 18(7), e0288109.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/kreps_2023.R. Single-profile conjoint, 5 tasks per respondent (article says four). Qualtrics/Lucid IDs, ZIP and state dropped; second (mediation) experiment not included.

Description: German state-parliament MPs (n=258) each read one coalition-negotiation vignette from a 2x2 factorial design (pressure to reach a decision high/low x election campaign imminent/far away) and rated, on 1-5 scales, how likely they were to publicize the negotiation through various channels, to keep it confidential, and to compromise; realism and manipulation-check ratings are included.
Reference: Philipps, G. (2024). Compromise-building in the spotlight of the media? Individual and situational influences on the self-mediatization of parliamentary negotiations. The International Journal of Press/Politics, 29(2), 570-590.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/philipps_2022.R. Factorial vignette, one vignette per respondent (task=1, profile=1); id = row number (no id in source). Level text is the codebook's English description of the 4 vignette variants; vignette prose not deposited.

Description: Vietnamese adults in the 2016 PAPI national face-to-face survey (n=12,893) chose which of two hypothetical National Assembly candidates they would vote for; candidates varied in age, gender, home province (respondent's own or Hanoi), nomination route, Communist Party membership, career and policy priority.
Reference: Malesky, E., & Schuler, P. (2020). Single-party incumbency advantage in Vietnam: A conjoint survey analysis of public electoral support. Journal of East Asian Studies, 20(1), 25-52.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/malesky_2020.R. 2016 wave only (2017/2018 held: unlabelled codes, misaligned labels, arms). One pair per respondent; profile from the authors' form variable; 1,147 don't know/refused omitted. cov_survey_weight = PSW_psweight (authors also post-stratify by province population).

Description: US online quota sample (Respondi, Sept/Oct 2016; n=2,721) compared up to 4 pairs of policy proposals described only by their income effects (-$5,000 to +$5,000) on the US average, the respondent's own income, their sector's average, and people earning about $10,000, $85,000 and $375,000 a year; they chose one and rated each 1-10 for referendum vote.
Reference: Bechtel, M. M., & Liesch, R. (2020). Reforms and redistribution: Disentangling the egoistic and sociotropic origins of voter preferences. Public Opinion Quarterly, 84(1), 1-23.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/bechtel_2020.R. Main study; 1-4 tasks per respondent (18,906 rated policies as in the article). cov_survey_weight = entropy-balancing weight used in all paper estimates. Pilot and validation studies are separate tables.

Description: US MTurk sample (May/June 2016; n=307) compared up to 4 pairs of policy proposals described by their income effects in percent (-5% to +5%) on the US average, own income, own sector, and people earning about $10,000, $85,000 and $375,000 a year, and chose one.
Reference: Bechtel, M. M., & Liesch, R. (2020). Reforms and redistribution: Disentangling the egoistic and sociotropic origins of voter preferences. Public Opinion Quarterly, 84(1), 1-23.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/bechtel_2020.R. Pilot (supplement C, Figure A.6). Task and profile inferred from row order (one chosen per consecutive pair verified). Choice only; no covariates deposited.

Description: US MTurk sample (n=2,003, of 2,300 fielded) compared up to 15 pairs of proposals described by their income effects (-$5,000 to +$5,000) on five income bands (under $18,000 to over $100,000), framed (randomly, per respondent) as generic, health care or trade policies or candidates' platforms, and chose one.
Reference: Bechtel, M. M., & Liesch, R. (2020). Reforms and redistribution: Disentangling the egoistic and sociotropic origins of voter preferences. Public Opinion Quarterly, 84(1), 1-23.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/bechtel_2020.R. Validation study (article Figure 6, supplement E). trial_version = framing arm. Profile inferred from row order within task. Choice only; no covariates deposited.

Description: Japanese adults (Rakuten Insight online panel, July 2022; n = 1,834 answering) made 10 forced choices between two hypothetical political parties varying on 11 valence attributes (ministers, MPs, bills, scandals, leader tenure and personality, ...) and 3 policy positions, 5 tasks for the district vote and 5 for the proportional-representation vote.
Reference: Hamzawi, Kato, & Endo (2025). What brings you to the party? Voter preferences on parties through policy and valence dynamics. Party Politics.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/hamzawi_2025.R. Attribute text is the authors' English labels (respondents saw Japanese). Context block order (district vs PR) was randomized but not recorded: tasks 1-5 are always the district block, so task is not the display order across blocks. Randomization restricted (Table 1 note). 524 skipped tasks omitted. Qualtrics ResponseId dropped.

Description: South Korean respondents (n = 1,687, during the COVID-19 pandemic) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical immigrants varying on 8 attributes (origin regime, trade, residence, home-country COVID-19 cases, vaccination, Korean ability, education, occupation) and judged for each whether entry should be allowed, allowed with a 14-day quarantine, or banned.
Reference: Kim, S. E., Shin, A. J., & Yang, Y. (2022). The usual suspects?: Attitudes towards immigration during the COVID-19 pandemic. Journal of Asian Public Policy, 17(2), 272-289.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/kim_2022.R. Profile position not recorded (profile = arbitrary file order within task). Attribute text is the authors' English labels (respondents saw Korean), typos kept. rating_entry recoded from Korean answer text to 1 ban / 2 quarantine / 3 allow. No codebook; article not consulted (paywalled). Qualtrics ResponseId re-keyed.

Description: Adults in Spain (bilendi online panel, 2022; n = 2,999) chose between and rated (1-7) 5 pairs of hypothetical trade agreements varying in yearly gains or losses (euro) for themselves, the average citizen and the average citizen of the partner country, plus partner size, current trade volume and implementation year.
Reference: Dür, A., Hee, S., & Huber, R. A. (2025). A fair deal: Inequity aversion and individual attitudes toward trade agreements. The Review of International Organizations.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/dur_2025.R (Study 1, Spain sample; the authors pool Spain and Poland with a country control, split here because the displayed text differs). Attribute text is an English rendering of the article's Table 1 example; respondents saw Spanish. No agreement had losses on all three payoffs. Respondent ids re-keyed.

Description: Adults in Poland (bilendi online panel, 2022; n = 2,999) chose between and rated (1-7) 5 pairs of hypothetical trade agreements varying in yearly gains or losses (zloty (5 x the euro value)) for themselves, the average citizen and the average citizen of the partner country, plus partner size, current trade volume and implementation year.
Reference: Dür, A., Hee, S., & Huber, R. A. (2025). A fair deal: Inequity aversion and individual attitudes toward trade agreements. The Review of International Organizations.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/dur_2025.R (Study 1, Poland sample; the authors pool Spain and Poland with a country control, split here because the displayed text differs). Attribute text is an English rendering of the article's Table 1 example; respondents saw Polish. No agreement had losses on all three payoffs. Respondent ids re-keyed.

Description: British adults (bilendi online panel, 2023; n = 2,128) chose between and rated (1-7) 5 pairs of hypothetical trade agreements varying in personal gains (small/medium/large), the average citizen's gains relative to the respondent, partner size, current trade volume and implementation year.
Reference: Dür, A., Hee, S., & Huber, R. A. (2025). A fair deal: Inequity aversion and individual attitudes toward trade agreements. The Review of International Organizations.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/dur_2025.R (Study 2). Level text as in the article's Table 3. Choice and rating coefficients of the article's Table 4 reproduce exactly. The deposit's list experiment (GB_exp1.rds) is not included.

Description: Adults aged 14+ in Austria and Italy (Marketagent online panel, July-August 2022; n = 6,357) compared 2 pairs of hypothetical autumn COVID-19 vaccination calls (virus variant, available vaccines, Omicron-adapted vaccine, incentive, and a testimonial's motivation, gender and age group), chose the more appealing one and rated the likelihood of getting vaccinated 0-10.
Reference: Stamm, T. A., Partheymüller, J., Mosor, E., Ritschl, V., Kritzinger, S., Alunno, A., & Eberl, J.-M. (2023). Determinants of COVID-19 vaccine fatigue. Nature Medicine, 29, 1164-1171.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/stamm_2023.R (experiment 1). Text vignettes; level text is the English version of Supplementary Table S3.1 (respondents saw German or Italian). The testimonial's first name and age were not saved: attr_testimonial_gender and attr_testimonial_age hold the design condition, not displayed text.

Description: Adults aged 14+ in Austria and Italy (Marketagent online panel, July-August 2022; n = 6,357) compared 2 pairs of fictional media reports on COVID-19 vaccination (expert consensus or false balance, celebrity news, Long Covid incidence, vaccination certificate rules, vaccine mandate), chose the one that made them trust vaccination more and rated the likelihood of getting vaccinated 0-10.
Reference: Stamm, T. A., Partheymüller, J., Mosor, E., Ritschl, V., Kritzinger, S., Alunno, A., & Eberl, J.-M. (2023). Determinants of COVID-19 vaccine fatigue. Nature Medicine, 29, 1164-1171.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/stamm_2023.R (experiment 2). Text vignettes; level text is the English version of Supplementary Table S4.1 (respondents saw German or Italian). Article AMCEs for the triple vaccinated reproduce.

Description: US citizens (Qualtrics panel, 2018; n = 980) chose between 6 pairs of hypothetical persons varying in citizenship, country of birth, education, gender, income-tax payment and residence, and rated each 1-7 on extending voting rights to them.
Reference: Hultin Rosenberg, J., & Wejryd, J. (2022). Attitudes toward competing voting-right requirements: Evidence from a conjoint experiment. Electoral Studies, 77, 102470.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/hultinrosenberg_2022.R. Level text from the authors' Stata value labels; question wording not deposited (article not consulted). 19 non-'good completers' dropped as in the authors' analysis. Unanswered choices kept as NA alongside ratings. Qualtrics ResponseId and free-text comments dropped.

Description: Adults in Chile (probability sample interviewed face to face, May-June 2019; 1,542 of 1,800 answering) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical presidential candidates varying in coalition, gender, age, positions on same-sex marriage and free university, and the emotions the candidate expresses about the country's past (pride/anger) and future (fear/optimism).
Reference: Segovia, C. (2021). Decidiendo por quién votar. Evidencia experimental del efecto de las emociones en el voto. Colombia Internacional, 107, 3-28.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/segovia_2020.R. The deposit ('Hoping for a better future') names no paper; the same experiment is Experimento 2 of Segovia (2021). Level text is the deposit's Spanish value labels (four truncated labels completed); the article words some levels differently. 2,245 tasks without a recorded choice omitted. Appendix Table A1 reproduces exactly with cov_survey_weight.

Description: UK farm veterinarians (n = 306, postal survey, March 2018) each rated 8 text vignettes in which a sheep or beef farmer asks for antibiotics without a farm visit, with 7 randomized factors (case type, farmer's habit, client relationship, colleagues' past prescribing, willingness to pay for a visit, time pressure, confidence in the farmer); outcomes are the likelihood the vet would prescribe and the share of vets who would.
Reference: Doidge, C., Hudson, C., Lovatt, F., & Kaler, J. (2019). To prescribe or not to prescribe? A factorial survey to explore veterinarians' decision making when prescribing antimicrobials to sheep and beef farmers in the UK. PLOS ONE, 14(4), e0213855.
Notes: data/conjoint/doidge_2019.R. Factorial vignette survey (presentation text, one vignette per task). attr_ text is each varying clause as printed in the article's S1 example survey, mapped from the deposit's short codes. rating stored 1-11 (= -5..+5); rating_others 1-10 (grouped percentages). Covariates are the authors' groupings.

Description: Swiss residents (German-language online survey; 2,499 respondents) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical persons varying occupation, education, income, place of residence, gender, sexuality, migration background and age: which person stands higher in Swiss society (choice, n = 2,382) and each person's place on a 1-10 status ladder (rating, n = 2,436).
Reference: Breyer, M. (2025). Perceptions of the social status hierarchy and its cultural and economic sources. European Journal of Political Research, 64(2), 810-833.
Notes: data/conjoint/breyer_2025.R. Choice and rating ship as separate files with different respondent numbering; joined by each respondent's unique 10-profile signature (2,319 matched; 63 choice-only, 117 rating-only respondents). Attribute text is the authors' English labels (survey in German). Occupation-education combinations restricted (observed). Covariates are the authors' respondent groupings only.

Description: US MTurk workers (n = 1,228, December 2019) chose one of three T-shirts in each of 5 tasks, varying country of manufacture (9 Asian countries), material, quality and price; covariates include their threat, hostility and labor-condition ratings of each country.
Reference: DiGiuseppe, M., & Barry, C. M. (2022). Do consumers follow the flag? Perceptions of hostility and consumer preferences. International Interactions, 48(6), 1200-1215.
Notes: data/conjoint/digiuseppe_2022.R. No codebook or questionnaire: question wording unknown; forced choice inferred from the data. Price levels stored as the value labels 5/10/15/20 (dollar display format unknown). MTurk worker/assignment/HIT IDs and ZIP codes dropped.

Description: Indian adults (n = 998, December 2019) chose one of three televisions in each of 5 tasks, varying country of manufacture (10 countries), resolution, customer reviews, brand and price; covariates include their hostility and labor-condition ratings of each country.
Reference: DiGiuseppe, M., & Barry, C. M. (2022). Do consumers follow the flag? Perceptions of hostility and consumer preferences. International Interactions, 48(6), 1200-1215.
Notes: data/conjoint/digiuseppe_2022.R. No codebook or questionnaire: question wording, survey firm and display language unknown; forced choice inferred from the data. Price stored as value-label text with Indian digit grouping (currency display unknown). Free-text city/occupation and the worker-ID column dropped; birth year as recorded (some implausible).

Description: Japanese adults (n = 1,800; urban and rural samples) compared 4 pairs of hypothetical plans to build a high-level radioactive waste disposal site in their municipality, varying distance, stated purpose, local opinion split, benefit offered, population and average income; each pair got a forced choice and a 1-7 acceptance rating per plan.
Reference: Hayashi, R., Asano, T., Morikawa, S., & Komatsuzaki, S. (2024). Public service motivation and not-in-my-backyard: The case of high-level radioactive waste disposal sites in Japan. International Public Management Journal, 27(6), 948-971.
Notes: data/conjoint/hayashi_2024.R. Survey in Japanese; attribute and question text are the deposit codebook's English translation. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_*). One recorded age of 3 set to NA; 13 respondents aged 14-17 kept. Municipality dropped. cov_sc undocumented codes.

Description: Danish adults (Epinion omnibus, n = 1,034, Oct-Nov 2024) chose between two fictitious candidates for their own party in 8 tasks, varying gender, age, country of origin, education and political experience; half first read the intelligence service's assessment that the terrorist threat is significant (trial_terror_threat).
Reference: Littmann, B., Nielsen, N. N. J., & Laustsen, L. (2026). Terrorist threat decreases citizens' relative preferences for women candidates: Insights from a Danish conjoint experiment. European Journal of Political Research.
Notes: data/conjoint/littmann_2026.R. Danish attribute text as displayed. Origin and education levels deliberately weighted (article; Danmark ~79%). Between-respondent terror-threat treatment in trial_terror_threat. Choice wording is the article's English.

Description: Internet-panel respondents in China, Germany and the USA (n = 4,876, February 2018) compared 4 pairs of passenger-transport policy packages varying a fuel tax, use of its revenues, downtown car restrictions, public-transport support, fuel-efficiency requirements, information campaigns and car-industry subsidies; forced choice plus a 1-7 support rating per package.
Reference: Wicki, M., Fesenfeld, L., & Bernauer, T. (2019). In search of politically feasible policy-packages for sustainable passenger transport: Insights from choice experiments in China, Germany, and the USA. Environmental Research Letters, 14(8), 084048.
Notes: data/conjoint/wicki_2019.R. Countries pooled with cov_country (authors pool). Attribute text is the authors' English labels; the fuel-efficiency attribute is stored in miles per gallon for all countries although German and Chinese respondents most likely saw l/100 km. Choice wording not published.

Description: US Prolific respondents (n = 700, fielded 2024-08-15) chose between two news stories in each of 6 tasks in the engagement conjoint, with randomized headline (authors' short label), news outlet, editor's note (displayed text) and photo (authors' description). One forced choice per task.
Reference: Darr, J. P., & Robinson, S. (2026). Assessing civic journalism training: A mixed-method applied research study. Political Communication.
Notes: data/conjoint/darr_2026.R. One of four separate conjoints in the deposit (one table each). Headline is the authors' short label, not the displayed wording. Photo levels are the authors' descriptions of photographs. Question wording not in the deposit (article paywalled). Prolific IDs, ResponseId and GPS coordinates dropped; IDs re-keyed per table.

Description: US Prolific respondents (n = 701, fielded 2024-08-12) chose between two news stories in each of 6 tasks in the good conflict conjoint, with randomized headline and note (the authors' value labels, e.g. 'Good: Eye to Eye'), news outlet and photo (authors' description). One forced choice per task.
Reference: Darr, J. P., & Robinson, S. (2026). Assessing civic journalism training: A mixed-method applied research study. Political Communication.
Notes: data/conjoint/darr_2026.R. One of four separate conjoints in the deposit (one table each). Headline and note are the authors' value labels (headline stored as codes GC1/GC2/GC bad 1/GC bad 2), not the displayed wording. Photo levels are the authors' descriptions of photographs. Question wording not in the deposit (article paywalled). Prolific IDs, ResponseId and GPS coordinates dropped; IDs re-keyed per table.

Description: US Prolific respondents (n = 702, fielded 2024-08-09) chose between two news stories in each of 6 tasks in the solutions journalism conjoint, with randomized headline and editor's note (displayed text; the respondent's state piped into the headline is stored as [your state]), news outlet and photo (authors' description). One forced choice per task.
Reference: Darr, J. P., & Robinson, S. (2026). Assessing civic journalism training: A mixed-method applied research study. Political Communication.
Notes: data/conjoint/darr_2026.R. One of four separate conjoints in the deposit (one table each). The respondent's state piped into the headline is stored as [your state]. Photo levels are the authors' descriptions of photographs. Question wording not in the deposit (article paywalled). Prolific IDs, ResponseId and GPS coordinates dropped; IDs re-keyed per table.

Description: US Prolific respondents (n = 607, fielded 2025-01-30) chose between two news stories in each of 8 tasks in the transparency conjoint, with randomized headline, note and pledge (authors' short labels), news outlet and photo (authors' description). One forced choice per task.
Reference: Darr, J. P., & Robinson, S. (2026). Assessing civic journalism training: A mixed-method applied research study. Political Communication.
Notes: data/conjoint/darr_2026.R. One of four separate conjoints in the deposit (one table each). Headline, note and pledge are the authors' short labels, not the displayed wording; 39 tasks of 7 respondents who left early are dropped. Photo levels are the authors' descriptions of photographs. Question wording not in the deposit (article paywalled). Prolific IDs, ResponseId and GPS coordinates dropped; IDs re-keyed per table.

Description: Jewish-Israeli adults in the July 2020 wave of an online panel (n = 1,586) chose between two Israeli COVID-19 policies toward the Palestinians in each of 5 tasks, with randomized policy type, effect on Palestinian illness, cross-infections, funding source and coordination (with the PA / Hamas).
Reference: Harsgor, L., & Yakter, A. (2024). Public preferences for intergroup assistance in conflicts facing joint external threats: Lessons from COVID-19 in Israel. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 68(7-8), 1522-1551.
Notes: data/conjoint/harsgor_2023.R. Levels are the authors' English labels (respondents likely saw Hebrew; displayed wording not in the deposit). Observed restriction: Medical Aid never with Deterioration, Monitor never with Improvement. 334 unanswered tasks dropped. Covariate labels taken from the panel survey .dta. Question wording not in the deposit.

Description: Dutch respondents (n = 1,309) compared 3 pairs of e-bike policy packages varying in registration/licence, road placement, enforcement, purchase support and helmet rules, and for each pair picked the preferred standard, the one more likely to increase e-bike use, the more restrictive one and the one needing more government intervention.
Reference: Pickering, S. (2026). Replication data for: Public opinion towards e-bike policy packages: A conjoint experiment in the Netherlands [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: data/conjoint/pickering_2026.R. Four forced-choice outcomes on the same pairs (authors' labels; question wording not in the deposit). Levels stored in English; display language not documented. Survey weight kept (authors analyse unweighted). No article found; the deposit is cited.

Description: Moroccan adults recruited on Facebook in 2021 (n = 2,008) compared 4 pairs of bank-account or TV deals whose owner (businessman, councillor, party official), headquarters, cost, party and vote-buying behaviour were randomized; they chose a deal (or both/neither), picked the deal more likely to go wrong, and rated trust in each deal 0-10.
Reference: Bhandari, A., & York, E. (2026). Political connections, patronage, and consumer attitudes: The non-electoral consequences of clientelism. World Development.
Notes: data/conjoint/bhandari_2026.R. Both/Neither answers coded 0 on both profiles (raw answer in trial_choice_response / trial_wrong_response; authors code Both as chosen). Levels are the authors' English labels. Party level stored for Businessman profiles though the codebook calls it vacuous there; display not documented. Product (bank rounds 1-2, TV rounds 3-4) in trial_product. Authors' AMCE table reproduces exactly (N = 13,420).

Description: Adult residents of the canton of Zurich sampled by the cantonal Statistical Office (n = 1,021, online, 2020) compared 4 pairs of battery-electric cars with randomized price, range, running and maintenance costs, charging time and guarantee, battery warranty, purchase subsidy and car/rail-pass exchange offers; they chose one car and said whether they would buy each.
Reference: Bernauer, T., Brückmann, G., Quoß, F., & Wicki, M. (2022). Registered design for survey experiment: Decision behaviour when purchasing electric vehicles [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: data/conjoint/bernauer_2022.R. German level text as stored. Forced choice plus a yes/no buy rating per car. trial_group = the source's two versions of the conjoint block (Conjoint Pos/Neg), difference undocumented. Attribute row order possibly randomized, not deposited. No article; the deposit is cited.

Description: Flemish voters of Vooruit, Groen, Open VLD and Vlaams Belang (n = 2,119) chose between two party manifestos in 10 tasks (5 social democratic, 5 liberal), each stating randomized positions on the welfare state, inheritance taxes, immigration and nature conservation.
Reference: Luypaert, J. (2024). Replication data for: Balancing an ideological trade-off: Electoral appeal of consistent and responsive party positions [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: data/conjoint/luypaert_2024.R. Social democratic (tasks 1-5) and liberal (tasks 6-10) manifestos in one table, trial_manifesto. Dutch level text; attribute order per respondent in attrpos_. The manifesto rating in the deposit's 'ranked' files is left out (scale and direction undocumented). N 2,119 vs 2,082 in the deposit description. Article not found; deposit cited.

Description: German survey respondents (IFES 2023; n = 1,882) chose between two hypothetical people in 6 tasks of a job-training conjoint, profiles varying in age, family, gender, occupation, criminal record and origin (Saxony, DE / Hamburg, DE / Bavaria, DE / Bucharest, RO). Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Brehm, N., Zhou, A. H., & Denney, S. (2025). From division to democracy: Integrating post-socialist citizens in Germany and South Korea. Communist and Post-Communist Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/brehm_2025_job_training.R. Attribute text is the authors' English translation (respondents saw German); Age levels were 'standardized' by the authors to 25/35/46/62. Question wording not deposited. Covariates are raw answer text in the survey language; cov_female 1 = female, 0 = any other answer. The authors' main analysis restricts to Western, ethnic Germans (derivable from cov_state_at_18 and cov_ethnicity); all 1,882 are kept. 245 respondents lack party vote and the Q60-Q63 items.

Description: South Korean survey respondents (IFES 2023; n = 1,768) chose between two hypothetical people in 7 tasks of a job-training conjoint, profiles varying in age, family, gender, occupation, criminal record and origin (North Hamgyong, DPRK / Busan, ROK / Gyeonggi, ROK / Hanoi, Vietnam). Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Brehm, N., Zhou, A. H., & Denney, S. (2025). From division to democracy: Integrating post-socialist citizens in Germany and South Korea. Communist and Post-Communist Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/brehm_2025_job_training.R. Attribute text is the authors' English translation (respondents saw Korean); Age levels were 'standardized' by the authors to 25/35/46/62. Question wording not deposited. Covariates are raw answer text in the survey language; cov_female 1 = female, 0 = any other answer.

Description: Albanian-speaking adults in Kosovo (face-to-face, n = 2,405) each heard 2 dispute vignettes (one civil: inheritance or debt; one criminal: domestic violence or murder) in which the character's wealth, expected speed of the state courts and whether everybody or nobody around them used the state were randomized, then said how the character tried to resolve it and how people should resolve it (state, religious cleric or Kanun mediation).
Reference: Krakowski, K., & Kursani, S. (2023). Why do people use informal justice? Experimental evidence from Kosovo. Journal of Experimental Political Science.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/krakowski_2023.R. Factor levels parsed from the stored Albanian vignette text with the authors' keywords and stored as the questionnaire's English wording; full displayed Albanian text in trial_vignette_text; clause order in attrpos_*. Each 3-option outcome is split into 0/1 indicators (rating_tried_*, rating_should_*). Survey weight kept. Lat/long in the deposit dropped.

Description: Albanian-speaking adults in Kosovo (face-to-face, n = 2,405) each heard 3 vignettes about a young man's political violence (going to fight in Syria, a riot against Serbs in Mitrovica, a violent protest in Prishtina) in which his job situation, attachment to the community and who encouraged him were randomized, and rated how expected his decision was (1 completely expected .. 5 completely unexpected).
Reference: Krakowski, K., & Kursani, S. (2023). Why do people use informal justice? Experimental evidence from Kosovo. Journal of Experimental Political Science.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/krakowski_2023.R. Second experiment of the survey, not analysed in the article. Levels parsed from the stored Albanian text and stored as the questionnaire's English wording (job wording is event-specific); full text in trial_vignette_text; clause order in attrpos_*. Rating stored raw: higher = more unexpected. Survey weight kept.

Description: US YouGov respondents (n = 2,654) made 5 forced choices between two hypothetical people described by up to 10 attributes (race, sex, age, party, ideology, where they grew up, religion, career, marital status, sexual orientation; each attribute omitted from a profile about 15% of the time), in one of five randomly assigned contexts (relative, neighbor, loan, charity, jury).
Reference: Theodoridis, A. G., Goggin, S. N., & Deichert, M. (2023). Separated by politics? Disentangling the dimensions of discrimination. Political Behavior, 45(4), 2025-2051.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/theodoridis_2023.R. Level text from the authors' factor() labels in replication.R; the authors' 'Not Asked' levels are coded (not shown) (assumed omitted from the display; not documented). Context arm in trial_context; question wording per context not deposited. Respondent covariates keep YouGov codes (_code suffix; no codebook). Author order follows Crossref; the replication script lists Deichert, Goggin, Theodoridis.

Description: White non-Hispanic US online panel respondents (Bovitz/Forthright, n = 450) each read 6 one-sentence newspaper excerpts in which a speaker insulted, threatened or slurred a target at a town hall meeting; headline, both people's party, job and name (names signal race and gender) and the uncivil phrase were randomized. Ratings: how uncivil and how newsworthy (1-5).
Reference: Gubitz, S. R. (2022). Race, gender, and the politics of incivility: How identity moderates perceptions of uncivil discourse. The Journal of Race, Ethnicity, and Politics, 7(3), 526-543.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/gubitz_2022.R. Level text is the displayed embedded-data text from the author's reshaped file; the author's race/gender coding of the names is in trial_speaker_*/trial_target_*; trial_fellow_partisan marks the 'a fellow Democrat/Republican' wording. PANAS emotion items dropped (column-to-emotion mapping undocumented). IP addresses, lat/long and ResponseIds in all deposited data files dropped.

Description: Argentine online panel respondents (IPSOS; n = 2,424, 2,267 after the authors' speed rule) chose between two hypothetical critical-mineral mining projects in 4 tasks and rated each 1-5 stars; projects varied in local community (agricultural/indigenous), owner (YPF/Chinese/North American), new jobs, importance for green technologies, damage to water and soil, and government tax incentives.
Reference: Brooks, S. M., Lacroix Eussler, S., & Voeten, E. (2026). Environmental, economic, and geopolitical trade-offs in critical mineral mining projects: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in Argentina. The Extractive Industries and Society, 27, 101925.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/brooks_2026.R. Spanish displayed level text from the Qualtrics text export; attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). The authors drop respondents faster than 200 seconds; they are kept here (cov_duration_sec). 77 star ratings are 0 (outside 1-5), kept. Duplicate panel uids: first record kept. IP addresses, lat/long, ResponseIds and panel uids in the deposit dropped.

Description: Chinese respondents chose between two hypothetical volunteer projects in each of 6 paired tasks, with 8 randomized attributes (schedule, training, compensation, contact with beneficiaries, Communist Party branch, objective, disclosure, slogan). 658 respondents; one forced choice per task.
Reference: Zhang, R. (2024). Volunteer participation preferences [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/zhang_2024.R. No article linked or found; no codebook or questionnaire: question wording unknown, attribute levels are the author's English Stata value labels (survey fielded in Chinese). Covariate codes undocumented, kept as codes (_code suffix); platform respondent token dropped, re-keyed by the source's sequential id2.

Description: Economically active Colombian adults (Netquest online panel, quota 50/50 formal/informal workers) read one vignette about a Venezuelan migrant whose name/sex, previous occupation, degree recognition (engineers and doctors only) and salary expectations were randomized, then rated immigrants like them on five questions (presence, right to stay, effect on own job chances and salary, likelihood of competing). 1,203 respondents.
Reference: Carreras, M. (2026). Informality and attitudes towards immigrants in Latin America [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse. Replication package for Argote, P., & Carreras, M., Informality and attitudes towards immigrants in Latin America (manuscript).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/argote_2026.R. One text vignette per respondent (task = profile = 1). Attribute text = Spanish questionnaire dimension text (gendered forms written ingeniero/a, Él/ella as in the list). Degree recognition shown only for engineer/doctor, else (not shown). Outcome codes stored raw: on D1, D2, D5 a LOWER code is the more favourable/likely answer. No article DOI found (EPSA 2025 paper). Netquest panelist code, UUID key, timestamps, municipality and a free-text item dropped.

Description: Canadian online-panel respondents (April 2025, English or French) compared two hypothetical federal election outcomes in each of 6 paired tasks, varying number of parties, the winning party's votes and seats, turnout, women's and visible minorities' representation and ballot type; they chose the better outcome for Canada and rated each 0-10. 2,487 respondents.
Reference: Sevi, S., Blais, A., & Mekik, C. (2026). What do voters want out of elections? Electoral Studies, 102, 103091.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/sevi_2026.R. Attribute text as displayed: English or French by respondent (cov_language), so each level has two spellings. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_*). All 2,487 conjoint completers kept; the authors analyse 2,015 good cases (citizens, 240-1,200 s), reproducible from cov_citizenship and cov_duration_sec. IP address, GPS coordinates, Qualtrics ResponseId and panel PID dropped.

Description: German online respondents each listened to one audio recording of a fictional public service encounter in which the employee's administrative language (control, informational, relational, or both) and the service decision (negative or positive) were randomized, then rated satisfaction, comprehensibility, reification, emotionality and complaisance on 10-point scales. 1,402 respondents.
Reference: Eckhard, S., & Friedrich, L. (2022). Linguistic features of public service encounters: How spoken administrative language affects citizen satisfaction. Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory, 34(1), 122-135.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/eckhard_2022.R. Between-subjects 4 x 2 audio vignette (task = profile = 1). Level text = the codebook's English condition names; the German audio script is not deposited. trial_listened_complete flags respondents who did not listen to the whole recording (124). Free-text answers dropped.

Description: Online respondents in Belgium (2021) compared two proposals for a new law requiring companies to disclose environmental and working conditions in their international supply chains, in 5 paired tasks varying which companies the law covers, reporting strictness and government enforcement; they chose one and said whether they favoured each. 2,000 respondents; part of a 12-country study.
Reference: Kolcava, D., Smith, E. K., & Bernauer, T. (2022). Cross-national public acceptance of sustainable global supply chain policy instruments. Nature Sustainability, 6(1), 69-80.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kolcava_2022.R (one script, 12 country tables). Level text as stored in the raw .dta (bold tags removed); the .tab ingest mangled dashes, so the original .dta is read. Level text is in the respondent's survey language (EN 246, BE 797, FR 957 respondents by Qualtrics language), so each level has several spellings. Covariates are only the deposited attitude items (no demographics). rating = favour (1) / oppose (0) each proposal.

Description: Respondents in the US (January-February 2020) chose which of two hypothetical military operations against a state that had invaded an ally they would approve, in 6 forced-choice pairs varying the operation's objective, its backers, the target's regime, religion and military strength, and the mode of operation. 1,490 US MTurk workers (via Qualtrics).
Reference: Kiratli, O. S. (2024). Policy objective of military intervention and public attitudes: A conjoint experiment from US and Turkey. Political Behavior, 46(2), 1257-1279.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kiratli_2024.R (one table per country, as the author analyses them). Level text from the article's Table 1 and Fig. 1; the source stores abbreviations (IPC/FPR/Peace/HI). The objective level stores the clause after the common 'Country A/B has deployed troops ...' prefix. Education kept as codes (cov_education_code): the value labels conflict with the appendix.

Description: Respondents in Turkey (January-February 2020) chose which of two hypothetical military operations against a state that had invaded an ally they would approve, in 6 forced-choice pairs varying the operation's objective, its backers, the target's regime, religion and military strength, and the mode of operation. 1,002 Turkish Cint panelists.
Reference: Kiratli, O. S. (2024). Policy objective of military intervention and public attitudes: A conjoint experiment from US and Turkey. Political Behavior, 46(2), 1257-1279.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kiratli_2024.R (one table per country, as the author analyses them). Level text from the article's Table 1 and Fig. 1; the source stores abbreviations (IPC/FPR/Peace/HI). The Turkish sample saw Turkish text; levels are stored in English (Table 1), with the backer levels as 'Government ...' as on the Turkish screen (appendix A-I). The objective level stores the clause after the common 'Country A/B has deployed troops ...' prefix. Education kept as codes (cov_education_code): the value labels conflict with the appendix.

Description: US Lucid respondents (June 2020) each read one short news article about a hypothetical COVID-19 contact-tracing app whose developer, name, technology, required uptake, data storage and expiry were randomized, then rated how likely they were to download it and report a positive test, its likely consequences, data-protection confidence and five statements about requiring it. 2,035 respondents.
Reference: Zhang, B., Kreps, S., McMurry, N., & McCain, R. M. (2020). Americans' perceptions of privacy and surveillance in the COVID-19 pandemic. PLOS ONE, 15(12), e0242652.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/zhang_2020.R. Single-profile text vignette (one article per respondent); levels are the slot text checked against each respondent's saved article HTML. The third technology level is Bluetooth plus a BBC illustration. Refusals (-99) and Don't know (-88) -> NA; the authors' mean imputation is not applied. Download/report asked of smartphone owners only. Authors' raking weight not deposited as a variable.

Description: German online-panel respondents (bilendi, March 2024) chose between and rated two proposals for spending wealth-tax revenue on climate policy, in 5 pairs varying compensation payments, public investment, subsidies for companies and subsidies for households. 4,653 respondents; choice and a 1-5 rating per proposal.
Reference: Ahrens, L., Bremer, B., & Hakelberg, L. (2026). Taxing uber-polluters: Carbon inequality and support for wealth taxation to finance the green transition. Climate Policy.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ahrens_2026.R. Dataverse lists CC0 1.0 but the package README licenses the data CC BY 4.0; the stricter label is carried. Levels are the German text from the deposited design file. Rating stored raw: 1 = very strongly in favour .. 5 = very strongly against (lower = more favourable). 4,393 of 23,265 tasks have ratings but no choice. Attribute order randomized per respondent, kept as the source string (trial_attribute_order). Weights: cov_survey_weight = wgt.3.

Description: 2,165 Canadian respondents (329 answering in French) each completed six paired candidate conjoints, one per ethical issue (death penalty, lying, bribery, cheating on a spouse, homosexuality, suicide), with candidates varying in age, gender, party, race, profession, government experience and their stated acceptability of that issue; they chose one candidate and rated both 0-100.
Reference: Islam, M. M., & Loewen, P. (2026). Ethical distance and electoral accountability: Voters punish politicians whose ethical views diverge from societal consensus.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/islam_2026.R (one table per country, as the authors analyse them). Article not yet located (no journal/DOI in the deposit). Task order is not recorded: tasks follow the modules' column order in the deposit; trial_issue names the module. Rating question wording is not in the deposit. French-language respondents' levels are stored in French (cov_language). Unweighted analyses in the paper; cov_survey_weight = wgtnotrestr.

Unweighted analyses in the paper; cov_survey_weight = wgtnotrestr.

Description: German voters (online survey, January 2012) rated and chose between two Eurozone bailout proposals in up to 4 comparisons, with proposals varying Germany's contribution and share, the creditor haircut, austerity conditions, the endorser and the receiving country. 4,655 respondents; 0-6 referendum-vote rating and a forced choice.
Reference: Bechtel, M. M., Hainmueller, J., & Margalit, Y. (2017). Policy design and domestic support for international bailouts. European Journal of Political Research, 56(4), 864-886.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bechtel_2017.R. Respondents saw German; levels are English text following the article's Figure 1 and Table 1 (source value labels are short codes). Rating stored 0-6 as in the source (article reports 1-7). The authors' main analyses keep only comparisons where rating and choice agree; all are kept here. Forced-choice wording is in the Online Appendix (not deposited).

Description: German party members (local party figures; Qualtrics e-mail survey, November 2018) chose between two constituency candidates in 5 tasks for the Bundestag and 5 for a state parliament, with candidates varying in local party work, local political experience, years living in the district, dissent from the party line, gender, education and age. 310 respondents.
Reference: Berz, J., & Jankowski, M. (2022). Local preferences in candidate selection: Evidence from a conjoint experiment among party leaders in Germany. Party Politics, 28(6), 1136-1149.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/berz_2022.R. Levels are the German text from the Qualtrics export. Task is display order (Bundestag and Landtag blocks in random order; trial_parliament); the authors number Bundestag 1-5, Landtag 6-10. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). 310 respondents (triage note expected 309; article not checked).

Description: German municipal public-administration employees (email invitation, 2019; n = 234) each chose which of two hypothetical job applicants to hire into the public service, in 6 pairs described by 9 randomized attributes (school-leaving grade, school education, work experience, English, volunteering, gender, physical disability, age, family origin). Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Jankowski, M., Prokop, C., & Tepe, M. (2020). Representative bureaucracy and public hiring preferences: Evidence from a conjoint experiment among German municipal civil servants and private sector employees. Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory, 30(4), 596-618.
Notes: data/conjoint/jankowski_2020.R. One of three sample tables (jankowski_2020_hiring_civil_servants / _students / _private), analysed side by side by the authors, never pooled. Level text is the German text displayed (raw Qualtrics export); attribute row order randomized per respondent, kept as attrpos_*. Respondents' e-mail addresses in the raw export dropped. 234 respondents (the authors' analysis set; 7 did not finish the survey but completed all tasks). Family origin Germany on ~50% of profiles and disability 'yes' on ~20% (observed).

Family origin Germany on ~50% of profiles and disability 'yes' on ~20% (observed).
