Description: University of New Mexico faculty (Oct 2016) (n = 870) each chose between 8 pairs of hypothetical faculty candidates described by 8 randomized attributes (gender, race/ethnicity, heritage, research record, teaching record, PhD institution, spouse/partner a faculty member, community service record); outcome: which candidate should be given priority to be hired.
Reference: Carey, J. M., Carman, K. R., Clayton, K. P., Horiuchi, Y., Htun, M., & Ortiz, B. (2020). Who wants to hire a more diverse faculty? A conjoint analysis of faculty and student preferences for gender and racial/ethnic diversity. Politics, Groups, and Identities, 8(3), 535-553.
Notes: data/conjoint/carey_2020.R. One of four sample tables (UNM/UNR x faculty/students), analysed separately by the authors. Sample = consented, finished, conjoint displayed (authors' filter); 870 respondents vs 869 in the authors' saved estimates, whose reader drops the first data row of each export (kept here). Gender Non-binary on ~10% of profiles by design. UNM: heritage Non U.S. Citizen never paired with American Indian or Alaska Native.

Description: University of New Mexico students (2016) (n = 1387) each chose between 8 pairs of hypothetical faculty candidates described by 8 randomized attributes (gender, race/ethnicity, heritage, research record, teaching record, PhD institution, spouse/partner a faculty member, community service record); outcome: which candidate should be given priority to be hired.
Reference: Carey, J. M., Carman, K. R., Clayton, K. P., Horiuchi, Y., Htun, M., & Ortiz, B. (2020). Who wants to hire a more diverse faculty? A conjoint analysis of faculty and student preferences for gender and racial/ethnic diversity. Politics, Groups, and Identities, 8(3), 535-553.
Notes: data/conjoint/carey_2020.R. One of four sample tables (UNM/UNR x faculty/students), analysed separately by the authors. Sample = consented, finished, conjoint displayed (authors' filter); 1387 respondents vs 1386 in the authors' saved estimates, whose reader drops the first data row of each export (kept here). Gender Non-binary on ~10% of profiles by design. UNM: heritage Non U.S. Citizen never paired with American Indian or Alaska Native.

Description: University of Nevada, Reno faculty (n = 203) each chose between 10 pairs of hypothetical faculty candidates described by 9 randomized attributes (department/program, position, race/ethnicity, gender, PhD institution, undergraduate institution, spouse/partner a faculty member, teaching record, research record); outcome: which candidate should be given priority to be hired.
Reference: Carey, J. M., Carman, K. R., Clayton, K. P., Horiuchi, Y., Htun, M., & Ortiz, B. (2020). Who wants to hire a more diverse faculty? A conjoint analysis of faculty and student preferences for gender and racial/ethnic diversity. Politics, Groups, and Identities, 8(3), 535-553.
Notes: data/conjoint/carey_2020.R. One of four sample tables (UNM/UNR x faculty/students), analysed separately by the authors. Sample = consented, finished, conjoint displayed (authors' filter); 203 respondents vs 202 in the authors' saved estimates, whose reader drops the first data row of each export (kept here). Gender Non-binary on ~10% of profiles by design.

Description: University of Nevada, Reno students (n = 622) each chose between 10 pairs of hypothetical faculty candidates described by 9 randomized attributes (department/program, position, race/ethnicity, gender, PhD institution, undergraduate institution, spouse/partner a faculty member, teaching record, research record); outcome: which candidate should be given priority to be hired.
Reference: Carey, J. M., Carman, K. R., Clayton, K. P., Horiuchi, Y., Htun, M., & Ortiz, B. (2020). Who wants to hire a more diverse faculty? A conjoint analysis of faculty and student preferences for gender and racial/ethnic diversity. Politics, Groups, and Identities, 8(3), 535-553.
Notes: data/conjoint/carey_2020.R. One of four sample tables (UNM/UNR x faculty/students), analysed separately by the authors. Sample = consented, finished, conjoint displayed (authors' filter); 622 respondents vs 621 in the authors' saved estimates, whose reader drops the first data row of each export (kept here). Gender Non-binary on ~10% of profiles by design.

Description: Swiss 8th graders in Luzern and St.Gallen (Oct-Dec 2022; n = 2,144) each made 4 choices between two hypothetical occupations described by 8 randomized two-level attributes (IT reliance, social interactions, creativity, routine work, entrepreneurial risk, salary, family friendliness, meaningful work); outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Bajka, S. M., Combet, B., Emmenegger, P., & Seufert, S. (2025). Skill requirements versus workplace characteristics: Exploring the drivers of occupational gender segregation. Socio-Economic Review.
Notes: data/conjoint/bajka_2025.R. The deposit has only one-word level labels; level text is the article's Table 1 (English as published; survey language not stated, the cantons are German-speaking). Question wording paraphrased (verbatim prompt is in the article's supplementary appendix). Attribute order was randomized but not recorded. cov_school_class is the deposit's undocumented class code.

Description: Women of reproductive age in New Delhi, India (n = 496; 2017-2018, interviewer-administered on a tablet) chose between two options of a hypothetical contraceptive microarray patch in 10 discrete-choice tasks, options described by 6 attributes (pain, skin reaction, location, size, duration of protection, effect on menstruation) with illustrations; level text in Hindi.
Reference: FHI 360. (2020). Discreet choice experiment survey for development of a contraceptive microarray patch in India and Nigeria (FHI360 2017-2018) [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: data/conjoint/fhi360_2020.R. One of three sample tables (India, Nigeria sample 1, Nigeria sample 2). Profiles decoded from the Sawtooth binary design file (.cgi) and the study file (.ssi) level text; decoding checked against the design's own summary and by the expected ordering of preferences. Fixed holdout task dropped; 31 respondents without a design version dropped; questionnaire covariates not included (numeric codes).

Description: Women of reproductive age in Ibadan, Nigeria (sample 1) (n = 530; 2017-2018, interviewer-administered on a tablet) chose between two options of a hypothetical contraceptive microarray patch in 10 discrete-choice tasks, options described by 6 attributes (pain, skin reaction, location, size, duration of protection, effect on menstruation) with illustrations; level text in Yoruba.
Reference: FHI 360. (2020). Discreet choice experiment survey for development of a contraceptive microarray patch in India and Nigeria (FHI360 2017-2018) [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: data/conjoint/fhi360_2020.R. One of three sample tables (India, Nigeria sample 1, Nigeria sample 2). Profiles decoded from the Sawtooth binary design file (.cgi) and the study file (.ssi) level text; decoding checked against the design's own summary and by the expected ordering of preferences. Fixed holdout task dropped; 13 respondents without a design version dropped; questionnaire covariates not included (numeric codes).

Description: Women of reproductive age in Ibadan, Nigeria (sample 2) (n = 416; 2017-2018, interviewer-administered on a tablet) chose between two options of a hypothetical contraceptive microarray patch in 12 discrete-choice tasks, options described by 5 attributes (pain, skin reaction, location, size, duration of protection) with illustrations; level text in Yoruba.
Reference: FHI 360. (2020). Discreet choice experiment survey for development of a contraceptive microarray patch in India and Nigeria (FHI360 2017-2018) [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: data/conjoint/fhi360_2020.R. One of three sample tables (India, Nigeria sample 1, Nigeria sample 2). Profiles decoded from the Sawtooth binary design file (.cgi) and the study file (.ssi) level text; decoding checked against the design's own summary and by the expected ordering of preferences. Fixed holdout task dropped; no menstruation attribute in this design; questionnaire covariates not included (numeric codes).

Description: Quota-representative Dutch respondents (n = 1,541) each chose between 8 pairs of proposed green investments described by 4 randomized attributes (type, effect, place of investment, financing); outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Beaucousin, J., Kantorowicz, J. J., & Moszoro, M. W. (2025). Building support for green investments. Applied Economics Letters.
Notes: data/conjoint/beaucousin_2025.R. Dutch level text as stored; attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Question wording not deposited (paraphrase). 33 unanswered tasks dropped. No covariates deposited.

Description: Supermarket shoppers in Can Tho, Vietnam (Sept 2020; n = 410) made 4 choices each among two certified premium rice options and a status-quo rice, options described by four certification labels (low-emission, eco-friendly, ethically produced, low glycemic index) and price; fixed blocked design.
Reference: Cuong, O. Q., Connor, M., Demont, M., Sander, B. O., & Nelson, K. (2022). How do rice consumers trade off sustainability and health labels? Evidence from Vietnam. Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems, 6, 1010161.
Notes: data/conjoint/cuong_2022.R. Discrete choice experiment; the status quo (no certification, VND 20,000/kg) is shown with attributes, so it is profile 3 (always), not an opt-out. Level text from the article's example card (Table 2, English); survey language not stated. Task order within block inferred from the deposit's running choice-set counter. Gender/education kept as codes (article Table 4 counts suggest 0 = female).

Description: US urban and suburban adults (online panel, 2024; n = 5,127) made 5 choices between two 3-policy platforms holding opposite positions on the same three randomly drawn issues (17 housing, 22 non-housing), plus a retest of the first choice; one attribute column per issue, '(not shown)' when absent.
Reference: Elmendorf, C. S., Nall, C., & Oklobdzija, S. (2024). What state housing policies do voters want? Evidence from a platform-choice experiment. Journal of Political Institutions and Political Economy, 5(1), 117-152.
Notes: data/conjoint/elmendorf_2024.R. Platform-choice design: each profile shows three policy positions; the two profiles hold opposite positions on the same issues. One attr_ column per issue (39), '(not shown)' when the issue is not in the task; attrpos_ = row. Task 6 repeats task 1 with sets swapped and an extra issue-name column (trial_repeat_of). Sample per the authors' filters (finished, screening items passed, speeders out). The deposit's raw export contains IP addresses and GPS coordinates; dropped. Article not read.

Description: Chilean Netquest panelists (October-November 2021) chose which of two hypothetical presidential candidates they would vote for, or neither, in 5 pairs varying coalition membership versus independence, occupation, age and gender. 3,965 respondents.
Reference: Argote, P., & Visconti, G. (2023). Anti-elite attitudes and support for independent candidates. PLOS ONE, 18(10), e0292098.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/argote_2023.R. Respondents saw Spanish; levels are English. attr_coalition stores the authors' own value labels as they are (Center-Right, Center-Left, Left, Right, Independents), not the displayed coalition names, because no deposited file maps the labels to the coalitions shown. Choice is the authors' choice_clean (raw answer column empty); opt-out allowed (6,908 tasks with neither chosen; 646 respondents never chose). Wave 1 of the same panel as argote_2025_ideology_candidates_chile.

Description: South Korean Qualtrics-panel respondents (Jan-Feb 2024) chose between two hypothetical candidates in 10 paired tasks varying age, origin, gender, career, scandal and five policy positions (labor, housing, social, foreign, nuclear). 1,983 respondents; forced choice.
Reference: Ward, P., & Denney, S. (2025). Partisan voters in party systems with ephemeral parties: Evidence from South Korea. Party Politics.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ward_2025.R. Attribute text is the authors' English labels (respondents saw Korean). The general- vs presidential-election framing arm (randomized half/half) is not in the deposit. 22 respondents with no recorded choice dropped (README); Qualtrics IDs re-keyed; open-text reason dropped. Design facts from the authors' 2024 working paper (published article not reachable).

Description: US Lucid respondents (December 2021) each evaluated 5 hypothetical COVID-19 vaccine (or booster) profiles one at a time, varying efficacy, protection duration, protection against future variants, manufacturer and financial incentive, after a randomized Omicron information prime. 2,121 respondents; would-get-it choice and a 1-7 likelihood rating.
Reference: Raman, S., Kriner, D., Ziebarth, N., Simon, K., & Kreps, S. (2022). COVID-19 booster uptake among US adults: Assessing the impact of vaccine attributes, incentives, and context in a choice-based experiment. Social Science & Medicine, 310, 115277.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/raman_2022.R. Single-profile design; choice = would choose to get it (rejecting is the outside option). All vaccination groups in one table (the piped noun was 'vaccine' for the unvaccinated, 'vaccine booster' otherwise); the article's main sample is cov_vax_status fully vaccinated with cov_booster_status No (548). Omicron prime arm in trial_omicron_info. 3 respondents with no attribute data dropped; Lucid IDs re-keyed; zip dropped. Article says 288 unique profiles; the deposited levels give 216.

Description: Dutch online-panel respondents (EMMAVID Netherlands, ethnic minorities oversampled) evaluated 3 pairs of text vignettes of hypothetical Dutch MPs varying name, gender, migration background, religion and a policy statement. 905 respondents; vote choice per pair plus 0-10 ratings of representation, trust and capability.
Reference: van Oosten, S., Mügge, L., Hakhverdian, A., & van der Pas, D. (2024). Dutch Ethnic Minority and Muslim Attitudes, Voting, Identity and Discrimination (EMMAVID) - EMMAVID Data the Netherlands [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/vanoosten_2024.R. Text vignettes; respondents saw Dutch, stored text is the deposit's English (value labels, authors' statement list). Ratings stored raw as .sav codes 1-11 (= displayed 0-10 plus 1). Names are drawn from background- and gender-specific lists, so name is tied to background and gender. Part 3a (2 profiles without policy, expected-position question) not included. trial_group (Group 1 / Group 2 control) is undocumented. Panel interview numbers re-keyed. Reference DOI is the OSF preprint that analyses the data (pools FR/DE/NL).

Description: Online panel respondents in China, Germany, India, the UK and the USA (Deltapoll, October 2020, n = 7,512) chose which of two climate-change statements, varying valence, theme, scale and time frame, would make them more likely to support climate policies, in 5 paired tasks.
Reference: Dasandi, N., Graham, H., Hudson, D., Jankin, S., vanHeerde-Hudson, J., & Watts, N. (2022). Positive, global, and health or environment framing bolsters public support for climate policies. Communications Earth & Environment, 3, 239.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/dasandi_2022.R. Text vignettes: attr_ hold the authors' level names (Fig. 4), not the full statement; the 'Country' scale level displayed the survey country's name. Statements in English (UK, USA, India), Chinese and German (translations not deposited). Monthly willingness-to-pay rating dropped (undocumented wording, currency and range). Survey weight kept; respondents answering gender 'In another way' are NA.

Description: Pilot fielding (file 'August pilot', n = 4,935) of the same design in China, Germany, India, the UK and the USA: respondents chose which of two climate-change statements, varying valence, theme, scale and time frame, would make them more likely to support climate policies, in 5 paired tasks.
Reference: Dasandi, N., Graham, H., Hudson, D., Jankin, S., vanHeerde-Hudson, J., & Watts, N. (2022). Positive, global, and health or environment framing bolsters public support for climate policies. Communications Earth & Environment, 3, 239.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/dasandi_2022.R. Text vignettes: attr_ hold the authors' level names (Fig. 4), not the full statement; the 'Country' scale level displayed the survey country's name. Statements in English (UK, USA, India), Chinese and German (translations not deposited). Monthly willingness-to-pay rating dropped (undocumented wording, currency and range). Survey weight kept; respondents answering gender 'In another way' are NA.

Description: Japanese adults (Lucid, n = 3,151) read one newspaper-style vignette about a hypothetical municipal council candidate whose gender (Yasuko vs Yasuhiko Takahashi) and motivation for running (ambition revealed vs encouraged by others) were randomized (2 x 2), and rated favorability, expected popularity and six personal traits.
Reference: Endo, Y., & Ono, Y. (2025). Emphasizing or downplaying political ambitions: Exploring the role of candidate gender in shaping voter perceptions. Electoral Studies, 98, 103004.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/endo_2025.R. One vignette per respondent (task = profile = 1). Vignette text is the working paper's English translation (shown in Japanese); question wording is a paraphrase. Trait items have no documented anchors. Education, ideology and prefecture are unlabelled codes (_code). Qualtrics ResponseId dropped.

Description: German citizens (online sample, February 2023, n = 1,690) chose between two hypothetical municipal e-government chatbots varying developer, chat-history storage, chat termination, automated decisions, workload reduction, time saving, and communication type and tone, in 6 paired tasks.
Reference: Hemesath, S., & Tepe, M. (2024). Public value positions and design preferences toward AI-based chatbots in e-government. Evidence from a conjoint experiment with citizens and municipal front desk officers. Government Information Quarterly, 41(4), 101985.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hemesath_2024.R. Attribute levels in German as stored. Question wording not deposited (paraphrase). A task-level -5..+5 relative-preference scale is dropped (undocumented wording/anchors). Covariates: gender and education labelled from the authors' Script.R; other attitudes kept as codes. Qualtrics IDs and GPS coordinates dropped.

Description: German municipal front desk officers (March 2023, n = 267) chose between two hypothetical municipal e-government chatbots varying developer, chat-history storage, chat termination, automated decisions, workload reduction, time saving, and communication type and tone, in 6 paired tasks.
Reference: Hemesath, S., & Tepe, M. (2024). Public value positions and design preferences toward AI-based chatbots in e-government. Evidence from a conjoint experiment with citizens and municipal front desk officers. Government Information Quarterly, 41(4), 101985.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hemesath_2024.R. Attribute levels in German as stored. Question wording not deposited (paraphrase). A task-level -5..+5 relative-preference scale is dropped (undocumented wording/anchors). Municipality characteristics (type, mayor, population, area) dropped as identifying; gender and education kept as codes. Qualtrics IDs and GPS coordinates dropped.

Description: Swiss car holders (non-EV and EV holders in four German-speaking cantons, 2018, n = 5,325 completes, 4,973 with outcomes) chose between and rated two electric-vehicle policy packages varying charging infrastructure, purchase subsidy, information requirements, registration ban and (for a random half) funding, in 5 paired tasks.
Reference: Brückmann, G., & Bernauer, T. (2020). What drives public support for policies to enhance electric vehicle adoption? Environmental Research Letters, 15(9), 094002.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bruckmann_2020.R. Level text is the article's English Table 1 (survey in German). Funding attribute shown only in a random half (trial_funding_shown; otherwise '(not shown)'); 'No additional funding' iff no chargers and no subsidy. Task index inferred from row order. Gender kept as codes (the authors' 'male'/'not male' labels look reversed).

Description: Adults with hypertension in urban Bengaluru and rural Kolar, Karnataka, India (household survey, 2021, n = 1,085) chose between two hypothetical public primary-care facilities varying staff courtesy, wait time, provider (doctor or nurse), carefulness of assessment and free-medication availability, in 8 choice sets (discrete choice experiment).
Reference: Leslie, H. H., Babu, G. R., Dolcy Saldanha, N., Turcotte-Tremblay, A.-M., Ravi, D., Shapeti, S. S., Kapoor, N., Prabhakaran, D., & Kruk, M. E. (2023). Population preferences for primary care models for hypertension in Karnataka, India. JAMA Network Open, 6(3), e232937.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/leslie_2023.R. Fixed blocked D-efficient design: 5 versions of 7 sets plus one common set (task 36); task is the choice-set id, not display order (not recorded). Level text from the article's choice card (eFigure 1); shown in English or Kannada with illustrations. 23 respondents skipped 1-2 cards.

Description: US adults (Lucid, July 2022, n = 4,191) read 5 text vignettes in which a president of randomized party, gender, age and electoral mandate responds to one of 9 situations (crises or a non-crisis control) with one of 10 actions, some undermining accountability, and rated their approval on a 6-point scale.
Reference: De Bruin, E., & Jones, C. W. (forthcoming). Public support for undermining executive accountability in times of crisis. European Journal of Political Research.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/debruin_2026.R. Attribute levels are the displayed text pieces stored as Qualtrics embedded data; the vignette template and question wording were not available (paraphrase). Task-5-only follow-up items dropped. One duplicate Lucid panelist reduced to the first completion. IP addresses, GPS coordinates, ZIP codes and panel IDs dropped. Article forthcoming (no DOI yet).

Description: Urban consumers in Kinshasa, DR Congo (three survey groups, n = 600) chose between two rice products varying price (700-1,200 FC), packaging, distance to the point of sale and origin (local or one of four import regions), in 8 choice cards (discrete choice experiment; one of five product experiments answered by the same respondents).
Reference: Thontwa, S. K., De Weerdt, J., & Van Passel, S. (2024). What do urban consumers want? Findings from a discrete choice experiment on the preference for locally produced food in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Agrekon, 63(4), 223-239.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/thontwa_2024.R. One of five per-product tables (RIZ). Fixed blocked design (8 versions x 8 cards, trial_version). Level text in French from the authors' choice-card coding sheets. trial_arm = survey group CG/IT/LT (meaning undocumented). GPS coordinates dropped; the deposit's xlsx files also hold IP addresses and Qualtrics IDs. Rice reproduces the authors' CG-RIZ conditional logit (Tables.xlsx Table 3) exactly.

Description: Urban consumers in Kinshasa, DR Congo (three survey groups, n = 600) chose between two maize products varying price (1,200-1,900 FC), packaging, distance to the point of sale and origin (local or one of four import regions), in 8 choice cards (discrete choice experiment; one of five product experiments answered by the same respondents).
Reference: Thontwa, S. K., De Weerdt, J., & Van Passel, S. (2024). What do urban consumers want? Findings from a discrete choice experiment on the preference for locally produced food in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Agrekon, 63(4), 223-239.

GPS coordinates dropped; the deposit's xlsx files also hold IP addresses and Qualtrics IDs.

Description: Urban consumers in Kinshasa, DR Congo (three survey groups, n = 600) chose between two sugar products varying price (2,200-3,000 FC), packaging, distance to the point of sale and origin (local or one of four import regions), in 8 choice cards (discrete choice experiment; one of five product experiments answered by the same respondents).
Reference: Thontwa, S. K., De Weerdt, J., & Van Passel, S. (2024). What do urban consumers want? Findings from a discrete choice experiment on the preference for locally produced food in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Agrekon, 63(4), 223-239.

GPS coordinates dropped; the deposit's xlsx files also hold IP addresses and Qualtrics IDs.

Description: Urban consumers in Kinshasa, DR Congo (three survey groups, n = 600) chose between two cooking oil products varying price (1,800-3,100 FC), packaging, distance to the point of sale and origin (local or one of four import regions), in 8 choice cards (discrete choice experiment; one of five product experiments answered by the same respondents).
Reference: Thontwa, S. K., De Weerdt, J., & Van Passel, S. (2024). What do urban consumers want? Findings from a discrete choice experiment on the preference for locally produced food in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Agrekon, 63(4), 223-239.

Description: UK online respondents compared 5 pairs of hypothetical internet-voting (i-voting) reform proposals varying pre-registration, voting method, voting window, past trials, pilot results, fraud risk, cost, administering body, proposing party and endorser. 1,200 respondents; a choice plus 0-6 support and trustworthiness ratings per proposal.
Reference: Turnbull-Dugarte, S. J., & Devine, D. (2023). Support for digitising the ballot box: A systematic review of i-voting pilots and a conjoint experiment. Electoral Studies, 86, 102679.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/turnbulldugarte_2023.R. Level text from the .dta value labels (typos kept). Administered-by is one stored 6-level attribute; the authors split it into platform x private-sector role. Question wording and rating anchors are not in the deposit and the article could not be retrieved: outcomes are paraphrased and rating direction (higher = more support / more trustworthy) is inferred from the authors' 0-1 rescaling. N vs paper not checked.

Description: French adults (Bilendi opt-in panel, April 2024) judged 5 hypothetical foreign acquisitions of a domestic company, varying the acquiring country, relative gains, reciprocity in openness, and the target's size, performance, technology and sector, and said whether the government should block each. 1,223 respondents who passed the attention screener.
Reference: Guidi, M., Moro, F. N., & Poletti, A. (2026). Geopolitics and opposition to foreign direct investment in the EU: Evidence from a conjoint experiment. Business and Politics.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/guidi_2026.R (one of three country tables: france/germany/italy, analysed separately by the authors). choice = 1 if the respondent wants the government to block the acquisition (single profile, opt-out). Level text is the article's English Table 1 wording with the country name filled in; respondents saw French. Task order inferred from row order. Covariates are only the authors' dichotomized subgroup codings.

Description: Chinese online-survey respondents (Feb-Mar 2018) compared 4 pairs of meat-and-fish policy packages varying a meat tax, use of its revenues, vegetarian-meal rules for public cafeterias, discounts for vegetarian alternatives, animal farming standards, information campaigns and producer subsidies; forced choice plus a 1-7 support rating per package. 1,626 respondents.
Reference: Fesenfeld, L. P., Wicki, M., Sun, Y., & Bernauer, T. (2020). Policy packaging can make food system transformation feasible. Nature Food, 1(3), 173-182.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/fesenfeld_2020.R (one of three country tables cn/de/us; the authors analyse each country separately). Same survey as wicki_2019_passenger_transport. Level text is the published English instrument; respondents saw Chinese (translation not published). 'No tax revenues' appears exactly with 'No new tax'. trial_info_treatment = earlier randomized information arm.

Reference: Fesenfeld, L. P., Wicki, M., Sun, Y., & Bernauer, T. (2020). Policy packaging can make food system transformation feasible. Nature Food, 1(3), 173-182.

Reference: Fesenfeld, L. P., Wicki, M., Sun, Y., & Bernauer, T. (2020). Policy packaging can make food system transformation feasible. Nature Food, 1(3), 173-182.

Crowdsourcing panel, 14-16 March 2021; n = 2848) chose, in 5 paired tasks, the more desirable of two vaccination situations, each setting whether they themselves, a familiar person they had picked, and society as a whole vaccinate, wait and see, or do not vaccinate against COVID-19.

PII (IP, GPS, e-mail, phone) dropped. Article N not checked.

Reference: Stoop, N., van der Windt, P., & Weber, S. (2025). Where to flee? Preferences for host communities among displaced people in Congo. PLOS ONE, 20.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/stoop_2025.R. English level text; respondents saw Tshiluba with drawings. Ranking and Likert outcomes stored 0-4 (codebook says 1-4). Attribute order randomized per respondent, not recorded. N 1,965 matches the article; the job-availability effect on the economic-contribution item (0.77) reproduces the article's 0.8.

Description: Swiss voters (n = 3,006) compared 3 pairs of proposals for a law obliging Swiss firms to protect people and the environment abroad, varying reciprocity (unilateral, only if Western economies, only if economies worldwide do so) and stringency (round tables, public report, liability); they rated each proposal 1-7 and chose the one they would accept in a referendum; half first read a UN-norms text.
Reference: Rudolph, L., Kolcava, D., & Bernauer, T. (2023). Public demand for extraterritorial environmental and social public goods provision. British Journal of Political Science, 53(2), 516-535.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/rudolph_2022.R (conjoint; the deposit's factorial vignette is rudolph_2022_supply_law_vignette). Level text = the .dta English value labels (the displayed German cells are not deposited). 38 tasks without saved levels dropped; unanswered choices NA. Profile order within task inferred from the element numbering.

Description: Swiss voters (n = 2,963) read one vignette describing an adopted law obliging Swiss firms to protect people and the environment abroad, with reciprocity (3 levels) and stringency (3 levels) randomized, and rated 7 statements about the law on a 1-5 agreement scale; half first read a UN-norms text.
Reference: Rudolph, L., Kolcava, D., & Bernauer, T. (2023). Public demand for extraterritorial environmental and social public goods provision. British Journal of Political Science, 53(2), 516-535.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint). Script data/conjoint/rudolph_2022.R (factorial vignette; the deposit's conjoint is rudolph_2022_supply_law_conjoint). Level text = the German vignette sentences from the instrument. 'Don't know' absent from the data.

Description: US Prolific respondents (May 2021; 1,501, recruited as White and Nonwhite samples) chose between and rated two versions of a city Community Activity Worker job in 3 pairs, varying total pay, performance bonuses, performance evaluation, community involvement, income and demographics, overtime and key job task. Forced choice plus a 1-7 ideal-job rating per job.
Reference: Pedersen, M. J., Favero, N., & Park, J. (2023). Pay-for-performance, job attraction, and the prospects of bureaucratic representation in public organizations: Evidence from a conjoint experiment. Public Management Review.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/pedersen_2023.R. Levels from the deposited profile generator (PFP v4.0_strong.php) with <strong> tags removed; uniform independent randomization, fixed attribute order. The two Prolific samples (White / Non-White prescreen) are pooled as in the paper, cov_sample marks them. The same survey also underlies Pedersen, Favero & Park (2023, Public Administration) on PSM and self-efficacy.

Description: Dutch adults (May 2024; 1,195 respondents) chose which of two hypothetical conversations about a risk they would rather take part in, over an example pair plus 8 pairs, described by topic, the other person's gender, relation and closeness to the respondent, and the person's apparent knowledge, concern and motivation. Forced choice.
Reference: Perlstein, S., Kantorowicz, J., & Kuipers, S. (2025). Preferences for risk conversations in everyday life: A conjoint analysis. Journal of Risk Research, 28(6), 611-627.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/perlstein_2025.R. Levels stored in Dutch as displayed (English translations in the authors' conjoint_clean_main.Rmd). Task 1 is the intro 'Voorbeeld' pair, which respondents answered and the authors analyse (trial_example = 1). Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Unequal level shares and some never-occurring combinations (closeness x relation, concern x motivation), not documented. Covariates are codes only (no labels deposited).

Description: South Korean adults (2,000 respondents) chose which of two policy packages, varying opportunity expansion, elite responsibility and economic security (4 levels each), would make Korean society fairer, in 6 pairs; a second pick between the same packages (wording not deposited) is choice_support.
Reference: Han, S. (2026). Replication data for: When opportunity is not enough: Mobility beliefs and fairness evaluations [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/han_2026.R. Levels are the deposit's Korean *_label text; the codebook's Korean mock-up words some levels slightly differently, so exact displayed text is not certain. choice_support wording unknown. Covariate codes kept with _code suffix (the codebook's coding table belongs to the other, observational data). No published article linked.

Description: Japanese adults (national online sample of 1,002 plus an Okinawa oversample of 387) chose which of two plans to deploy MV-22 Osprey aircraft in Japan they supported, over 10 pairs varying the host camp, operating force (US military / Self-Defense Forces), regional incentives, force size, night training and training range. Forced choice.
Reference: Horiuchi, Y., & Tago, A. (2024). U.S. military should not be in my backyard: Conjoint experiments in Japan. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 68(9), 1798-1824.
Notes:
Script data/conjoint/horiuchi_2024.R (Study 1). Levels in Japanese as displayed (
replaced by a space); English in the authors' step04 script. All 10 tasks kept; the authors analyse tasks 1-7. National and Okinawa samples pooled (cov_sample) as in the paper; the authors' reCAPTCHA >= 0.5 and Okinawa-residence filters are not applied (1,304 respondents pass them). Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_).

Description: Japanese adults (national online sample of 3,199 plus an Okinawa oversample, 4,268 respondents in all) chose which of two plans to deploy F-35 fighters in Japan they supported, over 8 pairs (the 8th repeats the 1st) varying the air base, operating force, soundproofing subsidy, regional incentives and night training. Forced choice.
Reference: Horiuchi, Y., & Tago, A. (2024). U.S. military should not be in my backyard: Conjoint experiments in Japan. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 68(9), 1798-1824.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/horiuchi_2024.R (Study 2). Levels in Japanese as displayed; task 8 re-shows task 1 (trial_repeat_of = 1, same order), the authors analyse tasks 1-7. National and Okinawa samples pooled (cov_sample); the authors' reCAPTCHA, residence and Finished filters are not applied (4,218 pass reCAPTCHA + residence). cov_frame is an arm of another project's experiment whose position in the survey is not documented.

Description: Australian adults (943 panel respondents, 925 with an answer; ANU/Life in Australia wave 7 variables) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical candidates described by 12 attributes (ideology stored as two source columns, 13 attr_ columns) including gender, party, ideology, country of birth, cultural background and other language spoken; forced choice with a don't-know option.
Reference: Snagovsky, F., Kang, W. C., Sheppard, J., & Biddle, N. (2020). Does descriptive representation increase perceptions of legitimacy? Evidence from Australia. Australian Journal of Political Science, 55(4), 378-398.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/snagovsky_2020.R. Levels are the .dta value-label text; no questionnaire deposited, so the choice question wording is unknown. Ideology is kept as the deposit's two labelled variables, attr_political_id ('Centre left/right' / 'Hard left/right') and attr_left_right ('left' / 'right', fixed by party); how they were combined on screen is not deposited. Other language is tied to cultural background (observed restriction). Don't know kept as opt-out; Refused tasks dropped.

Description: US local elected officials (CivicPulse, April 2020) saw 3 pairs of hypothetical refugee groups varying 7 attributes (age, education, group makeup, English, region of origin, religion, sponsor) and said whether they were receptive to either group, one, or neither settling in their community. 574 officials; per-group 0/1 receptivity.
Reference: Shaffer, R., Pinson, L. E., Chu, J. A., & Simmons, B. A. (2020). Local elected officials' receptivity to refugee resettlement in the United States. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 117(50), 31722-31728.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/shaffer_2020.R. The four-way answer (either / A only / B only / neither) is stored as the authors' per-group binary; the two ratings of a task recover it. 22 respondents whose attribute levels were not saved are dropped. No codebook in the deposit; trial_group_size and cov_cpss_03 are undocumented. Article AMCEs reproduce.

Description: English adults (YouGov, June 2023) saw 8 single hypothetical work-visa applicants varying age, gender, job (8 occupations crossing skill and labour demand), country of origin (India, Australia, Poland, Nigeria) and long/short-term visa, and said whether each should receive a work visa. 643 respondents; yes/no choice.
Reference: Kawakami, R., Scotto, T. J., Dorussen, H., Pickering, S., Reifler, J., Sunahara, Y., Tago, A., & Yen, D. (2026). Who gets in? A conjoint analysis of labour market demand and immigration preferences in England and Japan. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 52(1), 65-84.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kawakami_2026.R. Article reports 646 English respondents; the deposit has 643 (643 x 8 = the article's 5,144 responses). Job labels follow the authors' code and Figure 1 ('Retail worker'); Table 1 gives longer forms (Fruit and vegetable picker, Retail salesperson, Call Centre Telemarketer). Political-trust battery not kept (wording not deposited). Overall visa share reproduces the article.

Description: Japanese adults (Rakuten Insight, June 2023) saw 4 single hypothetical work-visa applicants varying age, gender, job (8 occupations crossing skill and labour demand), country of origin (Peru, China, Korea, Vietnam) and long/short-term visa, and said whether each should receive a work visa. 1,498 respondents; yes/no choice.
Reference: Kawakami, R., Scotto, T. J., Dorussen, H., Pickering, S., Reifler, J., Sunahara, Y., Tago, A., & Yen, D. (2026). Who gets in? A conjoint analysis of labour market demand and immigration preferences in England and Japan. Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies, 52(1), 65-84.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kawakami_2026.R. Respondents saw Japanese; level text is the authors' English labels. 27 unanswered tasks omitted. Job labels follow the authors' code and Figure 1 ('Retail worker'); Table 1 gives longer forms (Fruit and vegetable picker, Retail salesperson, Call Centre Telemarketer). Political-trust battery not kept (wording not deposited). Overall visa share reproduces the article.

Description: US full-time employees (Qualtrics, March 2022) chose between 10 pairs of hypothetical jobs varying work location (fully remote to mostly office), salary, supervision, schedule flexibility, expense reimbursement and support resources. 627 respondents; forced choice.
Reference: Wozniak-Jechorek, B., D'Urso, A. S., Thurston, C. N., & Patnaik, M. (2026). Understanding employee trade-offs in remote work: Toward more sustainable workplace design. Journal of Strategic Information Systems, 35(2), 101970.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/wozniakjechorek_2026.R. Level text as stored in the authors' cleaned file; question wording, attribute order and randomization rules not deposited (article paywalled). One respondent who took the survey twice keeps the first response only (627, as in the abstract); 2 unanswered tasks dropped. Deposit held IP addresses and GPS coordinates; dropped.

Description: German adults (online panel, Turkish- and former-Soviet-origin respondents oversampled) read 3 pairs of text vignettes of hypothetical Bundestag politicians varying name, gender, migration background, religion and a policy statement, rated each on representation, trust and capability (0-10) and chose one to vote for. 954 respondents.
Reference: van Oosten, S., Mügge, L., Hakhverdian, A., van der Pas, D., & Vermeulen, F. (2024). German Ethnic Minority and Muslim Attitudes, Voting, Identity and Discrimination (EMMAVID) - EMMAVID Data Germany [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/vanoosten_2024_de.R. Sibling of vanoosten_2024_politicians_nl. Level text is German as in the .sav labels (displayed language). Ratings kept as .sav codes 1-11 (= displayed 0-10). 228 Turkish-background profiles carry German first names, against the codebook name lists; kept as stored. Education kept as codes (labels doubtful). Part 3a profiles dropped. Reference DOI is the OSF preprint.

Description: Household heads along the Jamuna river in rural Bangladesh (panel wave 1, May-June 2021, face-to-face) heard one of six hypothetical riverbank-erosion and flood scenarios (3 damage levels x 2 future-risk levels) and said whether they would stay in their village or move. 1,534 respondents; one stay/move choice each.
Reference: Rudolph, L. (2026). Vignette experiments can replicate actual behavioral intent and partly actual behavior: Panel evidence on environmental migration from Bangladesh. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 1-22.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/rudolph_2026_migration.R. One vignette per respondent; attributes are the two parts of the scenario text (situation, outlook) from the English master questionnaire (interviews in Bengali), which form six fixed combinations; trial_design_cell gives the author's damage x risk label. choice is the author's narrow migration intent (move vs stay, with a forced follow-up after an unprompted 'depends'). Reproduces the author's main regression exactly.

Description: US adults (Lucid, April-May 2022) chose between 10 pairs of electricity energy mixes varying monthly bill (05-25), percentage of renewables (10-100%) and whether renewables are locally produced. 1,861 respondents; forced choice.
Reference: Wu, V. (2024). Replication data for: "Partisan energy mix priorities in the United States: Republicans prioritize price, Democrats also consider renewables" [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/wu_2024.R. Built from the raw Qualtrics export (CCA_Data.xlsx) with the author's sample filters (1,862, the deposit's n; one answered no task). Attribute order randomized per respondent; levels assigned to attributes by form, row kept as attrpos_. No published article found. Export held IP addresses, GPS coordinates, ZIP codes and Lucid IDs; dropped. trial_cca_treatment is an undocumented assignment from another survey block.

Description: German online respondents (Qualtrics panel, Dec 2019; n = 1,255) each rated three text vignettes about applying for a municipal service, randomizing the service (passport, certificate of good conduct, social-housing permit), the interface (app, self-service terminal, clerk) and service quality (on time, delayed, delayed with apology); ratings of satisfaction with the procedure and with the result (9-point).
Reference: Prokop, C., & Tepe, M. (2022). Talk or type? The effect of digital interfaces on citizens' satisfaction with standardized public services. Public Administration, 100(2), 427-433.
Notes: data/conjoint/prokop_2021.R. Factorial vignette, one profile per task, three tasks. Quality sentence names the service, so attr_quality has 9 texts (3 quality x 3 service). attr_image records the picture shown; in task 3 the survey flow shows the desk (clerk) picture with the self-service-terminal text (707 vignettes). Ratings stored as Qualtrics codes 1-9 (= -4..4). 1,255 respondents with any rating; authors' complete-case sample 1,234. IP address, ResponseId and panel token dropped.

Description: US adults in the CCES 2014 Yale team module (YouGov, pre-election wave; n = 1,000) each saw four randomly generated candidate profiles (gender, family, religion, military service, job, top three issue priorities) and guessed the candidate's party, said how sure they were, and rated the candidate 0-10.
Reference: Henderson, J. (2017). CCES 2014, Team Module of Yale University (JAH) [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: data/conjoint/henderson_2014.R. Single-profile tasks (4 per respondent). Level text from the .sav value labels; the on-screen profile table is not deposited. Favorability 'Not sure' (about 19%) stored NA. Post-election wave profiles exist but their answers are not in the deposit, so not built. CCES team weight kept.

Description: Representatives of Costa Rican firms (Qualtrics survey, 2013-2014) chose between two trade policies in up to 5 paired comparisons, the policies varying tariff/non-tariff barrier reduction, flexibility of commitments, use of dispute settlement, investment protection and export subsidies. 325 respondents; forced choice.
Reference: Kim, I. S., Milner, H. V., Bernauer, T., Osgood, I., Spilker, G., & Tingley, D. (2019). Firms and global value chains: Identifying firms' multidimensional trade preferences. International Studies Quarterly, 63(1), 153-167.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kim_2019.R. Levels are the Spanish text from the Qualtrics display columns (stored without accents); profile position recovered by matching each long-file row to the displayed profiles. The paper analyses the 214 firms in tradable industries (1,049 tasks); all 325 respondents are kept. The deposit's survey export (crsurvey_full.csv) holds names, e-mails, IPs, GPS and company names; none is carried here.

Description: Japanese voters (Rakuten Insight online panel, 2020) rated the favourability of 20 single hypothetical Diet candidates each (10 for a House of Representatives and 10 for a House of Councillors election), with candidates varying legacy (dynastic) status, gender, age, education, occupation, hometown, experience and party. 1,126 respondents; 1-8 rating.
Reference: Miwa, H., Kasuya, Y., & Ono, Y. (2023). Voters' perceptions and evaluations of dynastic politics in Japan. Asian Journal of Comparative Politics, 8(3), 671-688.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/miwa_2023.R. Levels are the deposit's English short labels (respondents saw Japanese sentences, Online Appendix E.1, not deposited). Task numbers are row order and not display order: the deposit lists each respondent's HoR block before the HoC block although election order was randomized. Level distributions follow real-world shares (legacy 85.3/3.6/4.2/6.9%).

Description: US adults chose between two laptop computers in up to 6 paired tasks, the products varying brand, price, processor, storage and RAM and four contract terms (warranty, conflict resolution, liability, privacy). 2,238 respondents; forced choice. The same respondents did the companion experiment kantorowicz_2026_rights_laundry.
Reference: Kantorowicz-Reznichenko, E., van Heusden, A., & Kantorowicz, J. (2026). Consumers' rights in the shadow of the brand: A conjoint experiment on the valuation and trade-offs of contractual rights. Journal of Law & Empirical Analysis, 3(1), 105-126.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kantorowicz_2026.R. Task and profile are inferred from the deposit's reshape layout (profile halves, stacked task blocks; verified one choice per pair). Privacy levels are the authors' short labels; the displayed sentences, question wording and article were not available. Derived respondent dummies dropped.

Description: US adults chose between two laundry machines in up to 6 paired tasks, the products varying brand, price, depth, noise and load capacity and four contract terms (warranty, conflict resolution, liability, privacy). 2,239 respondents; forced choice. The same respondents did the companion experiment kantorowicz_2026_rights_computers.
Reference: Kantorowicz-Reznichenko, E., van Heusden, A., & Kantorowicz, J. (2026). Consumers' rights in the shadow of the brand: A conjoint experiment on the valuation and trade-offs of contractual rights. Journal of Law & Empirical Analysis, 3(1), 105-126.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kantorowicz_2026.R. Task and profile are inferred from the deposit's reshape layout (profile halves, stacked task blocks; verified one choice per pair). Privacy levels are the authors' short labels; the displayed sentences, question wording and article were not available. Derived respondent dummies dropped.

Description: Japanese voters (2019 online survey) chose between two hypothetical House of Councillors PR-list candidates in 10 paired tasks, the candidates varying age, gender, incumbency, other political experience, hometown, education and occupation. 2,018 respondents; forced choice; respondents had been randomized to four information/voting-rule arms beforehand.
Reference: Reeves, J. F., & Smith, D. M. (2026). Getting to know her: Information and gender bias in preferential voting systems. Electoral Studies, 103120.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/reeves_2026.R. Levels are the Japanese display text; hometown and prefectural-assembly levels name the respondent's own prefecture, as designed. trial_treatment_group is the earlier voting experiment's arm (the paper estimates the conjoint by arm). The deposit is one zip (survey + candidate data); only the 2019 conjoint rows are used.

Description: US adults (NORC AmeriSpeak, June 2019, n = 3,107) each read one news story about a recovering opioid user whose race, gender, residential location, pathway to addiction and insurance were randomized, then rated federal spending on treatment and on law enforcement and whether addicts are to blame (5-point scales).
Reference: de Benedictis-Kessner, J., & Hankinson, M. (2024). How the identity of substance users shapes public opinion on opioid policy. Political Behavior, 46(1), 609-629.
Notes: Conjoint layout (irw_conjoint), one vignette per respondent. Script data/conjoint/debenedictiskessner_2022.R. Race and gender are the authors' condition coding (shown by name, hand colour in photo, pronouns); the displayed name is not in the deposit (trial_name_quartile = P_RNAME). Pathway text completed from Online Appendix B (deposit truncates it). Ratings in source code order (1 = increase a lot / strongly agree). The ACA favourability item is dropped (wording undocumented).

Description: Dutch respondents (quota-representative online sample, n = 1,529) chose between two hypothetical migrants in each of 6 tasks, with randomized reason for migration (persecution, economic, earthquake, drought, flood), country of origin, economic self-sufficiency, education, age and gender.
Reference: Faure, M., Kantorowicz, J., & Weiss, A. (2025). Is climate change a valid reason for migration? Evidence from a conjoint experiment. Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties, 36(3), 757-778.
Notes: data/conjoint/faure_2025.R. Levels in Dutch as displayed (authors' English translations in the script header). Choice question wording not in deposit (paraphrase). Country x reason restrictions observed (Maldives never with earthquake/drought; Pakistan, Vietnam never with drought). Attribute positions not deposited. Qualtrics response IDs dropped; education and party kept as unlabelled codes.

Description: Voters in North Maharashtra, India (in-person survey, n = 2,360) read one vignette about a village council president whose gender (Bharti/Rohit, female/male) and caste (Kamble/Marathe, Dalit/Maratha) were randomized 2x2, and judged whether the president would hold real decision-making authority, would resign under elite pressure, and would face backlash.
Reference: Heinze, A. R. (2025). Democratic deepening or elite persistence? How local elites adapt to electoral reform in rural India. American Political Science Review.
Notes: data/conjoint/heinze_2025.R. 2x2 factorial vignette, one vignette per respondent. attr_gender/attr_caste store the displayed category words; first name and surname moved with them (source stores only the names; mapping from the article). Three 0/1 judgements coded as the authors' clean.R. N 2,360 vs 2,347 in the article. Authority means by condition reproduce the article.

Description: Representatives of 609 interest groups worldwide (business associations, citizen groups, labour unions; online survey) compared two proposed trade agreements in each of 2 tasks, varying whether the agreement includes provisions on services liberalisation, intellectual property, environment and labour rights; they chose one (or neither) and rated each 1-10.
Reference: Dür, A., Huber, R. A., Mateo, G., & Spilker, G. (2023). Interest group preferences towards trade agreements: Institutional design matters. Interest Groups & Advocacy, 12(1), 48-72.
Notes: data/conjoint/dur_2023.R. Respondents are organisations (one representative per group). Four Yes/No provision attributes (article Table 1). Choice allows Neither (opt-out). Question wording paraphrased from the article (not deposited). Group descriptors kept as covariates. N 609 matches the article; mean ratings by group type reproduce.

Description: Hungarian adults (online survey 2022, n = 639) chose which of two protein-product cards (tofu, cheese, eggs, milk, pork, poultry, fish, almond) was more sustainable, or no choice, in 16 fixed choice sets where the card's nutritional score, ecological score and price were each shown or not.
Reference: Tompa, O., Kiss, A., Lakner, Z., Unger-Plasek, B., & Temesi, Á. (2024). Differences in perspectives on sustainability attributes of dietary protein sources between reduced animal-based dieters and nondieters. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 11, 1401.
Notes: data/conjoint/tompa_2024.R. Fixed orthogonal design, same 16 card pairs for all; 'no choice' opt-out. Score/price shown-or-not design: absent = (not shown); shown values are the product's own (not independent of product). Display order of the 16 sets undocumented. All 639 respondents kept; the article analyses 541 after exclusions. Table 3 nondieter clogit reproduces exactly.

Description: Bean farmers in north-western Nicaragua (2017 field days, n = 229) made 12 incentivized choices between two 1-lb bags of bean seed, identified only by the symbol of the blind field plot they came from (circle, square, triangle) and priced C$14-34, or neither; one choice was enforced.
Reference: Maredia, M. K., Posey, S., Reyes, B., Shupp, R., et al. (2020). Farmer willingness to pay for quality bean seeds: Data, tools and methods used in the field experiments conducted in Nicaragua, 2017 [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: data/conjoint/maredia_2020.R. Real (incentivized) choice experiment; fixed 12-pair orthogonal design shown in 4 orders (sets W-Z); task = display position in the set (verified by cross-set choice agreement). Seed symbols stand for certified (circle), QDS (square) and recycled (triangle) seed, not shown to farmers. Price has almost no effect on choice. Hypothetical choice experiment in the deposit not built (its sets cannot be decoded). Related thesis: Posey (2018), MSU.

Description: New York residents recruited on Prolific (n = 1,200) voted with real money ($15 endowment, binding group vote) on farmworker-assistance projects varying educational materials, winter clothing, emergency transportation and cost, in one of three randomized formats: a single project-vs-none vote (600), nine sequential binary votes (300), or nine sequential votes between two projects and none (300).
Reference: Vossler, C. A., & Zawojska, E. (2025). From simple to complex: A revealed preference test of discrete choice experiment designs. Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists.
Notes: data/conjoint/vossler_2025.R. Incentivized DCE; arms in trial_mechanism (single_binary, sequential_binary, sequential_trinary); binary arms have one profile per task, trinary two; 'No project' is the opt-out. Nine fixed projects, cost randomized. Level mapping from the instrument and the authors' Stata log. Prolific IDs dropped. Article DOI not found; manuscript JAERE 2025232.

Description: Candidates in Tunisia's 2018 municipal elections (Local Election Candidate Survey, n = 938) made four forced choices between two local development projects with randomized co-financing organization (local CSO, CPSCL, World Bank, GIZ, USAID), project type, supporters and municipal cost.
Reference: Blackman, A. D., Sasmaz, A., Singh, R., & Williamson, S. (2025). Anti-Americanism and foreign aid preferences among political elites: Evidence from Tunisia [Working paper]. University of Oxford.
Notes: data/conjoint/blackman_2025.R. Level text from the paper's Table 1 (English; survey language not stated). Profile position inferred from the stacked row blocks of the deposit. Attribute order randomized but not recorded. Municipality ID and Qualtrics IDs dropped. The zip also re-hosts Arab Barometer data (not used). USAID AMCE (-0.09) reproduces the paper. Publication venue/DOI not found.

Description: US MTurk workers (two waves, 2016 and 2018; n = 2,005, of whom 1,894 form the authors' analysis sample) chose between two hypothetical hospital birth scenarios of a first child in 7 paired tasks, varying the baby's sex, birth weight, season of birth and out-of-pocket cost.
Reference: Clarke, D., Oreffice, S., & Quintana-Domeque, C. (2021). On the value of birth weight. Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics, 83(5), 1130-1159.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/clarke_2021.R. All 2,005 completed responses kept; cov_main_sample = 1 marks the article's 1,894 (US IP, passed repeated education check, >= 2 minutes). Attribute order randomized once per respondent (attrpos_). cov_survey_weight is the authors' state-representativeness weight, defined for the main sample only. MTurk codes and noised IP coordinates dropped.

Description: German adults (online panel, 2021; n = 3,169) voted in a hypothetical referendum on 6 successive proposals for a levy on meat, whose justification (animal welfare or climate) and differentiation (uniform or by meat type / housing stage) were randomized between respondents and whose level rose across the 6 proposals; outcomes are a yes vote and a no vote (abstention possible).
Reference: Perino, G., & Schwickert, H. (2023). Animal welfare is a stronger determinant of public support for meat taxation than climate change mitigation in Germany. Nature Food, 4(2), 160-169.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/perino_2023.R. Level text is the German shown on the vote pages (questionnaire screenshots p.27-50), levy amounts hard-coded from those screenshots. Codebook and authors' code disagree on the vote coding; the data follow the code (1 = yes). Proposals shown in a fixed rising order. All 3,169 kept; the article trims survey time to the 5th-95th percentile.

Description: French adults (online panel, respondents of Turkish, North-African and Sub-Saharan African parentage oversampled) read 3 pairs of text vignettes of hypothetical French MPs varying name, gender, migration background, religion and a policy statement, rated each on representation, trust and capability (0-10) and chose one to vote for. 1,199 respondents.
Reference: van Oosten, S., Mügge, L., Hakhverdian, A., van der Pas, D., & Vermeulen, F. (2024). French Ethnic Minority and Muslim Attitudes, Voting, Identity and Discrimination (EMMAVID) - EMMAVID Data France [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/vanoosten_2024_fr.R. Sibling of vanoosten_2024_politicians_nl and _de. Level text is French as in the .sav labels (displayed language); 'pratique l'Islam' (Turkish, North-African profiles) and 'pratique l'islam' (others) kept as stored. Ratings kept as .sav codes 1-11 (= displayed 0-10). Sub-Saharan background drawn about twice as often as the others. 182 Turkish-background profiles carry North-African first names (codebook Table A1 lumps the two lists). Education kept as codes (labels doubtful). Part 3a dropped. Reference DOI is the OSF preprint.

Description: Mexican adults (Pollfish online survey, 2021-22; n = 2,401) rated agreement with paying more taxes, with the tax type (VAT, income tax or unnamed) and the spending area (health, roads, security or unnamed) randomized in the sentence (experiment 1).
Reference: Berens, S., López García, A. I., & Maydom, B. (2024). Classrooms or crackdowns? How violence affects security policy preferences in Mexico. Studies in Comparative International Development, 61(1), 10-33.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/berens_2024.R (one of four tables from the MigCrimeMexSurvey 2021 deposit). Level text is the Spanish clause from the questionnaire; '(not shown)' = the control version without the clause. One vignette per respondent. Balanced allocation (200-201 per cell).

Description: Mexican adults (Pollfish online survey, 2021-22; n = 2,401) rated agreement with a proposal to take the military off public-security duties, with the proposing party (PAN, PRI or unnamed) and the collaborating actor (municipal authorities, private sector, citizens or unnamed) randomized (experiment 4).
Reference: Berens, S., López García, A. I., & Maydom, B. (2024). Classrooms or crackdowns? How violence affects security policy preferences in Mexico. Studies in Comparative International Development, 61(1), 10-33.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/berens_2024.R (one of four tables from the MigCrimeMexSurvey 2021 deposit). Level text is the Spanish clause from the questionnaire; '(not shown)' = the control version without the clause. One vignette per respondent. Balanced allocation (200-201 per cell).

Description: Mexican adults (Pollfish online survey, 2021-22; n = 2,401) rated agreement that reducing crime needs more security forces on the streets, with the territorial scope and an accompanying social or punitive measure randomized (experiment 5, the article's experiment).
Reference: Berens, S., López García, A. I., & Maydom, B. (2024). Classrooms or crackdowns? How violence affects security policy preferences in Mexico. Studies in Comparative International Development, 61(1), 10-33.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/berens_2024.R (one of four tables from the MigCrimeMexSurvey 2021 deposit). Level text is the Spanish clause from the questionnaire; '(not shown)' = the control version without the clause. One vignette per respondent. Balanced allocation (200-201 per cell). This is the experiment analysed in the article (2_Analysis_E5.do).

Description: Mexican adults (Pollfish online survey, 2021-22; n = 2,401) judged newly recruited municipal police officers whose gender (female or unstated) and previous background (soldiers, private security, self-defence forces, human-rights activists, return migrants or unstated) were randomized: faith that they would catch criminals and likelihood of misconduct (experiment 6).
Reference: Berens, S., López García, A. I., & Maydom, B. (2024). Classrooms or crackdowns? How violence affects security policy preferences in Mexico. Studies in Comparative International Development, 61(1), 10-33.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/berens_2024.R (one of four tables from the MigCrimeMexSurvey 2021 deposit). Level text is the Spanish clause from the questionnaire; '(not shown)' = the control version without the clause. One vignette per respondent. Balanced allocation (200-201 per cell). Gender factor: female stated vs not mentioned (no male level).

Description: Adults in Belgium (Qualtrics online panel with age, gender and education quotas, MAPLE I wave 1, Feb-Apr 2019; n = 1,543) chose between two hypothetical parties in 2 paired tasks and rated each party's vote probability (0-10); parties varied in leader's ministerial experience, ideology, economic record, EU-integration stance, immigration stance and priority on corruption.
Reference: Lobo, M. C., Pannico, R., Heyne, L., Silva, T., Kartalis, Y., & Nina, S. R. (2023). MAPLE I Study – Public Opinion Panel Survey on European Attitudes and Political Behaviour, 2019 [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lobo_2023.R (one of six country tables from the same MAPLE I wave-1 conjoint: Belgium, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain). Level text is the codebook's English wording (Appendix 9); respondents saw Dutch or French (cov_language). Attribute order randomized per respondent, same in both tasks (attrpos_). cov_survey_weight = within-country rim weight. No linked article.

Description: German respondents (online survey, August 2020; 624 respondents) compared two climate-policy packages in four rounds, packages varying government support, public investment, producer standards, CO2 tax, restrictions and the proposing body (federal government, expert commission, citizens' assembly). Outcomes: forced choice and a 1-7 rating of each package.
Reference: Fesenfeld, L. P., Freudlsperger, C., Kuntze, L., & Ingold, K. (2023). Replication data for: Legitimizing climate action in democracies [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/fesenfeld_2023.R (one table per country, as the authors analyse them). Article not located (no DOI in deposit); reference is the dataset. Rating wording and anchors not deposited. Level text is English for both countries. cov_gender/cov_age_group/cov_education mapped from the deposit's German screener codebook (Descriptives_Germany_final.xlsx, from the sister descriptive survey; codes verified against App. Table 1).

Description: US respondents (online survey, December 2020; 1,350 of the 1,360 respondents) compared two climate-policy packages in four rounds, packages varying government support, public investment, producer standards, CO2 tax, restrictions and the proposing body (federal government, expert commission, citizens' assembly). Outcomes: forced choice and a 1-7 rating of each package.
Reference: Fesenfeld, L. P., Freudlsperger, C., Kuntze, L., & Ingold, K. (2023). Replication data for: Legitimizing climate action in democracies [Data set]. Harvard Dataverse.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/fesenfeld_2023.R (one table per country, as the authors analyse them). Article not located (no DOI in deposit); reference is the dataset. Rating wording and anchors not deposited. Level text is English for both countries. US gender and education keep source codes (cov_gender_code, cov_education_code: no codebook); cov_age in years. 93 single-package tasks dropped (10 respondents lost).

Description: Paired conjoint on fertility intentions: 8,330 adults aged 20-44 in Argentina, Germany, Italy and the US (May 2025) compared 5 pairs of hypothetical family scenarios varying the woman's age, children, home ownership, division of work, childcare, household income and four macro outlooks (climate, economy, politics, war); outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-10 rating of intention to have a child.
Reference: Aassve, A., et al. (2026). Parenthood decisions in uncertain times: Experimental evidence from four countries. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/aassve_2026.R. Levels are the authors' value labels (displayed wording not deposited); attr_income is the monthly amount shown, in local currency (five country-specific levels). Four countries pooled in one table (cov_country), as in the paper. Outcome wording paraphrased. Full author list not checked (cited as Aassve et al.).

Description: Italian online respondents (Qualtrics, July 2024; n = 1,174) chose which of two parties they would vote for in 8 pairs of party agendas (plus a repeat of pair 1 with sides swapped) and rated agreement with each agenda 0-10; agendas varied debt-reduction strategy (immigration, taxes, spending cuts, none), defence, civil-rights and energy policy. Outcomes: choice and rating.
Reference: Aspide, A., & DiGiuseppe, M. (2025). The mass politics of public debt, immigration, and austerity. Journal of European Public Policy, 33(7), 2010-2038.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/aspide_2025.R. Experiment 2 only (Experiment 1 is a single-factor info experiment). Italian level text as displayed; task 9 repeats task 1 with profiles swapped (trial_repeat_of). Covariates are uncodebooked codes (_code). Panel IDs dropped. N vs paper not checked (article page blocked).

Description: US adults (SSI online panel, July 2016, n=865) chose between two fictitious House candidates in 2 rounds, candidates varying anti-establishment, people-centrism and conflict statements, immigration and taxation stances and career background; vote choice plus a 0-100 feeling thermometer for each candidate.
Reference: Bakker, B. N., Schumacher, G., & Rooduijn, M. (2021). The populist appeal: Personality and antiestablishment communication. The Journal of Politics, 83(2), 589-601.
Notes: data/conjoint/bakker_2021.R. Study 2 of the deposit. Raw Qualtrics export with IP addresses, GPS coordinates, postcode/city, panel ids and free-text comments (all dropped). 13 answered tasks whose profiles were not saved dropped (865 respondents, 1,724 tasks vs 868 / 1,736 in the paper). Level text is the exact displayed text (differs slightly from the article's Table 2 paraphrases). Agreeableness and authoritarianism items kept raw for the paper's moderation analyses.

Description: 2,618 US citizens (Respondi online quota panel, December 2016) each split $10 million of disaster relief between two hypothetical disaster-hit counties in 4 tasks; counties varied economic damage, fatalities, household income, unemployment and 2012 presidential vote, with the president's party varied per task. Outcome: amount allocated (rating, $ million, 0-10).
Reference: Bechtel, M. M., & Mannino, M. (2022). Retrospection, fairness, and economic shocks: How do voters judge policy responses to natural disasters? Political Science Research and Methods, 10(2), 260-278.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bechtel_2022.R. Divide-the-dollar outcome: the two counties' ratings sum to 10 in every task. attr_president is constant within a task. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). cov_survey_weight = authors' entropy-balancing weight. IP addresses, GPS coordinates and county of residence in the deposit file were not read.

Description: Adult UK Prolific respondents (2023) compared 5 pairs of short news reports about crises under two governments, varying 9 attributes (crisis type, economic and household damage, expert warnings, prevention spending, opposition and prime-minister behaviour, speed and size of relief). 824 respondents (812 complete); three forced choices per pair: re-elect, handled better, more responsible.
Reference: Berz, J. (2026). Crises and electoral accountability: How do individual characteristics of crises affect performance and responsibility evaluations among voters? Government and Opposition, 61, e19.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/berz_2026.R. Levels are the text fragments inserted into the news report (Qualtrics F- columns), not the author's shortened plot labels. 12 break-off respondents keep their answered tasks; the article's sample is the 812 who completed all 5 tasks (matches). Prolific IDs dropped.

Description: Respondents in Bulgaria (n = 2,009) each compared 5 pairs of hypothetical EU sanction proposals against their country (framing of the accusation, consequence, number of supporting EU states, domestic opposition stance, government response procedure, trigger), choosing one and rating each 1-7. Outcomes: choice and rating.
Reference: Blauberger, M., Makaradze, S., & Spilker, G. (2025). International sanctions and domestic backlash. Exploring public support towards the EU's rule of law enforcement. European Union Politics, 27(1), 60-87.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/blauberger_2025.R (one table per country: hu, pl, bg; the authors analyse countries separately). Task/profile inferred from row order (10 stacked blocks; verified one choice per pair). Level text = .dta value labels (short English labels, not the displayed national-language text). Question wording paraphrased from variable labels; article not accessible.

Description: Respondents in Hungary (n = 2,018) each compared 5 pairs of hypothetical EU sanction proposals against their country (framing of the accusation, consequence, number of supporting EU states, domestic opposition stance, government response procedure, trigger), choosing one and rating each 1-7. Reference: Blauberger, M., Makaradze, S., & Spilker, G. (2025). International sanctions and domestic backlash. Exploring public support towards the EU's rule of law enforcement. European Union Politics, 27(1), 60-87.

Question wording paraphrased from variable labels; article not accessible. Covariates are the authors' dichotomised groupings plus gender and blame attribution.

Description: Online quota-sample respondents in Germany (Lucid, May-September 2021; n = 3,050 who reached the conjoint) each read 5 pairs of text descriptions of politicians (gender plus one further social characteristic, party and constituency link, justification style, a responsiveness quote, party-vs-own voting, and a stance on one policy issue) and chose who would better represent them. Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Blumenau, J., Wolkenstein, F., & Wratil, C. (2024). Citizens' preferences for multidimensional representation. Perspectives on Politics, 23(2), 588-610.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/blumenau_2024.R (one table per country: uk, us, de). Text vignettes: six sentences per politician, sentence order random per respondent (attrpos_). Gender and the second characteristic are split from one sentence; party and constituency phrase from another. The policy issue is the same for both politicians of a pair. Unequal level probabilities (ethnicity, sexuality). The article's sample excludes attention-check failures and speeders (cov_attention_pass, cov_duration_sec): all respondents kept here. DE personalization wording follows the politician's gender (seiner/ihrer) for 2 of 6 levels. Lucid/panel IDs, postcodes and free text dropped.

Description: Online quota-sample respondents in United Kingdom (Lucid, May-September 2021; n = 3,102 who reached the conjoint) each read 5 pairs of text descriptions of politicians (gender plus one further social characteristic, party and constituency link, justification style, a responsiveness quote, party-vs-own voting, and a stance on one policy issue) and chose who would better represent them. Reference: Blumenau, J., Wolkenstein, F., & Wratil, C. (2024). Citizens' preferences for multidimensional representation. Perspectives on Politics, 23(2), 588-610.

Description: Brazilian online respondents compared pairs of municipalities described by the mayor's party (PT/PSDB), a federal-municipal daycare agreement, and who runs a homeless shelter (NGO or city hall, with or without federal funds); 1,103 respondents, up to 4 tasks, mayor choice plus 7-point ratings of each mayor and of the federal government.
Reference: Bueno, N. S. (2017). Bypassing the enemy: Distributive politics, credit claiming, and nonstate organizations in Brazil. Comparative Political Studies, 51(3), 304-340.
Notes: data/conjoint/bueno_2017.R. Portuguese level text as stored; attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). rating_federal is asked once per task about the federal government and repeated on both profile rows. The deposit's separate 2x2 credit/blame vignette is not included. N matches the supplement (1,103 respondents, 8,602 rows).

Description: Recruiters in Germany, Norway, Poland and Romania (2024-2025, n=2,506) each rated 6 vignettes of fictional job candidates varying referral, gender, nationality (native/Ukrainian/Syrian, Nepali or Belarusian), education location, language level, partnership, parenthood and experience: 0-10 likelihood of interview and of employment, plus a final comparison of the two top-rated candidates.
Reference: Buttler, D., Imdorf, C., Bjørnshagen, V., et al. (2026). Hiring discrimination in the organisational context: A harmonized factorial survey dataset from four European countries (Germany, Norway, Poland, Romania). Scientific Data, 13, 896.
Notes: data/conjoint/buttler_2026.R. Factorial vignette survey, fixed blocked design (24 decks); one vignette per task. Level text = English codebook labels (display text in de/no/pl/ro not deposited). d2 (final pairwise comparison of the two highest-d11 candidates) kept raw as rating_final_comparison; whether code 1 is purely the respondent pick is not stated (1-coded never has lower d11). Respondent and vignette counts match the descriptor (2,506 / 15,036). Covariates as answer text from .dta labels.

Description: Partisan political donors (Bright Line Watch donor sample, Qualtrics, Feb-Apr 2019) chose between two hypothetical candidates in 10 pairs varying name (signalling race and gender), party, and six platform statements on voter-ID laws, investigations, compromise, courts, discrimination and taxes. 622 respondents (authors' analysis sample 573); binary choice.
Reference: Carey, J., Clayton, K., Helmke, G., Nyhan, B., Sanders, M., & Stokes, S. (2020). Who will defend democracy? Evaluating tradeoffs in candidate support among partisan donors and voters. Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/carey_2020_democracy.R (one of three tables: donors, March 2019 public, October 2018 public). Platform rows randomized once per respondent (attrpos_). Non-consenters and under-18s dropped; 3 respondents whose attribute levels were not saved dropped; insincere and non-US respondents kept with flags (cov_take_serious, cov_us_resident); the authors' filters give 573. Free-text comments dropped. Respondent count in the article not verified (article not read).

Description: US adults (YouGov matched sample, March 2019) chose between two hypothetical candidates in 10 pairs varying name (signalling race and gender), party, and six platform statements on voter-ID laws, investigations, compromise, courts, discrimination and taxes. 1,000 respondents; binary choice; YouGov weight included.
Reference: Carey, J., Clayton, K., Helmke, G., Nyhan, B., Sanders, M., & Stokes, S. (2020). Who will defend democracy? Evaluating tradeoffs in candidate support among partisan donors and voters. Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/carey_2020_democracy.R (one of three tables). YouGov MICH0038 'Bright Line Watch 6 - Conjoint', 12-18 March 2019. Choice question wording not in the YouGov codebook (paraphrase; the donor questionnaire uses the same design). Insincere respondents kept with cov_take_serious (the authors drop 'Most of the time'/'Always'). Attribute order not recorded. Respondent count in the article not verified.
