Description: US adults (YouGov matched sample, October 2018) chose between two hypothetical candidates in 10 pairs varying name (signalling race and gender), party, and six platform statements on voter-ID laws, investigations, compromise, courts, discrimination and taxes. 1,000 respondents; binary choice; YouGov weight included. Appendix replication sample.
Reference: Carey, J., Clayton, K., Helmke, G., Nyhan, B., Sanders, M., & Stokes, S. (2020). Who will defend democracy? Evaluating tradeoffs in candidate support among partisan donors and voters. Journal of Elections, Public Opinion and Parties.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/carey_2020_democracy.R (one of three tables). YouGov MICH0033 'Bright Line Watch 5 - Conjoint', 24-31 October 2018 (the paper's appendix sample). Choice question wording not in the YouGov codebook (paraphrase). Insincere respondents kept with cov_take_serious. Attribute order not recorded.

Description: 3,019 German panel respondents (wave 4, attention-check passers) each saw 5 screens of four Bundestag candidates, one each from Die Linke, SPD, CDU and AfD, varying experience, reason for running, chance of winning, refugee, border, pension and tax positions; they chose one candidate and rated each 1-7. Outcomes: choice and rating.
Reference: Chou, W., Dancygier, R., Egami, N., & Jamal, A. A. (2021). Competing for loyalists? How party positioning affects populist radical right voting. Comparative Political Studies, 54(12), 2226-2260.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/chou_2021.R. Four profiles per task, one per party (attr_party fixed by column; profile order = codebook party order, display order undocumented). Party-specific level sets (AfD lacks some levels) and 1-2 'likely winners' per screen: estimate within party. English attribute text from the codebook; respondents saw German. Panel pseudonyms re-keyed.

Description: Finnish respondents chose between pairs of political leaders varying in stance on media freedom, welfare spending, adoption rights and climate policy, plus gender, age and education, then said whether they would vote for the chosen leader; 2,406 respondents, 6 tasks each.
Reference: Christensen, H. S., & Saikkonen, I. (2023). Replication data: Does democratic backsliding depend on the policy issue [Data set]. OSF.
Notes: data/conjoint/christensen_2023.R. No article linked (do-file: 'Transgressions across issues'). Level text is the authors' English labels from the .dta/do-file; Finnish display text and question wording not deposited. choice_vote recodes the per-task follow-up 'would vote for selected profile'. Fixed design versions (vers_cbconjoint) kept as trial_design_version. Municipality dropped (re-identification risk).

Description: 247 political scientists (APSA members) each chose which of 2 hypothetical published studies was more ethical in up to 5 tasks; studies varied in author affiliation, author rank, outlet, conclusions, study type, location and sample size.
Reference: Costa, M., Crabtree, C., Holbein, J. B., & Landgrave, M. (2023). Is that ethical? An exploration of political scientists' views on research ethics. Research & Politics, 10(4).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/costa_2023.R. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_), in blocks; unanswered tasks dropped, so 247 of the 362 consenting respondents (353 shown the conjoint) remain. Levels as displayed; the authors' groupings of affiliations/outlets not applied.

Description: Ethiopian university students (n = 1,008 with a usable task; endline and expansion samples pooled) each chose between two hypothetical federal arrangements in up to 2 pairs, varying who hires civil servants, police structure, who decides language/history policy, and how state borders are drawn. Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Davis, B., Dow, D. A., Springman, J., & Tellez, J. F. (2026). Two dilemmas in the politics of ethnic federalism: Experimental evidence from Ethiopia. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 70(9), 1642-1669.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/davis_2026.R. Task inferred from row order (verified one choice per pair). 102 incomplete pairs dropped. cov_ethnic_violence_any is the authors' derived binary (source items not deposited). Question wording not deposited.

Description: Physicians and ECLS staff in Germany and Switzerland (2019; 510 respondents as deposited, article analyses 420 physicians) rated 5 text vignettes each of patients who might start extracorporeal life support (ECMO), varying age, circuit, costs, therapeutic goal, resources, comorbidities and neurological outcome: 1-6 agreement that ECLS should be used (own view) and would be used in their clinic.
Reference: Drewniak, D., Brandi, G., Buehler, P. K., Steiger, P., Hagenbuch, N., Stamm-Balderjahn, S., Schenk, L., Rosca, A., & Krones, T. (2022). Key factors in decision making for ECLS: A binational factorial survey. Medical Decision Making, 42(3), 313-325.
Notes: data/conjoint/drewniak_2022.R. Initiation scenario of a two-scenario factorial survey (withdrawal = drewniak_2022_ecls_stop, same respondents). Fixed blocked D-efficient design (120 vignettes, 24 decks). Vignette display order not recorded: task is not display order. Deposit holds more respondents than the article (exclusions of non-involved staff etc. not applied; cov_user, cov_work allow approximating). Level text = English translation from article Table 1.

Description: Physicians and ECLS staff in Germany and Switzerland (2019; 467 respondents as deposited, article analyses 420 physicians) rated 5 text vignettes each of patients on running extracorporeal life support (ECMO), varying age, circuit, days on ECLS, withdrawal criteria, patient condition, therapeutic goal, comorbidities and neurological outcome: 1-6 agreement that treatment should be (own view) and would be (clinic) discontinued.
Reference: Drewniak, D., Brandi, G., Buehler, P. K., Steiger, P., Hagenbuch, N., Stamm-Balderjahn, S., Schenk, L., Rosca, A., & Krones, T. (2022). Key factors in decision making for ECLS: A binational factorial survey. Medical Decision Making, 42(3), 313-325.
Notes: data/conjoint/drewniak_2022.R. Withdrawal scenario (initiation = drewniak_2022_ecls_start, same respondents). Fixed blocked D-efficient design (180 vignettes, 36 decks). Vignette display order not recorded: task is not display order. Deposit holds more respondents than the article (exclusions not applied). Level text = English translation from article Table 2.

Description: Online respondents in 16 countries (CANDOUR II, 2022) saw single government-leader profiles describing pandemic-era GDP and job growth, vaccine supplies, lockdown length, COVID deaths and vaccination rate, and said whether the leader should be re-elected and rated support 1-7; 22,180 respondents, 8 profiles each.
Reference: Duch, R., Loewen, P., Robinson, T., & Zakharov, A. (2025). Governing in the face of a global crisis: When do voters punish and reward incumbent governments? Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 122(4), e2405021122.
Notes: data/conjoint/duch_2025.R. Single-profile design (task = round, profile = 1). Authors' short labels mapped back to the English display text (SI Fig. S1 and the authors' translation targets); non-English countries saw translations. 221 Brazilian rounds with a mistranslated jobs level dropped. Country-level context, PCA indices and raw attitude batteries not kept (CSV size). Deposit N 22,180 vs article 22,147.

Description: Discrete choice experiment on collective investments in multi-apartment buildings: 1,531 Czech residents of housing cooperatives and homeowners' associations (online panel, Sept-Oct 2024) made 5 choices between two investment options varying beneficiaries, personal engagement, decision rule, change in monthly housing costs and change in property value; outcomes are the choice and a 0-100 confidence rating.
Reference: Frankowski, J., Stará, S., Bełch, W., Sokołowski, J., Mazurkiewicz, J., Nesládek, M., Prusak, A., & Vácha, T. (2026). Housing conditions, residents' attitudes and preferences towards investments in multi-apartment buildings in Poland and Czechia: ENBLOC survey and discrete choice experiment data [Data set]. Zenodo.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/frankowski_2026.R. Czech CAWI sample only: the Polish CAWI sample (4,488) has choices that are inconsistent across the attribute rows of an option (88% of tasks), and the two CAPI samples (1,503) have 7 property-value codes against 9 codebook levels; both held. Levels are the codebook's Czech labels; housing cost and property value were shown as amounts computed from the respondent's own fee/value and are stored as the percentage change. Respondent ids re-keyed.

Description: 248 adults recruited at two county fairs in Southwest Pennsylvania (July-August 2021) each chose between 2 government proposals to help fossil fuel workers and communities in 6 tasks; proposals varied in retraining program, retrained salary, retraining time, income support, benefit support, relocation support and community investment.
Reference: Gazmararian, A. F. (2024). Fossil fuel communities support climate policy coupled with just transition assistance. Energy Policy, 184, 113880.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/gazmararian_2024.R. County-fair convenience sample (tablet, a few paper surveys). Same design as gazmararian_2024_transition_national. SI Table 8.1 weight columns look swapped (col 2 'weighted' equals the unweighted fit). ResponseIds, paper ids, dates and free text dropped.

Description: 1,001 US adults (Lucid, February-March 2023) each chose between 2 government proposals to help fossil fuel workers and communities in 5 tasks; proposals varied in retraining program, retrained salary, retraining time, income support, benefit support, relocation support and community investment.
Reference: Gazmararian, A. F. (2024). Fossil fuel communities support climate policy coupled with just transition assistance. Energy Policy, 184, 113880.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/gazmararian_2024.R. National Lucid sample with census quotas; attention check was a screener. Same design as gazmararian_2024_transition_fair. ZIP codes, Lucid rid and ResponseIds dropped.

Description: German online respondents in Saxony, Thuringia and Western Germany (Aug-Sep 2024) chose between and rated two hypothetical CDU candidates in 3 rounds, varying age, gender, political experience, positions on refugee immigration, inequality and Ukraine, and willingness to cooperate with the far-right AfD. 2,773 respondents; binary choice and a -5..+5 thermometer.
Reference: Gross, M., Juen, C.-M., & Stecker, C. (2026). The cordon dilemma: How voters evaluate cooperation with the far-right in parliament. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/gross_2026.R. Levels are the German labels stored in the deposit; the authors' Table 1 renders some as longer English sentences, so the screen may have shown fuller text. Three regional samples pooled as in the paper (cov_survey_region). 45 unanswered rounds (coded 0/0 with no ratings in the source) dropped. Question wording not deposited (paraphrase). Panel member id (m) dropped. Respondent count in the article not verified.

Description: Bihar (India) voters chose between pairs of hypothetical MLA candidates varying in gender, caste/religion (surname), campaign appeal and, in two pairs, party (BJP/RJD); 1,999 respondents, 4 pairs each, binary vote choice.
Reference: Hankla, C. R., Banerjee, S., Thomas, A., & Banerjee, A. (2022). Electing women in ethnically divided societies: Candidates, campaigns, and intersectionality in Bihar, India. Comparative Political Studies, 56(9), 1433-1469.
Notes: data/conjoint/hankla_2022.R. Level text mapped from the authors' dummies via the survey instrument (Appendices pp. 9-14); caste shown only by surname (Ansari Muslim, Pandey forward, Sahu OBC, Paswan SC). Task and profile inferred from the file's 8-block layout; display order of tasks and sides not documented. Reproduces Appendix Table 1 Model 1 coefficients exactly.

Description: Paired conjoint: 2,211 German adults (TGM panel, December 2024) made 7 choices between refugee-policy packages varying admission policy (third-country transfer and resettlement), refugee selection criteria, partner-country conditions and welfare access, and rated each package 1-7; respondents had first been assigned one of three framing primes.
Reference: Hillenbrand, T. (2025). Reforms welcome? Evidence on the nature of asylum backlash and orderly admissions as a remedy (UNU-MERIT Working Paper 2025-026). UNU-MERIT.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hillenbrand_2025.R. Level text is the working paper's English translation (Table 3) of the German levels, matched via the author's recode. Attribute order randomized per respondent, attrpos_* from the recorded AttributeOrder. Prime arm in trial_prime; cov_attention_pass marks the ~2/3 the paper analyses. Data deposit is Chapter 4 of the author's doctoral thesis.

Description: 4,000 Japanese adults (Lucid, January 2024) each rated 4 factorial vignettes about a hypothetical 25-year-old rejected for a job or snubbed in a board game club, with target attribute (gender, nationality, sexuality, university), advantaged/disadvantaged group and mechanism randomized; outcome is a 1-6 rating of how likely the scenario is discriminatory.
Reference: Igarashi, A., Kano, Y., & Miwa, H. (2025). ChatGPT versus humans in judging discriminatory scenarios: Experimental evidence from a Japanese context. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 12, 1776.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/igarashi_2025.R. Human survey only (ChatGPT output files not used). Attribute text is the article's English translation (Tables 1-2) of the phrases inserted into Japanese vignettes, rebuilt from the authors' scenario code; free-text reasons dropped.

Description: Factorial vignette (4x3x3x3, one vignette per respondent): 2,045 German adults (Bilendi & respondi panel, June 2022) read a terrorist-attack scenario varying the attackers' motivation, personal threat, the party proposing a surveillance policy and whether the policy targets everyone or suspects; outcomes are support for the policy and four further 1-10 ratings.
Reference: Jäger, F. (2023). Security vs. civil liberties: How citizens cope with threat, restriction, and ideology. Frontiers in Political Science, 4, 1006711.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/jager_2023.R. Levels are the author's short factor labels (German vignette wording not deposited); control levels ('not specified or mentioned') stored as (not shown). Outcome wording from the OSF preregistration (paraphrase). Reproduces the article's AMCEs exactly.

Description: Straight US respondents from a Qualtrics opt-in panel (2019-20) each read one fictitious news story about a gay teacher fired by a Christian school, with six randomized factors (relationship size and exclusivity, teacher gender, race/ethnicity via name, relationship length, school level). 3,541 respondents; three 0-1 outcomes: support for the teacher's case, feeling similar to the teacher, support for LGB job protections.
Reference: Jones, P. E. (2022). Respectability politics and straight support for LGB rights. Political Research Quarterly, 75(4), 935-949.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/jones_2022.R. Study 2 only (Study 1 manipulates one factor). Factorial vignette, one story per respondent (task = profile = 1). Levels are the author's factor labels; the displayed story template is in the script header (gender and race were shown through first name/surname and pronouns). Outcomes are deposited already recoded to 0-1 by the author (higher = more support) and kept so. Author's 3-item LGB-rights index dropped. Table A9 marginal means and the two-person AMCE (0.05) reproduce.

Description: Online respondents in China (SSI, fall 2017; 1,047 business elites and nonelites, 532 in the authors' screened sample) chose between six pairs of tax-reform proposals varying tax type, tax rate, the government services funded and the institutional political influence granted.
Reference: Kao, J. C., Lü, X., & Queralt, D. (2024). Do gains in political representation sweeten tax reform in China? It depends on who you ask. Political Science Research and Methods, 12(1), 146-165.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kao_2024.R. Levels are the .dta value labels (authors' short English labels; respondents saw Chinese). Choice wording not deposited (paraphrase). All respondents with choices kept; the article's screened sample is cov_elite_t10 non-missing (270 elites, 262 nonelites with choices). Attribute order randomized but not recorded. The Taiwan file (shadow case) is not built: no task/profile columns and row order does not pair profiles. Figure 2 elite coefficients reproduce exactly from log_file.txt.

Description: US online respondents (Nov 2022) chose between pairs of border-security policies varying in implementing agency, strategy, budget change and effects on illegal immigration, human trafficking, drug trafficking and terrorism; 776 respondents, 5 tasks each.
Reference: Kenwick, M. R., & Maxey, S. (2024). Explaining public demands for border militarization. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 69(6), 1005-1032.
Notes: data/conjoint/kenwick_2024.R. Survey 1 of 2 (the other is kenwick_2024_border_treatments). Level text from the Qualtrics display strings; choice wording not in deposit; article Ns not checked (paywalled).

Description: US online respondents (Dec 2022) read one of four status-threat vignettes (trial_arm) and then chose between pairs of border-security policies varying in agency, strategy, budget and effects on immigration, trafficking and terrorism; 3,228 respondents, up to 5 tasks.
Reference: Kenwick, M. R., & Maxey, S. (2024). Explaining public demands for border militarization. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 69(6), 1005-1032.
Notes: data/conjoint/kenwick_2024.R. Survey 2 of 2; free-text answers in the deposit not included. Level text from the Qualtrics display strings; choice wording not in deposit; article Ns not checked (paywalled).

Description: South African respondents (n=1,591) compared two hypothetical service-delivery protests (size, grievance, who is blamed, tactics, duration, police response) in 3 tasks, choosing for each pair the protest they sympathize with more, whose demands they support, that is more of a public disorder, and whose protesters are more deserving.
Reference: Koob, S. A., & Justesen, M. K. (2026). Fighting for a better life: Protests and public opinion in South Africa. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: data/conjoint/koob_2026.R. Four forced-choice outcomes on the same tasks (authors' four outcome frames merged; rows identical). Exact question wording not deposited; outcome names are the authors' labels. Fixed attribute order (recorded positions constant). Covariates Q3.1 and race (Q3.2) kept as unlabelled codes; cov_vignette_arm = arm of the paper's earlier vignette experiment. Article not read (paywalled): respondent count not checked against it; descriptive means agree with the abstract (peaceful tactics most sympathy, riots most disorder).

Description: Paired conjoint: 2,007 Greek adults (Cint/Qualtrics) chose between two hypothetical immigrants in each of 5 tasks; profiles varied gender and skin tone (apparently via photo), region of origin, occupation, language skills, religion, marital status and residence, with levels in Greek.
Reference: Kyrkopoulou, E., & Sambanis, N. (2026). O Xenos: Racial difference, colorism, and attitudes toward immigrants in Greece. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kyrkopoulou_2026.R (paper's Study 2; Study 1 photo thermometer not built). Greek levels kept as exported, gendered forms separate; attr_gender/attr_skin are English codes most likely conveyed by a photo (inferred). Question wording not deposited. Observed restriction: very good Greek never with 'in home country'.

Description: US MTurk respondents (2021; 1,458, of whom 1,249 form the authors' quota sample) chose four times between two hypothetical societies varying bottom-20%, middle-60% and top-20% incomes and upward income mobility, under a 'distant society' or 'nearby society' framing.
Reference: Lara E., B., & Shores, K. A. (2024). Measuring preferences for income equality and income mobility. Review of Economics and Statistics, 106(6), 1542-1557.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lara_2024.R. Built from the full-sample file (superset); cov_preferred_sample marks the article's 1,249 (matched by response signature, the files use different ids); cov_survey_weight = full-sample raked weight, cov_weight_preferred = main-analysis weight. Source society labels are swapped relative to the README (the 'socB' columns hold Society A); choice pairing is certain, left/right position inferred. Level text in the format of the article's Table 1; displayed average income and 90/10 ratio (computed) not stored; attribute order randomized per respondent but not recorded; choice wording not deposited. Article Table 3 MRS reproduce to rounding (2.738/1.224 vs 2.744/1.228). Adaptive questionnaire not included.

Description: US MTurk respondents (spring 2019, second wave of a panel; 1,233 respondents) compared five pairs of hypothetical cyberattacks varying target, damage, deaths, perpetrator type and origin, purpose, intelligence-community confidence, expert agreement and a policymaker's reaction. Outcomes per scenario: 0-100 confidence in the attribution, 0-100 severity, and support (1/0) for six foreign-policy responses or six criminal sentences.
Reference: Leal, M., & Musgrave, P. (2022). Cheerleading in cyberspace: How the American public judges attribution claims for cyberattacks. Foreign Policy Analysis, 18(2), orac003.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/leal_2022.R. Attribute text from the raw anonymized export (F-task-profile fields), linked to the authors' analysis file by reproducing their caseid (verified on every level). No choice between scenarios was asked: all outcomes are ratings. Support items follow display logic: foreign-policy measures only when the perpetrator is foreign, sentences only when from 'the United States' (NA otherwise). Terrorist/government-agency origins restricted (observed). The CCES 2018 one-factor experiment in the deposit is not a conjoint and is not built. Appendix confidence model (n = 12,290) reproduces exactly.

Description: 204 members of the Hong Kong People Representative Panel (probability) each compared 5 pairs of highly-skilled immigration schemes varying eligibility, change of employment, nationality, language requirement, welfare entitlement, tax and quota; forced choice plus a 0-10 rating of each scheme.
Reference: Lee, S.-y. (2025). Procedure matters: The distinct attitudinal feedback effects of immigration policy. Political Behavior, 47(1), 191-215.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lee_2024.R. Hong Kong probability panel of survey IMMPOLICY21 (the other panel is a separate table). Attribute text in Chinese as displayed; profile inferred from row order; rating labelled 1-10 in the dictionary but stored 0-10; article not read, so N and question wording unverified.

Description: 1,432 members of the Hong Kong People Volunteer Panel (non-probability) each compared 5 pairs of highly-skilled immigration schemes varying eligibility, change of employment, nationality, language requirement, welfare entitlement, tax and quota; forced choice plus a 0-10 rating of each scheme.
Reference: Lee, S.-y. (2025). Procedure matters: The distinct attitudinal feedback effects of immigration policy. Political Behavior, 47(1), 191-215.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lee_2024.R. Hong Kong volunteer (non-probability) panel of survey IMMPOLICY21 (the other panel is a separate table). Attribute text in Chinese as displayed; profile inferred from row order; rating labelled 1-10 in the dictionary but stored 0-10; article not read, so N and question wording unverified.

Description: Conjoint among 573 US local elected officials, who rated two hypothetical pieces of constituent feedback on each of three local issues (park, retail development, school tax), varying mode (office visit vs social media), number of constituents, who they were, the type of argument and the position; outcomes are 1-4 ratings of how informative and how influential each message is.
Reference: Lee, N. R., Chen, K., Marble, W., & Bram, C. (2025). Voice and value: How elected officials evaluate online and offline constituent feedback. Public Opinion Quarterly, 89(1), 31-48.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lee_2025.R. task = issue (park, dev, tax); display order of issues not deposited; position fixed within an issue; constituent and argument lists are issue-specific. Question wording paraphrased (article closed, instrument not deposited). Officials without saved attributes (149) dropped; county/state/PersonID dropped.

Description: Paired city conjoint: 1,164 Mexican-born immigrants in the US (online, English or Spanish) chose between 4 pairs of destination cities varying jobs, rent, social network, share Mexican, local deportation policy, immigrant healthcare access and community type; also ten 0/1 judgements of each city (five per randomized question version).
Reference: Lueders, H. (2025). Local immigration policies shape immigrants' relocation preferences regardless of immigration status. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lueders_2025.R (pull experiment only; the push experiment is a single-factor vignette). Task/profile from city letters A-H (pairs A/B..G/H). Levels are the deposit's factor labels (English; Spanish text not deposited). Question wording paraphrased (article closed, instrument not deposited). Zip-code latitude/longitude dropped.

Description: Online respondents in New Zealand (Cint, fall 2018; 1,285 respondents) chose between six pairs of hypothetical candidates of their preferred party, varying sexual orientation, gender (incl. transgender), race, religion, age, health, education and political experience, and rated each candidate 1-7.
Reference: Magni, G., & Reynolds, A. (2021). Voter preferences and the political underrepresentation of minority groups: Lesbian, gay, and transgender candidates in advanced democracies. Journal of Politics, 83(4), 1199-1215.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/magni_2021.R (one table per country, as the authors report them). Task and profile rebuilt from row order and the choice columns (verified); attribute order randomized per task and recorded (attrpos_). Rating wording/anchors not deposited. Mechanism items (more liberal/left, neighbor, electability) not kept: the meaning of their 0 code is undocumented. 38 tasks without a usable choice dropped. Article AMCEs reproduce (gay -0.033, transgender -0.085). The NZ file has six tasks per respondent; the article says five.

Description: Online respondents in the United Kingdom (Cint, fall 2018; 1,120 respondents) chose between five pairs of hypothetical candidates of their preferred party, varying sexual orientation, gender (incl. transgender), race, religion, age, health, education and political experience, and rated each candidate 1-7.
Reference: Magni, G., & Reynolds, A. (2021). Voter preferences and the political underrepresentation of minority groups: Lesbian, gay, and transgender candidates in advanced democracies. Journal of Politics, 83(4), 1199-1215.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/magni_2021.R (one table per country, as the authors report them). Task and profile rebuilt from row order and the choice columns (verified); attribute order randomized per task and recorded (attrpos_). Rating wording/anchors not deposited. Mechanism items (more liberal/left, neighbor, electability) not kept: the meaning of their 0 code is undocumented. 63 (incl. 2 with scrambled level text) tasks without a usable choice dropped. Article AMCEs reproduce (gay -0.046, transgender -0.107).

Description: Online respondents in the United States (Cint, fall 2018; 1,827 respondents) chose between five pairs of hypothetical candidates of their preferred party, varying sexual orientation, gender (incl. transgender), race, religion, age, health, education and political experience, and rated each candidate 1-7.
Reference: Magni, G., & Reynolds, A. (2021). Voter preferences and the political underrepresentation of minority groups: Lesbian, gay, and transgender candidates in advanced democracies. Journal of Politics, 83(4), 1199-1215.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/magni_2021.R (one table per country, as the authors report them). Task and profile rebuilt from row order and the choice columns (verified); attribute order randomized per task and recorded (attrpos_). Rating wording/anchors not deposited. Mechanism items (more liberal/left, neighbor, electability) not kept: the meaning of their 0 code is undocumented. 64 tasks without a usable choice dropped. Article AMCEs reproduce (gay -0.067, transgender -0.110).

Description: Women who had recently given birth in Naivasha Sub-County, Kenya (466 respondents, enumerator-administered) chose between two hypothetical delivery facilities varying quality of care, staff attitude, cost, equipment, distance and referral services, or home delivery (opt-out), in 16 choice sets.
Reference: Oluoch-Aridi, J., Adam, M. B., Wafula, F., & Kokwaro, G. (2020). Understanding what women want: Eliciting preference for delivery health facility in a rural subcounty in Kenya, a discrete choice experiment. BMJ Open, 10(12), e038865.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/oluocharidi_2020.R. DCE; opt-out (home delivery) has no attributes, so it is not a profile (both profiles 0 in 794 tasks). Level text from the article's sample choice card (Table 2); the deposit holds dummy pairs. Article says one block of 8 sets per respondent, but the deposit has 16 sets for everyone and several design versions; kept as deposited. Several covariates do not match the Readme codings and keep codes (_code). Conditional logit with an opt-out constant gives coefficients close to the article's (attitude 1.18, equipment 1.08, quality 0.80 vs 1.184, 1.073, 0.826).

Description: Online respondents in Spain and Portugal (Sept-Oct 2019) chose among two hypothetical conservation programs and a no-program status quo in 4 choice sets, varying the change in numbers of vulnerable, endangered and critically endangered waterbird species in SW Iberian coastal salt marshes and a one-time income-tax payment. 979 respondents; choice among three alternatives.
Reference: Oviedo, J. L., Campos, P., Caparrós, A., Muñoz Arroyo, G., & De la Cruz, A. (2026). Integrating threatened biodiversity in monetary ecosystem accounting: Choice experiments and simulated exchange values. Environmental and Resource Economics, 89(8).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/oviedo_2026.R. DCE; the NO PROGRAM status quo shows fixed outcomes and is profile 3. Species levels are rebuilt from the coded change vs the status quo using the English questionnaire's cell template; respondents presumably saw Spanish or Portuguese. Tax amounts stored as coded (presumably euros; displayed format unknown). Fixed blocked design (30 distinct profiles). No respondent covariates other than country deposited. Article DOI from a web search; article not read.

Description: 315 family physicians and physician assistants in Vietnam each answered 9 choice cards between two hypothetical jobs varying in income change, promotion timing, urban/rural location and chance of opening a private clinic; a forced A/B preference and a real-world choice among A, B and their current job.
Reference: Pham, C. A. T., Le, N. Q. T., & Kim, D. (2026). What drives family physicians to rural practice? A discrete choice experiment in Vietnam. Health Policy OPEN, 11, 100175.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/pham_2026.R. Fixed blocked design (2 blocks x 10 cards); the repeated reliability card is excluded in the deposit, so task (original position 1-10) skips one position per respondent. The current-job alternative had no displayed attributes and is the opt-out of choice_final. Attribute text is the English line of the bilingual Vietnamese/English cards.

Description: Licensed psychotherapists in Germany (DocCheck panel, 2020) chose between pairs of blended-care application scenarios varying in recommendation source, effectiveness of the online component, online vs face-to-face time split and reimbursement; 200 respondents, 16 forced choices each (DCE).
Reference: Phillips, E. A., Himmler, S., & Schreyögg, J. (2022). Preferences of psychotherapists for blended care in Germany: A discrete choice experiment. BMC Psychiatry, 22, 112.
Notes: data/conjoint/phillips_2022.R. Fixed Bayesian D-efficient design in blocks (trial_block: block 1 = design before a programming change, 37 respondents; blocks 2-3 = final design). German option text from designmain.xlsx; typo 'von 10 von Klienten' normalized. Free-text answers dropped. N, female share (43%) and mean age (48) match the article.

Description: US online respondents (August 2023) chose between two hypothetical Medicare-based health-insurance programs in 9 pairs, varying the transition from private insurance, who benefits most, who bears the tax burden, and total cost. 1,638 respondents; forced binary choice.
Reference: Qi, H. (2025). Understanding public attitudes toward redistribution: Analysis by ideological subgroups. Public Opinion Quarterly.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/qi_2025.R. Levels are the author's Stata value labels (short forms). Cost: value labels say $2/$3/$4/$6 trillion but the author's figure labels say $2.4/$3.2/$4.3/$6.2 trillion per year; the displayed amounts are unresolved. Task and profile inferred from the profile identifier (pairs verified: one chosen per pair). IP addresses dropped. The log's liberal-subgroup AMCEs (N = 7,308) reproduce exactly.

Description: 1,996 US adults (online survey, June 2022) each chose between two hypothetical social welfare programs in 8 tasks; programs varied the program described (SSI, WIC, housing assistance), the tax source, the level of government levying the tax, the progressivity of the tax burden and the annual cost. Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Qi, H., & Dorssom, E. I. (2026). Tax burden, tax types, and public support for social welfare programs. American Politics Research, 54(5), 638-651.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/qi_2026.R. Restriction: Properties tax source only with State and local. Program descriptions shown only as 'SSI/WIC/HA description' labels. Screener pass flags kept (paper's main analyses use screener_count >= 2). IP addresses and ResponseIds dropped. Question wording not deposited.

Description: Online respondents in the UK, the US and Germany (Qualtrics, 2019; 16,808 respondents, 9,317 passing the authors' checks) read up to two vignettes (hybrid-car tax cut, sugar restrictions) about a legislative decision after an interest-group consultation, randomizing group representation, whose positions the decision matched, and public support. Outcomes: six 0-4 agreement items on the legitimacy of the process and decision.
Reference: Rasmussen, A., & Reher, S. (2023). (Inequality in) interest group involvement and the legitimacy of policy making. British Journal of Political Science, 53(1), 45-64.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/rasmussen_2023.R. Factorial vignette, one profile per task; task = position in the randomized issue order, issue in trial_issue. Levels are the codebook's labels (vignette wording not deposited; German respondents saw German text). Countries pooled as in the authors' models (cov_country). Respondents failing the attention/manipulation checks are kept with flags (authors drop them in main models). 5,900 source rows with no outcome omitted. Paper N 9,357 after checks vs 9,317 here. Table 1 model 1 coefficients (None -0.947 etc.) reproduce.

Description: Adults in Germany, France, Italy and the United Kingdom chose between pairs of strategies to end the war in Ukraine varying in casualties, destruction, own-country aid costs, nuclear risk, territorial cessions and Ukrainian self-determination; 8,008 respondents (YouGov, 2023), 4 tasks each.
Reference: Rudolph, L., Haggerty, F., & Thurner, P. W. (2026). Examining public support for Ukraine's defense against autocratic aggression. Nature Communications, 17.
Notes: data/conjoint/rudolph_2026_western.R. US respondents (2,003) omitted: same YouGov 2023 survey and design as rudolph_2026_ukraine_support (US, POQ). Authors' English level labels; displays were in German/French/Italian/English. The 1-7 strategy rating is omitted (scale-endpoint alignment undocumented in this deposit). Postcode in the master file dropped.

Description: 923 Swiss residents (Bilendi online panel, May 2025) chose between 2 natural-hazard adaptation cost-sharing policies in 6 tasks (who bears the costs, exemptions, which municipalities are protected) and rated each option's acceptability 1-6; attribute text as displayed in German, French, Italian or English.
Reference: Schick, V., Metz, F., Joon, K., Hanger-Kopp, S., & Lieberherr, E. (2026). Distributive preferences in natural hazard adaptation [Data set]. Zenodo.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/schick_2026.R. Attribute levels stored as displayed in the respondent's survey language (cov_language); task 6 repeats task 1 with options swapped (trial_repeat_of). File has 923 respondents but README says final n = 891 (unresolved). Covariates are the authors' collapsed recodes.

Description: Mexican respondents (Study 2, n=1,949) read 4 vignettes each about a victim of violence varying the nature of violence, perpetrator, crime and the victim's occupation, nationality, ethnicity and gender, then decided whether and how much to donate and rated the victim (feeling thermometer, social distance, compassion, helping norms).
Reference: Skigin, N. (2023). Prosocial behavior amid violence: The deservingness heuristic and solidarity with victims. Political Psychology.
Notes: data/conjoint/skigin_2023.R. Study 2 only (Study 1 is a single-factor vignette study). Single-profile tasks; choice = donated (yes/no, opt-out). No question wording or scale anchors deposited (article not read): outcome meanings from the author's variable names. Level text = author's English labels. 8 duplicated panel ids deduplicated, 1 id with two different sessions dropped. Task = grp (g1-g4), display order not documented.

Description: Private forest owners in Denmark (1,716) and Finland (1,631) made 9 choices each between a management-based and a results-based biodiversity contract (objective, compensation per ha, payment threshold, payment schedule, measuring and reporting) or neither.
Reference: Süring, C., & Lundhede, T. (2025). Private forest owner preferences for action- and result-based biodiversity restoration contracts – A discrete choice experiment in Denmark and Finland. Forest Policy and Economics.
Notes: data/conjoint/suring_2025.R. Labelled DCE with opt-out (neither); profile 1 = management-based, 2 = results-based. Objectives come in fixed pairs. Compensation shown in DKK (Denmark) and EUR (Finland; file stores DKK at 7.45, converted back). Task inferred from row order. Danish pilots and unavailable tasks dropped; Danish N 1,716 vs 1,795 in the Zenodo description (gap unexplained). Free-text fields dropped (some identifying detail). ha_enroll follow-up not kept. Article not read (repository bot check).

Description: Paired candidate conjoint: 2,550 US online respondents (2023) made 7 choices between two candidates, each shown with five issue positions drawn from a pool of 27 issues and an ideology label (eight labels or none), in a general-election or a Democratic/Republican primary arm; outcome is a 4-point A-vs-B preference stored as choice plus the raw code.
Reference: Trexler, A., & Johnston, C. D. (2025). An ideology by any other name. Political Behavior, 47(1), 385-409.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/trexler_2025.R (Study 2 of the deposit; Study 1 is not a conjoint). One attr_ column per issue (displayed sentence or (not shown)) with attrpos_ = its row 1-5. Empty ideology label coded (not shown) by inference from the authors' code. Level shares differ strongly by arm (primary sets favour the party's labels and positions): condition on trial_election x trial_embed_pid. Keeps all 2,550 who answered; the paper analyses 2,433 after quality filters. Zip codes and free text dropped.

Description: Paired conjoint in Chile: 2,145 adults (online quota sample, 2024) chose between two hypothetical news outlets in 3 tasks, each described by seven generative-AI policies (journalistic tasks, visual and textual content creation, topics, personalization, human oversight, disclosure); outcomes are which outlet is more credible and which they would pick to stay informed.
Reference: Valenzuela, S., Bachmann, I., Borah, P., & Solís Valdés, N. (2026). The effects of generative AI in news on media credibility and selectivity: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in Chile. Digital Journalism.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/valenzuela_2026.R. Level text (Spanish, as shown) and per-respondent attribute order come from the randomizer's JSON (G012_01), checked against the coded attribute columns. Uniform levels, no restrictions except no identical profiles within a task. Panel reference hash, comuna and open text dropped.

Description: Dutch citizens in municipalities over 100,000 (Study 3, n=650) rated two hypothetical neighbourhood participatory budgets per task (who can submit, which projects, municipal support, who picks the winner, final cost overrun of the winning project); 6 pairs each, 1-7 approval rating.
Reference: van der Does, R., & Kantorowicz, J. (2021). Why do citizens (not) support democratic innovations? The role of instrumental motivations in support for participatory budgeting. Research & Politics, 8(2).
Notes: data/conjoint/vanderdoes_2021.R. Study 3 of the deposit. The randomized winning-project attribute is not deposited (only the authors' respondent-derived favorability, dropped). Forced choice not deposited: rating only. Attribute text = authors' English labels. Article's 50%-overrun AMCE (about -0.4) reproduced (-0.43).

Description: Dutch citizens in municipalities over 100,000 (Study 2, n=538) rated two hypothetical neighbourhood participatory budgets per task (who can submit, which projects, municipal support, who picks the winner, and how far from home the respondent's own top-ranked project would be built); 6 pairs each, 1-7 approval rating.
Reference: van der Does, R., & Kantorowicz, J. (2021). Why do citizens (not) support democratic innovations? The role of instrumental motivations in support for participatory budgeting. Research & Politics, 8(2).
Notes: data/conjoint/vanderdoes_2021.R. Study 2 of the deposit. The winning project shown was the respondent's own top-ranked project in both budgets (constant). Forced choice not deposited: rating only. Attribute text = authors' English labels. Study 1 of this deposit is a subset of vanderdoes_2022_participatory_budgeting and not built. Article's location AMCEs (four streets away negative, about -0.2) reproduced in direction and size.

Description: Mexican adults from a Netquest online panel (March-May 2020) chose between two hypothetical candidates in 2 tasks varying party, security-policy proposal, previous experience and gender. 2,317 respondents with at least one answered task; binary choice.
Reference: Ventura, T., Ley, S., & Cantú, F. (2024). Voting for law and order: Evidence from a survey experiment in Mexico. Comparative Political Studies, 57(2), 551-583.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ventura_2024.R. Spanish level text from the Qualtrics export; attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Question wording not deposited (paraphrase). No-answer tasks (-999) dropped as in the authors' cleaning. IP address, GPS coordinates, Netquest respondent URLs and panel ids dropped. A tweet-sharing experiment in the same file stores its attributes only as image URLs and is not built. Respondent count in the paper not verified (article paywalled).

Description: Discrete choice experiment: 1,571 residents of the Sapporo metropolitan area (online panel, December 2023) made 8 choices between two urban-green-space visits or no visit, with visits varying maximum temperature, humidity, water-play facilities, indoor cooling facilities and travel time.
Reference: Wang, J., Mameno, K., Owake, T., Aikoh, T., & Shoji, Y. (2026). Extreme heat and humidity reduce the recreational value of urban green spaces. Communications Earth & Environment.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/wang_2026.R. Fixed blocked Ngene design (6 versions x 8 sets, trial_version); opt-out 'no UGS visit' is not a profile. Level text rebuilt from numeric quantities per the article (Japanese card wording and question not deposited). Reproduces the authors' CLOGIT exactly. Authors' exclusion flags kept as cov_reject_1..3; article analyses 1,325 (code: 1,365 / 1,003).

Description: 1,038 authors who had published in conservation journals (worldwide online survey) each made 12 choices among three hypothetical journals varying in scope, open access, impact factor, editorial support, peer-review model, society affiliation and publication cost, or chose none (discrete choice experiment). Outcome: choice, with opt-out.
Reference: Yoh, N., Holle, M. J. M., Willis, J., Rudd, L. F., Fraser, I. M., & Veríssimo, D. (2024). Understanding author choices in the current conservation publishing landscape. Conservation Biology, 39(2), e14369.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/yoh_2024.R. Fixed Ngene D-efficient design, same 12 cards for everyone; task = card number, not presentation order (not recorded). Level text as stored in the deposit (CamelCase short words), except 'No impact factor' and 'Free' from the paper. 91 skipped sets dropped.

Description: Residents of Nordland, Troms and Finnmark (Norway; electronic survey, n = 517, the deposited with-jobs half of a split sample) chose among the current-regulation scenario and two stricter-regulation scenarios on 8 cards varying coastal landscape (aquaculture/fishing-tourism facilities), new jobs, beach waste, recreational catch and household tax; outcome is the preferred scenario.
Reference: Aanesen, M., Falk-Andersson, J., Vondolia, G. K., Borch, T., Navrud, S., & Tinch, D. (2018). Valuing coastal recreation and the visual intrusion from commercial activities in Arctic Norway. Ocean & Coastal Management, 153, 157-167.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/aanesen_2018.R. Only the with-jobs split sample is deposited (the without-jobs file the ReadMe describes is absent). Levels coded per the Variable Explanation, shown in the questionnaire's Norwegian card wording; the questionnaire's printed cards do not match the data's card combinations (probably another version), so level text rests on the codebook. 81 tasks without a recorded choice and 1 with two choices dropped.

Description: Paired conjoint on family reunification: 4,119 adults in Germany, Italy and Sweden (online, Feb-Mar 2024) chose which of two fictitious resident family members should be allowed to bring a family member, in 6 pairs varying migration background, language, legal status, work, economic resources, gender, religion and religiosity, and rated each 1-7.
Reference: Ahlén, A., Borevi, K., Gschwind, L., Hultin Rosenberg, J., & Wejryd, J. (2026). Universalist attitudes to family migration in Germany, Italy and Sweden: A new 'opinion-policy gap'. European Union Politics.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ahlen_2026.R (one of two tables). Levels are English value labels of the authors' recodes (screen text in German/Italian/Swedish not deposited). Wording paraphrased (article not accessible). Incoming family member's origin fixed per respondent (trial_incoming_origin). Tasks are survey tasks 7-12 renumbered 1-6. Countries pooled (cov_country).

Description: Paired conjoint on migrant admission: 4,119 adults in Germany, Italy and Sweden (online, Feb-Mar 2024) chose between two migrant profiles in 6 pairs varying reason for migrating, education, work experience, language, gender, religiosity and religion-by-country of origin.
Reference: Ahlén, A., Borevi, K., Gschwind, L., Hultin Rosenberg, J., & Wejryd, J. (2026). Universalist attitudes to family migration in Germany, Italy and Sweden: A new 'opinion-policy gap'. European Union Politics.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ahlen_2026.R (one of two tables). The deposit labels this conjoint 'for reference' (only an appendix figure in the article). Levels are English value labels of the authors' recodes; wording not deposited. Countries pooled (cov_country).

Description: Online respondents in ten large emitting countries (Dynata, Oct 2021, n=12,646) chose in 3 tasks which of two hypothetical climate pledges their own country should make; pledges varied unconditional commitment (0-50%), an additional conditional 10%, the sector that must reduce and who monitors; forced choice.
Reference: Aklin, M., Buntaine, M. T., & Mildenberger, M. (forthcoming). Public opinion and the political logic of international climate pledges. Global Environmental Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/aklin_2026.R. Experiment 1 (home-country pledges). Ten countries pooled (cov_country); level text is the English instrument as stored (respondents saw translations). Profile order inferred from row order. Same respondents and ids as the companion table. Only respondents who chose in all tasks of both conjoints (12,646). No demographics (no key to the vignette files). Pooled AMCEs (fig02/figS05 estimates CSV) reproduced exactly. Article forthcoming in Global Environmental Politics (no DOI yet).

Description: Online respondents in ten large emitting countries (Dynata, Oct 2021, n=12,646) chose in 3 tasks which of two hypothetical developing countries should receive financial and technical climate assistance; countries varied unconditional and conditional emission commitments, income level and who monitors; forced choice.
Reference: Aklin, M., Buntaine, M. T., & Mildenberger, M. (forthcoming). Public opinion and the political logic of international climate pledges. Global Environmental Politics.
Notes: data/conjoint/aklin_2026.R. Experiment 3 (international transfers). Ten countries pooled (cov_country); level text is the English instrument as stored (respondents saw translations). Profile order inferred from row order. Same respondents and ids as the companion table. Only respondents who chose in all tasks of both conjoints (12,646). No demographics (no key to the vignette files). AMCEs not re-run (Experiment 1 table reproduced exactly from the same pipeline). Article forthcoming in Global Environmental Politics (no DOI yet).

Description: Syrian refugee household heads in Lebanon (face-to-face, Aug-Oct 2019, n=2,998) heard 5 vignettes about conditions one year from now (safety, jobs/services in Syria, conscription, jobs/services in Lebanon, where friends and relatives are) and said whether they would be willing to return to Syria.
Reference: Alrababa'h, A., Masterson, D., Casalis, M., Hangartner, D., & Weinstein, J. M. (2023). The dynamics of refugee return: Syrian refugees and their migration intentions. British Journal of Political Science, 53(4), 1108-1131.
Notes: data/conjoint/alrababah_2023.R. Level text = article's English rendering of the Arabic vignette, matched to the authors' short data labels. Jobs and services share one slot in Syria and in Lebanon (by design). Attribute order randomized by respondent but not recorded. Sampling weight kept. AMCEs reproduce article Figure 3 (hometown safe 0.35, all Syria safe 0.42, conscription ended 0.18).

Description: Online quota-sample respondents in 10 European countries and the USA (2016, n = 11,716) each read one employment and one education vignette about a protagonist who decides to use a cognitive enhancer, with randomized gender, enhancer type (pill or brain-stimulation device), current performance and efficacy (10% or 50%), and rated whether they would make the same choice (0-10).
Reference: Bard, I., Gaskell, G., Allansdottir, A., da Cunha, R. V., Eduard, P., Hampel, J., Hildt, E., Hofmaier, C., Kronberger, N., Laursen, S., Meijknecht, A., Nordal, S., Quintanilha, A., Revuelta, G., Saladié, N., Sándor, J., Santos, J. B., Seyringer, S., Singh, I., Somsen, H., Toonders, W., Torgersen, H., Torre, V., Varju, M., & Zwart, H. (2018). Bottom up ethics - Neuroenhancement in education and employment. Neuroethics, 11(3), 309-322.
Notes: data/conjoint/bard_2018.R. Two single-profile vignettes per respondent with the same four 2-level factors: task 1 = employment, task 2 = education (trial_context); their display order was randomized but not recorded, so task is not display order. Level text = authors' labels (protagonist gender was conveyed by a first name). Rating stored 0-10 as deposited (the article describes the scale as -5 to +5). 11 countries pooled, cov_country. The 14 attitude claims kept as cov_claim_* (0-10). Article N matches (11,716); its vignette-on-claims regressions reproduce (e.g. employment high efficacy +0.097 on the proactionary scale).

Description: 1,058 Canadian adults (Lucid, June 2021; English and French) chose between and rated (0-100) two post-COVID recovery policy packages in 3 tasks, varying climate action, infrastructure investments, assistance to individuals, assistance to corporations and cost.
Reference: Bergquist, P., De Roche, G., Lachapelle, E., Mildenberger, M., & Harrison, K. (2023). The politics of intersecting crises: The effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on climate policy preferences. British Journal of Political Science, 53(2), 707-716.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bergquist_2023.R (one of three tables: US, Canada, US follow-up, estimated separately in the article). Article n = 1,058. 116 respondents answered in French; the level text stored (and in the table) is English for everyone, the French screen text is not deposited. Qualtrics ResponseIds dropped. Attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). trial_climateexperiment is the arm of an earlier, separate text experiment (labels not deposited).

Description: 1,022 US adults in a follow-up survey chose between and rated (0-100) two post-COVID recovery policy packages in 3 tasks; same five attributes as the main US conjoint plus COVID-19 management (test funding, vaccine requirement, mask mandate, none).
Reference: Bergquist, P., De Roche, G., Lachapelle, E., Mildenberger, M., & Harrison, K. (2023). The politics of intersecting crises: The effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on climate policy preferences. British Journal of Political Science, 53(2), 707-716.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bergquist_2023.R (one of three tables: US, Canada, US follow-up, estimated separately in the article). Follow-up study (article footnote 2; n not given in the main text): 1,040 reached the conjoint, 1,022 answered at least one task. ZIP codes and Qualtrics ResponseIds dropped. Attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). trial_climateexperiment is the arm of an earlier, separate text experiment (labels not deposited).

Description: 1,642 US adults (Lucid, April 2021) chose between and rated (0-100) two post-COVID recovery policy packages in 3 tasks, varying climate action, infrastructure investments, assistance to individuals, assistance to corporations and cost.
Reference: Bergquist, P., De Roche, G., Lachapelle, E., Mildenberger, M., & Harrison, K. (2023). The politics of intersecting crises: The effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on climate policy preferences. British Journal of Political Science, 53(2), 707-716.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bergquist_2023.R (one of three tables: US, Canada, US follow-up, estimated separately in the article). Article n = 1,695 reached the conjoint; 53 answered no task and are not in the table. Political party, gender, education and ethnicity keep the panel's codes (no codebook). ZIP codes and Qualtrics ResponseIds dropped. Attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). trial_climateexperiment is the arm of an earlier, separate text experiment (labels not deposited).

Description: Quota samples of adults in Australia, Canada and the UK (Qualtrics, Nov-Dec 2024; n = 3,033) each compared three pairs of hypothetical societies varying the economy, crime and five dimensions of democracy (elections, media, checks and balances, accountability, free speech); forced choice plus a 0-10 rating of each society.
Reference: Bordeleau, J.-N. (2024). Are people equally willing to trade different dimensions of democracy for material and physical security? [Data set]. OSF.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bordeleau_2024.R. Three countries pooled in one table (cov_country) as in the author's main models; identical English attribute text. Level text as stored per profile (differs slightly from Conjoint_Levels.docx). Party ID kept as unlabelled country-specific codes (cov_party_id_code). Article not yet published (EPSA 2025 paper / uOttawa thesis chapter).

Description: Factorial clinical-vignette survey: 140 Dutch primary-care providers (60 GPs, 80 practice nurses, 2014) each rated 12 text vignettes of a COPD or diabetes patient varying 11 patient factors, on the likelihood of providing self-management support, its expected success, and their confidence (each 1-5).
Reference: Bos-Touwen, I. D., Trappenburg, J. C. A., van der Wulp, I., Schuurmans, M. J., & de Wit, N. J. (2017). Patient factors that influence clinicians' decision making in self-management support: A clinical vignette study. PLoS ONE, 12(2), e0171251.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bostouwen_2017.R. Dryad deposit (mirrored as Zenodo record 4987374, whose own DOI does not resolve). Fixed blocked design (96 vignettes, 8 blocks of 12; unrealistic combinations removed). Levels are the SPSS value labels (English short forms; vignettes were Dutch prose). Prov_SM value label 3 'somewhat unlikely' vs questionnaire 'somewhat likely'.

Description: US MTurk respondents (n=1,208) compared two countries in 5 paired tasks varying alliance with America, military size, trade-induced military growth, conflict likelihood, impact on the US economy and government type; chose which country America should increase trade with and rated support for trade with each (1-10).
Reference: Carnegie, A., & Gaikwad, N. (2022). Public opinion on geopolitics and trade: Theory and evidence. World Politics, 74(2), 167-204.
Notes: data/conjoint/carnegie_2022.R. Levels and wording from the deposit (displayed text + codebook). Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Observed restriction: allies always 'Likelihood stays the same' on conflict. Separate single-factor vignette experiment and India vignette data not included. Paper N not checked (paywalled).

Description: Finnish respondents (Qualtrics panel, May 2019, n=829) chose between two hypothetical European Parliament candidates in 7 pairs varying gender, ideology, issue focus, experience, representative focus, citizenship and EU-integration position, each attribute possibly not shown.
Reference: Christensen, H. S., La Rosa, M. S., & Grönlund, K. (2020). How candidate characteristics affect favorability in European Parliament elections: Evidence from a conjoint experiment in Finland. European Union Politics, 21(4), 563-583.
Notes: data/conjoint/christensen_2020.R. Levels = article Table 1 English text (Finnish display text not deposited). Each attribute's 'NOT SHOWN' level stored as (not shown); whether the row was omitted or showed a placeholder is undocumented. Outcome wording paraphrased. N 829 matches; AMCEs vs not-shown baseline reproduce article text (Female 0.04, human rights 0.09, all people in Finland 0.12, Finnish 0.15).

Description: US respondents (957; Black and White samples) compared 7 pairs of descriptions of an act of violence varying perpetrator, target, tactic, location, casualties, motivation and label; chose which made them angrier and which perpetrator to punish more, and rated support for life in prison (1-5) for each.
Reference: Crabtree, K. (2026). Racial identity and evaluations of civilian-perpetrated violence in the United States. Political Behavior.
Notes: data/conjoint/crabtree_2026.R. Attribute levels are the author's stored labels (full displayed sentences not deposited). Outcome wording not deposited (paraphrases from author's code); rating_punish direction from author's code and agreement with choice_punish. Article paywalled; N not checked. Qualtrics ResponseIds re-keyed.

Description: US Qualtrics respondents (fall 2020; 2,418 in wave 1 plus 530 recontacted in wave 2) voted in three mock local elections (mayor, district council, at-large council) of four candidates shown by name (signalling race and gender) and, for half, party, under randomly assigned plurality or ranked-choice rules. Outcomes: top choice (single-winner races), plurality vote marks and RCV ranks.
Reference: Crowder-Meyer, M., Gadarian, S. K., & Trounstine, J. (2023). Ranking candidates in local elections: Neither panacea nor catastrophe for candidates of color. Journal of Experimental Political Science, 11(2), 117-134.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/crowdermeyer_2023.R. Candidates are shown by name only (plus party in the partisan arm); the authors' race/gender coding of the names is not stored as attributes (gender in crosswalk.csv). Wave 2 (530 recontacts, all RCV) carries new ids that cannot be linked to the same people's wave-1 ids. Order of the three office screens not recorded (task = office). Question wording not deposited. Qualtrics ResponseIds dropped.

Description: German respondents in four samples (a general-population online sample, n = 2,482, and three student samples; May-June 2019; total n = 3,882) acted as job-centre caseworkers and in 8 paired tasks chose whose application for basic income support (ALG II) to approve first, with applicants varying in gender, age, citizenship, education, benefit duration, household composition, reason for unemployment and cooperation.
Reference: Dietrich, B., Jankowski, M., Schnapp, K., & Tepe, M. (2023). Prioritizing exceptional social needs: Experimental evidence on the role of discrimination and client deservingness in public employees' and citizens' discretionary behavior. Public Policy and Administration.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/dietrich_2023.R. Four Qualtrics samples pooled with cov_sample (as the authors pool them); civic respondents carry the authors' public/private-sector variable (cov_sector). German level text; attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Authors' exclusions applied (preview, incomplete, no consent). The deposit publishes IP addresses and GPS coordinates (dropped). N not checked against the article.

Description: Paired job-choice conjoint on sexual harassment: 3,925 employed Swedes (Swedish Citizen Panel, January 2020) chose between two job offers in 3 tasks varying wage, skill development, schedule flexibility and work environment (including three sexual-harassment vignettes whose victim sex depended on the respondent's workplace sex composition).
Reference: Folke, O., & Rickne, J. (2022). Sexual harassment and gender inequality in the labor market. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 137(4), 2163-2212.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/folke_2022.R. Levels are the English text stored in the deposit (authors' translation; respondents saw Swedish). Two vignette sets pooled as in the paper (trial_job_set: female-dominated set has male victims). Pairs with a dominant job kept (the paper drops them). Authors' probability weight not kept (built from population totals in the .do). Covariates mostly codes.

Description: Kenyan adults in face-to-face interviews (n=2,072; Nairobi, Mt. Kenya, Nyanza, Garissa) compared 3 pairs of hypothetical digital ID policies varying use for social protection, data sharing for public services, police access to biometric photos, tax-ID linkage and voter registration; choice, support and willingness to register for each policy, plus five round-1 mechanism ratings.
Reference: Garbe, L., McMurry, N., Scacco, A., & Zhang, K. W. (2025). Who wants to be legible? Digitalization and intergroup inequality in Kenya. Comparative Political Studies, 58(9), 1803-1853.
Notes: data/conjoint/garbe_2025.R. Sample = consent and survey-firm 'Approved' interviews, as in the authors' code (2,072 = article). Level text is the showcard wording printed in the authors' 2023 WZB working paper appendix (the article's Figure 1 is an image); binary codes mapped via the form's yes/no showcard images. Refused choices resolved by the follow-up 'Are you sure?' as the authors do; 17 tasks remain without a choice. Device/SIM IDs, phone numbers and GPS in the deposit are not read.

Description: Syrian refugees in Lebanon (face-to-face survey, n=417 in the deposit) chose in up to 5 tasks which of two places in Syria a person like themselves should return to, places varying harm risk on route, chance of lasting peace, number of people known there and ease of finding work; forced choice.
Reference: Ghosn, F., Chu, T. S., Simon, M., Braithwaite, A., Frith, M., & Jandali, J. (2021). The journey home: Violence, anchoring, and refugee decisions to return. American Political Science Review, 115(3), 982-998.
Notes: data/conjoint/ghosn_2021.R. Attribute codes 1-3 mapped to text from the questionnaire in Journey_Home_Appendix.pdf (Appendix C); direction agrees with the article's findings. Profile inferred from row order. Don't know/no response tasks are not in the deposit, so choice is forced. 417 respondents in file vs 406 in the article. Respondent covariates are the authors' 0/1 dummies; gender code direction undocumented (cov_gender_code).

Description: Canadian respondents outside Quebec (Dynata, May 2020, n=2,830 before the article's exclusions) chose between two parliamentary candidates in 6 tasks varying gender, age, experience, party, COVID-19 economic-aid and lockdown positions, and a randomized executive-aggrandizement position (Parliament or courts version by respondent).
Reference: Gidengil, E., Stolle, D., & Bergeron-Boutin, O. (2022). COVID-19 and support for executive aggrandizement. Canadian Journal of Political Science, 55(2), 342-372.
Notes: data/conjoint/gidengil_2022.R. Built from the raw Qualtrics export (level text as displayed). Both executive-aggrandizement versions in one table (trial_checks_version); authors analyse them separately. All 2,830 respondents with answers kept; article sample 2,322 after attention/duration/straightlining/citizenship exclusions (flags kept except straightlining); tasks under 5 s kept (trial_task_time_sec). Share choosing the norm-violating candidate 44%/44% vs article 43%/44%.

Description: 3,162 US adults (YouGov, December 2024) each read three newspaper-style vignettes about a state-legislature candidate, randomizing the candidate's photo/name (race, gender, age), party, and (in ~80% of vignettes) a controversial remark (type, target, wording), its timing, planning and history, and the politician's response. Outcomes: would ever consider voting (yes/no), 0-100 thermometer, 1-7 objectionableness.
Reference: Gift, T., & Lastra-Anadón, C. X. (2025). Can politicians say that? What shapes public responses to speech scandals? Journal of Experimental Political Science.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/gift_2025.R. Levels are the authors' category labels (Tables A.1-A.4), not the full screen text; candidate names reconstructed from Appendix Table A.4 (inferred). Remark-related attributes are (not shown) in the clean controls. Three omnibus polls stacked as by the authors (cov_omnibus); YouGov weight kept. Open-ended free-text answers dropped.

Description: Factorial vignette on legislators' credit claiming: 952 US online respondents (MTurk, June 2013) each read one press release varying the legislator's party, whether credit was claimed alone or with a Democrat/Republican, the stage (requested, secured, will request), the amount ($20 million or $50 thousand) and the project type; outcomes are 1-5 approval and a 0-100 thermometer rating of the legislator.
Reference: Grimmer, J., Messing, S., & Westwood, S. J. (2017). Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects and the effects of heterogeneous treatments with ensemble methods. Political Analysis, 25(4), 413-434.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/grimmer_2017.R. One vignette per respondent; 122 control respondents (no press release) dropped. Levels are the inserted text from the data (along-with levels are the authors' shorthand); full vignette, question wording and anchors not deposited. Approval: lower = more approval (authors code 1-2 as approve), stored raw. Covariates are codes without a codebook (_code). IP addresses and MTurk worker IDs in the source dropped.

Description: British online-panel respondents (2017, n = 1,635) chose, in 5 pairs, which of two hypothetical applicants they would prefer as the next Director General of the BBC; applicants varied in name, age, BBC experience, degree, 2017 party support, EU-referendum side and former occupation.
Reference: Hobolt, S. B., Leeper, T. J., & Tilley, J. (2021). Divided by the vote: Affective polarization in the wake of the Brexit referendum. British Journal of Political Science, 51(4), 1476-1493.
Notes: data/conjoint/hobolt_2021.R. One of two conjoints in the deposit (companion hobolt_2021_brexit_lodger). Names are gendered but the authors do not code them, so no crosswalk. Attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_ columns; name is the column header). Weight kept. Right-hand profile chosen 2 points less often, as the authors' analysis PDF reports. Paper N not checked (article not accessible); deposit n matches the analysis PDF.

Description: British online-panel respondents (2017, n = 1,669) chose, in 5 pairs, which of two hypothetical lodgers they would prefer; lodgers varied in name, age, occupation, volunteering, 2017 vote, EU-referendum vote and hobby.
Reference: Hobolt, S. B., Leeper, T. J., & Tilley, J. (2021). Divided by the vote: Affective polarization in the wake of the Brexit referendum. British Journal of Political Science, 51(4), 1476-1493.
Notes: data/conjoint/hobolt_2021.R. One of two conjoints in the deposit (companion hobolt_2021_brexit_bbc_dg). Names are gendered but the authors do not code them, so no crosswalk. Attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Weight (W8) kept. Paper N not checked (article not accessible); deposit n matches the analysis PDF.

Description: British YouGov panel respondents (April 2017, n = 3,293) compared 5 pairs of possible Brexit negotiation outcomes varying on immigration, citizens' rights, trade, EU law, budget contributions, one-off payment, Irish border checks and timing; choice plus per-outcome acceptability, whether each respects the referendum result, and likelihood of the chosen outcome.
Reference: Hobolt, S. B., Tilley, J., & Leeper, T. J. (2022). Policy preferences and policy legitimacy after referendums: Evidence from the Brexit negotiations. Political Behavior, 44(2), 839-858.
Notes: data/conjoint/hobolt_2022.R. rating_acceptable stored raw (1 = completely acceptable .. 4 = completely unacceptable; lower = more favourable). rating_respects_referendum recoded per profile from one A/B/both/neither/DK question (DK -> NA; the authors code DK as 0). rating_likely asked only of the chosen outcome (NA on the other; DK -> NA). Attribute row order shuffled once per respondent (attrpos_). Fixed sixth pair dropped. Weight kept. Paper N not checked (article page not reachable); row count matches the authors' cleaning script (32,930).

Description: Zambian phone-survey respondents (ZEPS wave 2, July-August 2021, n = 1,525) each heard one vignette in which a local authority urges them to campaign for or attend a meeting with a parliamentary candidate, with 11 randomized factors (candidate co-ethnicity, co-partisanship, gender, origin, residence; leader and community monitoring; friends joining; payment); they rated their likelihood of participating, expected sanctions, enjoyment and whether the authority would back the candidate.
Reference: Jöst, P., Krönke, M., Lockwood, S. J., & Lust, E. (2024). Drivers of political participation: The role of partisanship, identity, and incentives in mobilizing Zambian citizens. Comparative Political Studies, 57(9), 1441-1474.
Notes: data/conjoint/jost_2024.R. Single-vignette factorial (one task per respondent). attr_ethnicity and attr_partisanship are relative levels (respondent's own group/party or a random other one piped in; the name actually read out was not saved). Sanctioning/social-benefit labels keep the script's {0} placeholder for the activity phrase. All ratings raw: 1 = very likely/very much (lower = more willing). 6 respondents with missing attribute levels and 5 with no answers dropped (1,525 of 1,536). Paper AMCEs reproduced (co-partisan .10, co-ethnic .04, friends join .05).

Description: Paired conjoint on judging resolve in international disputes: 2,003 US adults (January 2015) compared 8 pairs of countries described by regime type, military capabilities, stakes, leader background (tenure, military service, gender), relation to the US, previous and current crisis behaviour; outcomes are which country is more likely to stand firm and a 0-100 likelihood that each will.
Reference: Kertzer, J. D., Renshon, J., & Yarhi-Milo, K. (2021). How do observers assess resolve? British Journal of Political Science, 51(1), 308-330.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kertzer_2021.R. Levels are the full displayed sentences; leader background and previous behaviour each cross several factors in one sentence (the authors split them by regex). Attribute row order randomized per respondent (attrpos_*). Tasks in which one country is 'the United States' are kept; the paper's main analysis drops them. Outcome wording paraphrased from the codebook.

Description: Paired conjoint on carbon-tax design in South Korea: 845 adults (the control, no-information arm) chose between 5 pairs of carbon-tax proposals varying the monthly household cost, the main taxed energy, and two revenue uses (redistributive and environmental); the outcome is a forced choice.
Reference: Kim, S. E., Kim, S. Y., & Suh, J. (2024). Public support for carbon tax in South Korea: The role of tax design and revenue recycling. Asia & the Pacific Policy Studies, 11(2), e385.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kim_2024.R. Only the control (no-information) arm is deposited; the information-treatment arm the paper also analyses is not. Levels are the Korean display text; English names in the script header. No covariates deposited. Tasks without an answer were dropped by the authors (7 respondents have fewer than 5 tasks).

Description: Paired candidate conjoint on crime policy: 2,688 online respondents in Argentina and Brazil each chose between two candidates in 5 pairs varying sex and positions on abortion, taxes, same-sex marriage, the environment and crime (social programs vs punitive policing).
Reference: Laterzo, I. G. (2023). Progressive ideology and support for punitive crime policy: Evidence from Argentina and Brazil. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/laterzo_2023.R. Task/profile structure inferred from row blocks (no task/profile columns); display position is not recorded, so profile numbering is arbitrary and outcome-independent (profiles sorted by their attribute text; identical pairs alternate by id + task parity) - do not use profile for position effects. Levels are the codebook's English wording (respondents saw Spanish/Portuguese). Choice wording not deposited. Countries pooled (cov_country) as in the paper; 100 Argentine tasks with missing levels dropped.

Description: Paired conjoint on proposals to ration petrol and diesel in Sweden: 3,247 adults compared 5 pairs of rationing proposals varying stringency (20/30/40/50 liter/month), allowance allocation, tradability, price and whether the cap declines over time; outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-5 rating from strongly against to strongly in favor.
Reference: Lindgren, O., Jagers, S. C., & Lindvall, D. (2026). The impact of policy design on opposition to restrictive climate policies. Ecological Economics, 240.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lindgren_2026.R. One of two conjoints done by the same respondents (fuel and red meat, random block order: trial_block_position); the twin table is lindgren_2026_meat_rationing. Levels are the authors' English value labels (shown in Swedish); question wording not deposited. All respondents kept; the authors drop speeders and attention-check failures (analytic n 3,175; cov_attention_pass, cov_duration_sec). Profile order inferred from the deposit's row index.

Description: Paired conjoint on proposals to ration red meat in Sweden: 3,247 adults compared 5 pairs of rationing proposals varying stringency (0.6/1/1.4/1.8 kg/month), allowance allocation, tradability, price and whether the cap declines over time; outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-5 rating from strongly against to strongly in favor.
Reference: Lindgren, O., Jagers, S. C., & Lindvall, D. (2026). The impact of policy design on opposition to restrictive climate policies. Ecological Economics, 240.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lindgren_2026.R. One of two conjoints done by the same respondents (fuel and red meat, random block order: trial_block_position); the twin table is lindgren_2026_fuel_rationing. Levels are the authors' English value labels (shown in Swedish); question wording not deposited. All respondents kept; the authors drop speeders and attention-check failures (analytic n 3,175; cov_attention_pass, cov_duration_sec). Profile order inferred from the deposit's row index.

Description: Canadian online respondents (2017, n=779) read one pair of short candidate descriptions: an incumbent (C) vs challenger (D) varying age, gender, race, occupation, party and daycare position, with the incumbent's illness (flu, skin cancer, depression) and voting attendance randomized, and a challenger military sentence; chose whom to vote for and who is most prepared, trustworthy and of best character.
Reference: Loewen, P. J., & Rheault, L. (2021). Voters punish politicians with depression. British Journal of Political Science, 51(1), 427-437.
Notes: data/conjoint/loewen_2019.R. One of four tables from this deposit (open-seat/incumbent session x US/Canada; same respondents in both sessions of a country). Attributes are the text fragments piped into an undeposited vignette; health/illness levels for A are the authors' factor labels. Outcome wording paraphrased from codebook; article paywalled. Empty D military sentence (375 of 779) stored as (not shown) (inferred).

Description: US online respondents (2017, n=967) read one pair of short candidate descriptions: an incumbent (C) vs challenger (D) varying age, gender, race, party and healthcare position, with the incumbent's illness (flu, skin cancer, depression) and voting attendance randomized; chose whom to vote for and who is most prepared, trustworthy and of best character.
Reference: Loewen, P. J., & Rheault, L. (2021). Voters punish politicians with depression. British Journal of Political Science, 51(1), 427-437.
Notes: data/conjoint/loewen_2019.R. One of four tables from this deposit (open-seat/incumbent session x US/Canada; same respondents in both sessions of a country). Attributes are the text fragments piped into an undeposited vignette; health/illness levels for A are the authors' factor labels. Outcome wording paraphrased from codebook; article paywalled.
