Description: Canadian online respondents (2017, n=779) read one pair of short candidate descriptions: an open-seat pair of candidates (A, B) varying age, gender, race, occupation, experience, party, abortion, military and tax positions, with Candidate A's health condition (blood pressure, cancer, depression) and leave of absence randomized; chose whom to vote for and who is most prepared, trustworthy and of best character.
Reference: Loewen, P. J., & Rheault, L. (2021). Voters punish politicians with depression. British Journal of Political Science, 51(1), 427-437.
Notes: data/conjoint/loewen_2019.R. One of four tables from this deposit (open-seat/incumbent session x US/Canada; same respondents in both sessions of a country). Attributes are the text fragments piped into an undeposited vignette; health/illness levels for A are the authors' factor labels. Outcome wording paraphrased from codebook; article paywalled.

Description: US online respondents (2017, n=966) read one pair of short candidate descriptions: an open-seat pair of candidates (A, B) varying age, gender, race, experience, party, abortion, guns and tax positions, with Candidate A's health condition (blood pressure, cancer, depression) and leave of absence randomized; chose whom to vote for and who is most prepared, trustworthy and of best character.
Reference: Loewen, P. J., & Rheault, L. (2021). Voters punish politicians with depression. British Journal of Political Science, 51(1), 427-437.
Notes: data/conjoint/loewen_2019.R. One of four tables from this deposit (open-seat/incumbent session x US/Canada; same respondents in both sessions of a country). Attributes are the text fragments piped into an undeposited vignette; health/illness levels for A are the authors' factor labels. Outcome wording paraphrased from codebook; article paywalled. US leave text mapped from the Canadian wording (inferred). Vote by illness reproduces authors' lm log (Depression -0.096).

Description: US adults (Morning Consult, n=12,052, weighted) each judged one hypothetical immigrant whose country (Mexico, India, Canada), skill (farm laborer with no formal education vs doctor with a graduate-equivalent degree) and the presence of a sentence on how prevalent such immigrants are were randomized; a binary admit question plus three ordinal admission ratings.
Reference: Malhotra, N., & Newman, B. (2017). Explaining immigration preferences: Disentangling skill and prevalence. Research & Politics, 4(4).
Notes: data/conjoint/malhotra_2017.R. Factorial vignette (3x2x2), one vignette per respondent. Only the randomized fragments are deposited (country, education, profession, prevalence sentence); the full vignette and outcome wording are not, so questions are paraphrased from the authors' do-file. Two of the four outcomes are reverse-coded in the source (low = favourable), stored raw. The deposit's re-hosted Hainmueller-Hopkins and Wright et al. files are not built. Demographics are unlabelled codes; ZIP codes dropped.

Description: US Prolific respondents (n=1,503) chose between two hypothetical therapists in 3 scenarios and rated each 1-7; therapists varied sex/gender, race/ethnicity, availability, session format, star rating, degree, experience and specialties, with one of three versions omitting two attributes.
Reference: McCrea, A. M., & Favero, N. (2026). Preferences for symbolic representation: Identity, context, and selection of mental health providers. International Public Management Journal, 1-21.
Notes: data/conjoint/mccrea_2026.R. Three respondent-level versions (trial_version) each hide two of nine attributes ('(not shown)'); the authors' analysis drops the no_sessioninfo version, kept here. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Question wording and rating anchors not deposited. Prolific IDs present in the deposit despite README (dropped). Paper N not checked (paywalled).

Description: Online panel respondents in Denmark, Germany, Poland and Portugal (Jan-Feb 2022; n = 4,103) each made 8 forced choices between two designs of a future renewable regional electricity supply varying technology, transmission expansion, land use, import share, price change and ownership.
Reference: Mey, F., Lilliestam, J., Wolf, I., & Tröndle, T. (2024). Visions for our future regional electricity system – citizen preferences in four EU countries. iScience.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mey_2024.R. Choices and levels from the raw conjointly exports (Zenodo 10463074); analytic sample (pre-test respondents removed) and English-recoded covariates from the authors' pre-processed twin (Zenodo 10463114, CC BY 4.0). Four countries pooled (cov_country) as in the authors' hierarchical model. Levels are conjointly's short English labels; respondents saw national-language text with pictograms. Within-task level overlap is rare (6-10%), so the design limited overlap although described as fully randomised. Article DOI not given in the deposit.

Description: Online panel respondents in Brazil, Germany, Italy, Poland and the US (Sep-Dec 2020, n=4,354) chose in 4 tasks which of two hypothetical persons should be prioritized for a COVID-19 vaccine; persons varied gender, age, children, job, citizenship, pre-existing condition and early registration; forced choice.
Reference: Munzert, S., Ramirez-Ruiz, S., Çalı, B., Stoetzer, L. F., Gohdes, A., & Lowe, W. (2022). Prioritization preferences for COVID-19 vaccination are consistent across five countries. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 9, 439.
Notes: data/conjoint/munzert_2022.R. Five countries pooled (cov_country), as in the paper. Levels stored in English (survey shown in local languages); citizenship stored as the authors' labels 'Country'/'Other Country'. Teacher job level only in Germany. The deposit repeats 237 respondents' conjoint rows 2-6 times (de-duplicated here; the paper's regressions appear to include the repeats: 36,936 obs). 4,354 respondents = paper's cluster count. Pooling weight (per-country sample-size) not kept.

Description: Paired conjoint on international COVID-19 vaccine agreements: 1,749 US adults (Lucid, April 2021) chose which of two agreements the US should join in 4 pairs varying participating countries, household cost, cost and benefit distribution, external supply deals, technology sharing and monitoring, and rated their likelihood of voting for each 1-7.
Reference: Nair, G., & Peyton, K. (2022). Building mass support for global pandemic recovery efforts in the United States. PNAS Nexus, 1(4), pgac123.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/nair_2022.R (one of three tables). Levels as stored in the authors' .rds factors. Same respondents as nair_2022_vaccine_recipients. 36 tasks without a choice keep ratings.

Description: Paired conjoint on international COVID-19 recovery agreements: 4,204 US adults (NORC AmeriSpeak probability panel, Sep-Oct 2021) chose which of two agreements the US should support in 2 pairs varying overall cost, US share, funding use, beneficiaries and duration, and rated their likelihood of voting for each (5-point, deposited rescaled to 0-1).
Reference: Nair, G., & Peyton, K. (2022). Building mass support for global pandemic recovery efforts in the United States. PNAS Nexus, 1(4), pgac123.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/nair_2022.R (one of three tables). Rating deposited only as the authors' 0-1 rescale of the 1-5 vote item (0 = definitely against); stored as deposited. Duration levels in data are 1/3/5/7/9 years though SM lists 1-5 years. Derived burden_ (cost x share) dropped. NORC panel weight kept.

Description: Paired conjoint on COVID-19 vaccine priority: 1,747 US adults (Lucid, April 2021) chose which of two people waiting for a vaccine should get priority, in up to 5 pairs varying sex, age group, exposure and illness risk, occupation, working from home and country of origin, and rated each 1-7.
Reference: Nair, G., & Peyton, K. (2022). Building mass support for global pandemic recovery efforts in the United States. PNAS Nexus, 1(4), pgac123.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/nair_2022.R (one of three tables). Levels as stored in the authors' .rds factors. 25 respondents answered fewer than 5 tasks. Same respondents as nair_2022_covax_agreement_lucid (conjoint order randomized, cov_conjoint_first). Authors' raking weight kept.

Description: Swiss adults (IPSOS online panel, November 2017, n = 2,843) chose between two agricultural-subsidy proposals in each of 6 tasks, each proposal allocating direct payments to six goals (environmentally friendly farming, small farms, food security, countryside, animal welfare, food quality) at None/Moderate/Large; outcomes are the forced choice and a 1-7 rating of each proposal. Half the sample first saw a cost prime (trial_cost_frame).
Reference: Nguyen, Q., Spilker, G., & Bernauer, T. (2021). The (still) mysterious case of agricultural protectionism. International Interactions, 47(3), 391-416.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/nguyen_2021.R. Levels coded 0/1/2 (labels none/medium/high) mapped to the displayed None/Moderate/Large of the article's Tables 1-2. Task and profile inferred from the source's 1-12 row index (rows c and c+6 form a pair; exactly one chosen in every pair). US and Swiss samples are separate tables, as analysed by the authors. Deposit N exceeds the article's count of valid answers (2,605 US / 2,310 CH).

Description: US adults (IPSOS online panel, November 2017, n = 2,854) chose between two agricultural-subsidy proposals in each of 6 tasks, each proposal allocating direct payments to six goals (environmentally friendly farming, small farms, food security, countryside, animal welfare, food quality) at None/Moderate/Large; outcomes are the forced choice and a 1-7 rating of each proposal. Half the sample first saw a cost prime (trial_cost_frame).
Reference: Nguyen, Q., Spilker, G., & Bernauer, T. (2021). The (still) mysterious case of agricultural protectionism. International Interactions, 47(3), 391-416.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/nguyen_2021.R. Levels coded 0/1/2 (labels none/medium/high) mapped to the displayed None/Moderate/Large of the article's Tables 1-2. Task and profile inferred from the source's 1-12 row index (rows c and c+6 form a pair; exactly one chosen in every pair). US and Swiss samples are separate tables, as analysed by the authors. Deposit N exceeds the article's count of valid answers (2,605 US / 2,310 CH).

Description: Paired conjoint on who counts as American: 1,500 US adults (750 White, 750 Black respondents, 2020) compared 5 pairs of profiles of people from immigrant families varying photo (skin tone x gender), immigration background, self-identification, language, education, profession, religion, party and spouse; outcomes are a forced choice of the more American person and a 1-7 rating of how American each is.
Reference: Ocampo-Roland, A. N. (2025). Group prototypicality and boundary definition: Comparing White and Black perceptions of whether Latinos are American. American Political Science Review, 119(4), 1581-1598.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ocampo_2025.R. Level text from the questionnaire's Table A1; attr_faces is a photograph stored as the authors' coding (e.g. 'Brown woman'); 'Latino' identity level is absent from Table A1 and kept as the codebook label; spouse level 5 stored as 'Spouse is (same identity as profile)' (displayed identity not recorded). White and Black respondents pooled (cov_race), as in the paper's pooled AMCE. A 1-7 'want as friend' rating was asked but not deposited.

Description: Single-profile conjoint on cross-Strait peace agreements: 3,446 Taiwanese online respondents (April 2022) each judged 5 hypothetical China-Taiwan agreements made of randomly shown concessions (4 by China, 4 by Taiwan), supporting or opposing each, under a randomized US-support / China-threat framing.
Reference: Pan, H.-H., Kastner, S. L., & Pearson, M. M. (2025). Is China-Taiwan rapprochement possible? Experimental evidence from Taiwan. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 69(7-8), 1143-1171.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/pan_2025.R. Each concession is shown or not: hidden clauses are '(not shown)'. Clause text is the authors' English rendering from the analysis do-file (respondents saw Chinese). Task = row order within respondent (display order not recorded). Deposit has 3,446 respondents vs 2,905 in published summaries (not reconciled). Support wording paraphrased. Covariates are the authors' binary recodes.

Description: 1,307 adults in Belgium (YouGov web panel, July-August 2022) chose which of two fictitious patients should be prioritised for publicly funded care in 4 tasks, varying nationality (Belgian, Danish, Italian, Bulgarian), migration status, responsibility for ill health and employment status; the chosen patient was also rated 0-10.
Reference: Perna, R., & Umpierrez de Reguero, S. (2025). Intra-EU migration and healthcare deservingness: A conjoint experiment in Belgium and Spain. Social Science & Medicine, 367, 117714.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/perna_2025.R (one table per country; the other is perna_2025_healthcare_es). Levels are the codebook's English labels; the screen text in the national languages is not deposited. Profile order is inferred from row order. Rating only on the chosen patient. One corrupt respondent dropped (1,308 -> 1,307 = article). Panel IDs re-keyed.

Description: 1,307 adults in Spain (YouGov web panel, July-August 2022) chose which of two fictitious patients should be prioritised for publicly funded care in 4 tasks, varying nationality (Spanish, Danish, Italian, Bulgarian), migration status, responsibility for ill health and employment status; the chosen patient was also rated 0-10.
Reference: Perna, R., & Umpierrez de Reguero, S. (2025). Intra-EU migration and healthcare deservingness: A conjoint experiment in Belgium and Spain. Social Science & Medicine, 367, 117714.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/perna_2025.R (one table per country; the other is perna_2025_healthcare_be). Levels are the codebook's English labels; the screen text in the national languages is not deposited. Profile order is inferred from row order. Rating only on the chosen patient. Region keeps codes (the codebook mapping looks doubtful). Panel IDs re-keyed.

Description: US online respondents in three experiments (n = 7,348) each read one hypothetical US economic-statecraft proposal (sanctions or inducements) against a target country, with randomized target, bad behaviour, country background, economic effect, outcome of inaction, rationale and proposal author; six 0-100 ratings (support, US interests, cost, effectiveness, US strength, message).
Reference: Peterson, T. M., & Miller, S. M. (2024). Contextualizing individual attitudes on economic statecraft. Foreign Policy Analysis, 20(3), orae016.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/peterson_2024.R. Three experiments (different target-country sets and second bad behaviour) pooled as the authors do, trial_experiment 1-3. Single vignette per respondent; four table rows in randomized order (attrpos_*). Rating anchors not in the deposit. Demographic codes (gender, ethnicity, hispanic, education) kept as unlabelled panel codes. 5 respondents with no saved attributes and 39 with no ratings dropped (7,392 exported).

Description: Serbian university-student participants (n = 432) made 8 choices among 4 hypothetical job candidates varying in an AI employability score (7-91%), required education, gender, age and hobby, then said whether they would actually advance the chosen candidate (dual response).
Reference: Petrović, N., Kuzmanović, M., Anđelković Labrović, J., Kovačević, I., & Llorens, A. (2026). Data for: How much weight does an AI score carry in hiring? Qualification conflict and evaluator heterogeneity in a choice-based conjoint experiment [Data set]. Zenodo.
Notes: data/conjoint/petrovic_2026.R. Accompanying manuscript unpublished (no article DOI). Record description adds a no-re-identification use condition to CC BY 4.0. choice = forced first-stage pick; choice_commit = dual-response outcome (pick if the participant would advance that candidate, else none; matches the export's model matrix). Level text = the survey tool's level names (Serbian; 'No info'/'Nema informacije' levels kept as text, display of those rows undocumented). Question wording not deposited. N 432 as the record states.

Description: Sworn Yonkers Police Department officers (June 2021, n = 246) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical police-officer applicants varying in sex, age, race/ethnicity, education, residency, exam score, motivation and previous occupation, and rated each 1-7.
Reference: Peyton, K., Weiss, C. M., & Vaughn, P. E. (2022). Beliefs about minority representation in policing and support for diversification. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 119(52), e2213986119.
Notes: data/conjoint/peyton_2022.R. Police-officer sample; companion table peyton_2022_police_recruit_residents. Level text = authors' short factor labels in conjoints_stacked.rds (displayed wording was longer, e.g. 'Scored in top 10% of applicants'; full displayed text not deposited). Restricted randomization on occupation x education. Deposit 250 officers (paper 250), 4 with no outcome dropped. No covariates deposited. Paper AMCEs reproduced closely (Top 1% exam 0.27 vs 0.28; >10 y residency 0.28 vs 0.29).

Description: Yonkers, NY residents (municipal panel baseline, May 2021, n = 1,409) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical police-officer applicants varying in sex, age, race/ethnicity, education, residency, exam score, motivation and previous occupation, and rated each 1-7.
Reference: Peyton, K., Weiss, C. M., & Vaughn, P. E. (2022). Beliefs about minority representation in policing and support for diversification. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 119(52), e2213986119.
Notes: data/conjoint/peyton_2022.R. Resident sample; companion table peyton_2022_police_recruit_officers (same design, YPD officers). Level text = authors' short factor labels in conjoints_stacked.rds (displayed wording was longer, e.g. 'Scored in top 10% of applicants'; full displayed text not deposited). Restricted randomization on occupation x education. Deposit 1,412 respondents (paper 1,413), 3 with no outcome dropped. Raking weight kept as cov_survey_weight (authors do not use it). Paper AMCEs reproduced closely (Top 1% exam 0.14 vs 0.15; >10 y residency 0.22 vs 0.22).

Description: Swedish consumers (online panel, Jan-Feb 2021, n=1,541) chose between two 400 g tofu variants varying production country, soybean origin, organic cultivation and price, or neither, in 9 choice sets each, after a randomized information treatment (environment, health, recipe, control).
Reference: Sagebiel, J., Castellari, E., Rommel, J., Weigel, M., & Welling, M. (in press). Swedish consumers' preferences for tofu sustainability characteristics: A choice experiment with information treatments. German Journal of Agricultural Economics.
Notes: data/conjoint/sagebiel_2026.R. Levels in Swedish from the deposit dictionary. Fixed 27-row design, variants always differ on every attribute. All 1,541 respondents with an answered choice set kept (incl. 82 timeouts; cov_status); article reports ~1,400 (exclusions not reproduced). Licence from the Zenodo record (authors' own migration of OSF a986e, which shows no licence). PII in source covariates (pseudo IP, session/panel ids, survey URLs) dropped.

Description: 1,195 US adults (national online survey, January 2023; the authors' cleaned sample) chose between two plans for a direct air capture facility sited in their community in 13 tasks, varying funding source, owner, energy source, community involvement, CO2 storage, share of costs reinvested locally and job creation.
Reference: Scott-Buechler, C., Cain, B., Osman, K., Ardoin, N., Fraser, C., Adcox, G., Polk, E., & Jackson, R. B. (2024). Communities conditionally support deployment of direct air capture for carbon dioxide removal in the United States. Communications Earth & Environment, 5.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/scottbuechler_2024.R. Choice is taken from the recorded answers (wide C1-C13); the deposit's long-format Choice column only flags the first plan and is not used. Fixed CBC design in 210 versions (trial_version). Only the authors' cleaned sample (1,195 of 2,198) has conjoint data. cov_survey_weight = authors' raking weight. Date of birth, ZIP codes, panel and supplier ids, free text dropped.

Description: University of Warsaw students (December 2017, survey app, n = 297) made 26 stated choices among mobile-data options in three within-subject treatments: free campus Wi-Fi status quo vs two 4G LTE packages (SP1), the same with a possible 1-3 zl Wi-Fi fee (SP2), and two 4G packages without a status quo (SP3), varying Wi-Fi fee, 4G monthly fee, data limit and number of devices; outcome is the chosen alternative.
Reference: Tjiong, J., Dekker, T., Hess, S., Giergiczny, M., Ojeda-Cabral, M., & Czajkowski, M. (2026). Capturing zero-price effects in stated choice surveys: Implications for willingness-to-pay and welfare. Journal of Choice Modelling, 58, 100582.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/tjiong_2026.R. Fixed blocked D-efficient designs; three treatments in one table (trial_treatment), as the authors also estimate them jointly. Level text = the app's display strings in the deposit's design sheets; the status quo is a profile with displayed Wi-Fi fee and '-' elsewhere. 5 students recorded twice dropped (N 297 vs 302). Student index numbers in the deposit (quasi-identifiers) re-keyed; questionnaire items without codebook dropped.

Description: Canadian respondents (n = 1,131) each chose between and rated (1-7) three pairs of hypothetical candidates varying gender, experience, six policy positions and, in a randomized arm, party label (Conservative/Liberal).
Reference: Treger, C., Galipeau, T., Bergeron, T., Lachance, S., Goel, N., Islam, M. M., Lee-Whiting, B., Magistro, B., & Loewen, P. J. (2026). Party or policy? The role of policy partisanship in voter decision-making. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/treger_2026.R. Task/profile inferred from row order (6 rows per respondent; one chosen per pair verified). Question wordings, rating anchors and experience display text are not in the deposit (paper paywalled, not read); experience levels use the authors' labels (1/4/12 years). Party shown only in the Partisanship arm (trial_arm), else '(not shown)'. 339 tasks have a rating but no recorded choice. Covariates are the authors' recodes (no codebook).

Description: German adults aged 40+ (Kantar online, Dec 2022; representative sample plus an affluent oversample, n = 2,992) each rated four vignettes about parents dividing a family business, house and cash between two siblings, on whether the focal child's share was too little (-5), appropriate (0) or too much (+5).
Reference: Trinh, N. A., Tisch, D., & Schechtl, M. (2026). The (in)appropriateness of inequality: A factorial survey experiment on wealth transfers within families. Social Forces.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/trinh_2026.R. Factorial survey, D-efficient blocked design (162 decks of 4; transfer type between respondents; trial_deck). Levels are the authors' English value labels; respondents read German vignette text (template in the script header). Focal child's gender shown via first name (attr_name) and sibling noun. Representative and affluent samples pooled (cov_subsample) as in the main models. task = vig_order (display position).

Description: German adults (online panel, February-March 2022, n = 1,870) compared 5 pairs of policy packages for phasing out fossil heating systems (building sector), varying the phase-out year, a purchase measure, a use measure (purchase taxes/bans on fossil heating, fuel taxes or mandatory replacement of old fossil heating) and a supporting measure; outcomes are a forced choice and a 1-5 support rating of each package. A framing (phase-out vs renewables) was randomized between respondents.
Reference: Tröndle, T., Annaheim, J., Hoppe, J., Hanger-Kopp, S., & Patt, A. (2023). Public preferences for phasing-out fossil fuels in the German building and transport sectors. Environmental Research Communications, 5(8).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/trondle_2023.R. Heating and transport experiments (same respondents, sector order randomized) are separate tables because their levels differ. Levels are the German displayed text. Complete responses only, as the authors; 1,870 respondents vs n = 1,777 in the paper's supplementary figures (gap undocumented). Hashed panel return token dropped.

Description: 2x2x2 factorial vignette on proposals to build wind turbines: 3,984 Swiss adults (respondi panel, September 2019) each read one vignette varying locality (own vs different canton), exposure (landscape photo with vs without a turbine) and politicisation (people vs named parties disagree); outcomes are 1-5 support for the proposals and 1-5 likelihood of turnout and of voting SP and SVP.
Reference: Umit, R., & Schaffer, L. M. (2022). Wind turbines, public acceptance, and electoral outcomes. Swiss Political Science Review, 28(4), 712-727.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/umit_2022.R. One vignette per respondent (task = profile = 1). Levels are the English design text of the article; respondents saw German, French or Italian (not deposited); the canton named in the 'different canton' arm is not recorded. Don't know already recoded NA by the authors. Vote-intention outcomes only for eligible voters. 145 respondents with no treatment recorded dropped.

Description: 301 respondents in Germany (April 2025) each compared 5 pairs of text scenarios about a cyberattack on a pharmaceutical wholesaler, varying societal harm, the medium of the hackers' statement, the legitimation strategy in the statement (11 levels) and an apology, and chose the scenario in which the group's actions seemed more appropriate/legitimate; the chosen scenario was also rated (1-5) on the group's responsibility, legal accountability and deserved punishment.
Reference: Weißmüller, K. S., van den Broek, T. A., Kaufmann, A., & Watson, S. J. (2026). Discrete choice experiment on the effectiveness of criminal organizations' legitimation strategies [Data set]. OSF.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/weissmuller_2026.R (one table per sample; the other is weissmuller_2026_legitimation_uk). Fixed design of 18 choice sets transcribed from the authors' .do files (the data store only the chosen scenario's levels; they match the design in every row). Level text is the codebook vignette text; no-apology level = (not shown). Display order of the 5 sets not recorded (task numbered by choice set). Ratings only on the chosen scenario. No article yet.

Description: Study 1: US Lucid respondents (2021; n = 2,339 with outcomes) each read one vignette of a Democratic state legislator varying age, race (Black/White), sex and two or three policy positions, and rated the candidate's ideology (3 items), issue priorities (7) and fairness to eight groups.
Reference: Wu, J. D., & Huber, G. A. (2024). How and when candidate race affects inferences about ideology and group favoritism. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/wu_2024_candidate_race.R (study 1). One vignette per respondent; policies stored per issue with '(not shown)' and attrpos_ (display rank). Answer texts coded to ordered integers (ideology 1 = Extremely Liberal). Three predicted-policy items dropped (wording not recoverable). 128 break-offs without outcomes dropped (export 2,467 = article N). Panel demographic codes kept as _code.

Description: Study 2: US Lucid respondents (January 2022; n = 1,447 after the pre-registered attention check) each rated five Democratic candidate vignettes varying race (White/Black/Asian/Hispanic), age, sex, experience, district racial composition, Biden vote share and policy positions: vote likelihood, perceived ideology and how much the candidate would prioritize eight groups.
Reference: Wu, J. D., & Huber, G. A. (2024). How and when candidate race affects inferences about ideology and group favoritism. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/wu_2024_candidate_race.R (study 2). task = candidate number (1-5). attr_district rebuilt from the exported shares in the template wording; CAUTION: the appendix lists the Hispanic and Asian shares in the opposite slots from the export's field names (header). Answer texts coded to ordered integers. Panel demographic codes kept as _code.

Description: 1,600 Chinese online respondents each chose between and rated two public servants in three scenarios (traffic stop, subway ID check, government service hall), varying sex, age, accent and whether they wore a Communist Party badge. Outcomes: forced choice and two 1-10 ratings (willingness to cooperate, would protect my interests).
Reference: Zhang, Y., & Wang, H. (2024). Symbolic bureaucratic representation and client cooperation: Experimental insights from four daily public service scenarios in China. Public Administration.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/zhang_2024_bureaucrat.R. Experiments 1-3 of four (experiment 4, hotline operator, has a different attribute set: zhang_2024_hotline_operator). Level text is the Chinese questionnaire text; codes were mapped through the authors' congruence variables (sex, age, party badge), except accent, whose code order is inferred from the questionnaire option order. Education, respondent accent and area keep codes (_code). Article respondent count not checked.

Description: 1,600 Chinese online respondents chose between and rated two 12345 government-hotline operators, varying sex, apparent age (sounds young / older), accent and whether the operator was a human or an AI chatbot. Outcomes: forced choice and two 1-10 ratings.
Reference: Zhang, Y., & Wang, H. (2024). Symbolic bureaucratic representation and client cooperation: Experimental insights from four daily public service scenarios in China. Public Administration.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/zhang_2024_bureaucrat.R. Experiment 4 of four (shown after the three in zhang_2024_bureaucrat_cooperation; task = 1 here). Level text is the Chinese questionnaire text; codes mapped through the authors' congruence and dummy variables, except accent (code order inferred from the questionnaire). Article respondent count not checked.

Description: Residents of Nordland, Troms and Finnmark (Norway; electronic survey, n = 490, the without-jobs half of a split sample) chose among the current-regulation scenario and two stricter-regulation scenarios on 8 cards varying coastal landscape (aquaculture/fishing-tourism facilities), beach waste, recreational catch and household tax; outcome is the preferred scenario.
Reference: Aanesen, M., & Armstrong, C. W. (2019). Trading off co-produced marine ecosystem services: Natural resource industries versus other use and non-use ecosystem service values. Frontiers in Marine Science, 6, 102.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/aanesen_2019.R. The other (with-jobs) half of the same split-sample survey is aanesen_2018_coastal_recreation (doi:10.18710/OFG1XW); different attribute set, so separate tables. Levels coded per the Variable Explanation, shown in the questionnaire's Norwegian card wording; the questionnaire's printed cards do not match the data's card combinations (probably another version), so level text rests on the codebook. 75 tasks without a recorded choice dropped.

Description: Participants in 7 Irish valuation workshops (2014, n = 139) chose among two cold-water coral protection options and the status quo on 12 cards varying protected area, attractiveness to business, importance as fish habitat and household cost, once before and once after a group discussion.
Reference: Aanesen, M., Armstrong, C., & van Rensburg, T. M. (2021). Do we choose differently after a discussion? Results from a deliberative valuation study in Ireland. Land Economics, 97(1), 207-223.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/aanesen_2021.R. Tasks 13-24 repeat cards 1-12 after the discussion (trial_round, trial_repeat_of). Business attribute text built from the codebook's oil/fish dummies with the questionnaire wording; status quo shown with its printed levels. Two card versions (A: municipalities 1-2, not printed in the questionnaire; B: as printed). 40 version-A tasks with an invalid cost code '2' and 16 tasks without exactly one choice dropped.

Description: US MTurk workers (2018, n = 1,991; 1,507 pass the authors' quality filter) read one 'James' vignette with race, spouse's name (Karen/Keith), free-time activity (Baptist/secular scouting/sports) and demonstrations (anti-tax/living-wage/student government) randomized, and chose which statement about James is most likely (sales / sales and Democrat / sales and Republican).
Reference: Ahler, D. J., & Sood, G. (2022). Typecast: A routine mental shortcut causes party stereotyping. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/ahler_2022.R. Outcome is a NOMINAL 3-category code (1 sales, 2 sales + Democrat, 3 sales + Republican) stored as rating. cov_untrustworthy = authors' filter (paper analyses the 1,507 with 0). GPA belief item dropped (no labels). Other studies in the deposit are single-factor and not built.

Description: US Qualtrics-panel respondents (June-July 2019, n=2,427) chose in 3 tasks between two climate policy packages varying carbon tax design, fossil fuel company policy, electricity generation standard, investments, household energy cost, government spending and transportation (Experiment 2); forced choice, raked weights.
Reference: Bergquist, P., Mildenberger, M., & Stokes, L. C. (2020). Combining climate, economic, and social policy builds public support for climate action in the US. Environmental Research Letters, 15(5), 054019.
Notes: data/conjoint/bergquist_2020.R. Experiment 2 of 2 (companion table bergquist_2020_gnd_social, same respondents and ids). Early respondents saw Sponsor instead of Transportation as the 7th attribute; the authors dropped them from this experiment (2,427 kept; the article reports 2,476 for both). Built from the authors' re-raked weighted file. No policy in a category stored as '(not shown)'. Article AMCEs for the clean energy standard (+10 to +11) reproduce.

Description: US Qualtrics-panel respondents (June-July 2019, n=2,476) chose in 3 tasks between two climate policy packages varying economic programs, social programs, carbon tax design, household energy cost, annual government spending and sponsor (Experiment 1); forced choice, raked weights.
Reference: Bergquist, P., Mildenberger, M., & Stokes, L. C. (2020). Combining climate, economic, and social policy builds public support for climate action in the US. Environmental Research Letters, 15(5), 054019.
Notes: data/conjoint/bergquist_2020.R. Experiment 1 of 2 (companion table bergquist_2020_gnd_energy, same respondents and ids). Built from the authors' weighted analysis file (2,476 respondents after their filters). No policy in a category stored as '(not shown)'. Between-respondent benefits framing in trial_benefits. Article AMCEs (job guarantee +12, energy cost -12/-21, spending -4/-9) reproduce. The raw Qualtrics exports in the deposit hold latitude/longitude, ZIP codes and panel IDs (not used).

Description: Norwegian adults (Kantar online panel, May-June 2023, n = 3,300 answering) chose between two party platforms (Parti A/B) in 5 tasks varying tax, refugee, environmental, indigenous-minority, Ukraine and municipality-merger policy; outcome is the chosen party.
Reference: Binningsbø, H. M., Dyrstad, K., & Finseraas, H. (2025). How does public opinion respond to government injustices against historically discriminated minorities? Evidence from Norway. British Journal of Political Science, 55, e91.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/binningsbo_2025.R. Levels = Norwegian Stata value labels. Question wording not deposited (paraphrase). Task 5 repeats task 1 with profiles swapped (trial_repeat_of). Deposit has 3,317 respondents vs article 2,962 native Norwegians (no nativity flag deposited). Kantar weight kept; the authors do not weight.

Description: Adults in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa and the Philippines (English text; cov_country), TGM Research online panels (n = 1883), chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical foreign bailout loans for a government in financial crisis varying interest rate, collateral, lender (IMF, Chinese government, US government, private banks) and conditions. One of 8 tables (2 experiments x 4 display-text groups) from the same study.
Reference: Bulman, D., Leng, N., & Ratigan, K. (2025). Foreign borrowing, sovereignty, and public opinion in the Global South: Traditional lenders or China? The Review of International Organizations.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/bulman_2025_loans.R. Built from the wide CleanData file with the displayed (survey-language) text; each respondent did only one of the two experiments. Countries with identical displayed level text pooled with cov_country, as the authors pool. cov_gender_code kept as codes: the supplement's gender counts are the reverse of d_female in every country.

Description: Polish adults (face-to-face representative survey, fall 2022; 2,476 of 2,500 with an answer) compared pairs of hypothetical refugees (3 Syrian, then 3 Ukrainian tasks) varying family status, economic status, suffering, religion and skin tone; outcomes are a forced choice, willingness to host (1-4), donating food/money (1-5) and three yes/no judgements (in need, crime, burden).
Reference: Charnysh, V., Peisakhin, L., Stoop, N., & van der Windt, P. (2026). Understanding refugee assistance: Evidence on Syrian and Ukrainian refugees in Poland. Comparative Political Studies.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/charnysh_2026.R. Task and profile inferred from row order (verified: exactly one chosen per pair). Level text = authors' English figure labels (Polish survey text not deposited); outcome wording from Stata variable labels (paraphrase). Syrian/Ukrainian block kept as trial_refugee_origin; preceding survey-experiment arm as trial_treatment. Food/money/need/crime/burden asked only in tasks 1 and 4.

Description: Lab-in-the-field respondents in Madhepura, Bihar, India (spring 2015, n=1,021) each evaluated 3 single fictitious state legislators varying photo, district, subcaste, party, record, family background, criminal charges, 2010 wealth, wealth increase and suspected illegality; outcomes are whether they would consider voting for him and four 1-5 ratings (job addressing problems, personal help, corruption, violence).
Reference: Chauchard, S., Klasnja, M., & Harish, S. P. (2019). Getting rich too fast? Voters' reactions to politicians' wealth accumulation. The Journal of Politics, 81(4), 1197-1209.
Notes: data/conjoint/chauchard_2019.R. Level text is the authors' English Stata value labels, not the displayed wording (the example vignette and questionnaire, Appendix A9/A13, are not deposited); photos stored as 'Photo 1-6'; subcaste as recorded. One vignette per respondent carries the respondent's own subcaste (design). Legality '(not shown)' when there is no wealth increase. Outcome wording paraphrased from the article; scale anchors unknown. 88 vote don't-knows are NA. Article reports N = 1,020; deposit has 1,021.

Description: Paired conjoint on participatory processes: 1,050 Finnish adults (Qualtrics panel) chose between two hypothetical participatory processes in 5 comparisons, varying policy issue, inclusiveness, number of gatherings, transparency, online vs face-to-face meetings, how participants form judgements and whether the outcome is binding or advisory; outcome is a forced choice.
Reference: Christensen, H. S. (2020). How citizens evaluate participatory processes: A conjoint analysis. European Political Science Review, 12(2), 239-253.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/christensen_2020_participatory.R. Levels are the English wording of the article's Table 1 (Finnish display text not deposited), mapped from the .dta value labels. task and profile inferred from pair id order and row order. Authors' dichotomized process-preference item dropped.

Description: Finnish respondents (n = 1,021) chose between two hypothetical candidates in 7 pairs varying gender, age, education, ideological closeness, political experience, endorsement source (nobody, VAA, social media, family/friend) and likelihood of election, each attribute possibly not shown.
Reference: Christensen, H. S., Järvi, T., Mattila, M., & von Schoultz, Å. (2021). How voters choose one out of many: A conjoint analysis of the effects of endorsements on candidate choice. Political Research Exchange, 3(1).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/christensen_2021.R. Levels = .dta value labels (English; Finnish display not deposited). 'NO INFO' level stored as (not shown) following the sibling christensen_2020_ep_candidates; whether a 'no information' text was displayed is undocumented. Article not retrievable (403): question wording paraphrased.

Description: Respondents in Egypt (n = 1,008) compared 3 pairs of hypothetical countries described by 9 three-level attributes (elections, civil liberties, executive constraints, populism, obedience, economic and gender equality, expert influence, direct democracy); outcomes: which country is more democratic, and a 1-10 democracy rating of each. One of six country tables from the same study.
Reference: Chu, J. A., Williamson, S., & Yeung, E. S. F. (2024). People consistently view elections and civil liberties as key components of democracy. Science, 386(6719), 291-296.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/chu_2024.R. Built from the raw Qualtrics export (displayed Egypt text, attribute positions recorded); six tables, one per country, because each sample saw its own language (authors pool them). attr_gender_equality is the equality of men's and women's rights, not a profile gender.

Description: Public servants in Germany (n = 379) and Taiwan (n = 365) rated 4 citizen candidates each for a citizen initiative, varying the candidate's traits (prototypical vs antiprototypical), gender and position (leader vs member), with policy field and collaboration type varied between respondents; outcome: willingness to collaborate, 1-7.
Reference: Dahlweg, A., Guo, Y., Liu, H. K., & Vogel, R. (2026). Public servants' implicit citizenship theories and willingness to collaborate with citizens: A cross-country study. Public Performance & Management Review.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/dahlweg_2026.R. Attribute levels are the codebook's English descriptions (the German/Chinese vignette text is not deposited); outcome wording is a paraphrase from the codebook. Task order = row order within respondent (no display index). Between-respondent scenario factors kept as trial_policy_field / trial_interaction. Article DOI not in the record.

Description: Researchers, tech-startup members and computing students in Adama City, Ethiopia (Aug-Dec 2025, n=150) ranked in 5 fixed choice sets three hypothetical open-government-data portals (search, download format, API, data quality, visualization) plus a status quo; the table stores each portal's rank 1-4 (1 = most preferred).
Reference: Debele, G. (2026). Dataset for: User-centered design for open government data platforms in developing smart cities: A discrete choice experiment in Adama City, Ethiopia [Data set]. Zenodo.
Notes: data/conjoint/debele_2026.R. Fixed design: all respondents saw the same 15 profiles in the same 5 sets and positions. Outcome is a rank (lower = more preferred); the status quo (no attributes, not a profile) takes the missing rank. Very regular structure (50 per stratum) flagged at triage; nothing shows the data are simulated. Manuscript not found published.

Description: Dutch secondary-school teachers (n = 140, convenience sample, 2025) each evaluated up to 6 of 32 hypothetical-student vignettes (full 2^5 factorial: gender, SES, ethnicity, work effort, class type), giving a transfer recommendation (lowest/highest track) and a 1-5 expectation of graduating at the highest track.
Reference: Drent, N., Timmermans, A. C., & Strijbos, J. W. (2026). Dataset: Beyond achievement: A vignette experiment on how intersecting student characteristics shape teachers' expectations and recommendations [Data set]. DANS Data Station Social Sciences and Humanities.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/drent_2026.R. Dutch vignette text (Magister-style mock-up) not deposited: levels are the codebook's English category labels. Display order not recorded (task inferred from row key). One row's missing characteristics filled from its vignette number. 722 rows vs codebook's 721; teachers 34 and 116 have 12 and 8 rows. Free-text comments dropped.

Description: Respondents in 14 EU countries (Dynata, 2021, n = 19,775) rated four vignettes in which a new party (populist or anti-government attack, one of eight policy demands) challenges their first-ranked party, which responds in one of six unified/divided ways; outcome is a 1-7 liking rating of the response.
Reference: Duell, D., & Kaftan, L. (2025). Voices of the party base: How supporters want established parties to respond to new parties. European Political Science Review.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/duell_2025.R. Vignette text (14 languages) not deposited: attack and party-response levels are the authors' short labels; policy demands are the article's English paraphrases mapped from codes (direction verified against the authors' congruence variable). Topics repeat within respondents although the article says one per policy area. Qualtrics ResponseIds dropped.

Description: German civil servants (online survey, n=276) read a vignette about a municipal employee (Frau or Herr Müller, randomized between subjects) who overlooked a tender quote and chose between two options in 4 of 18 fixed choice sets; each option combined error type, party aggrieved and error magnitude with the employee's response (reporting vs hiding, correcting vs ignoring).
Reference: Fischer, C., & Weißmüller, K. S. (2024). What determines civil servants' error response? Evidence from a conjoint experiment. American Review of Public Administration, 54(8), 747-770.
Notes: data/conjoint/fischer_2024.R. Fixed 18-set design transcribed from the authors' .do file; level text = German original from the operationalization docx with Frau/Herr substituted. ERROR-TYPE LABEL CONFLICT: the .do (and docx code numbering) call code 0 skill-based and 1 rule-based, the authors' R analytic CSV calls the same rows rule-based and skill-based; this table follows the .do. Display order not recorded (task = ascending set number; trial_choiceset = set). Choice question wording not deposited.

Description: Qatari citizens and resident expatriates (interviewer-administered survey, Qatar University SESRI, n=1,680) heard three hypothetical survey invitations varying sponsor, mode (in person / telephone), length (nested in mode) and topic, and said how likely they would be to take part (1 very likely to 4 very unlikely).
Reference: Gengler, J. J., Tessler, M., Lucas, R., & Forney, J. (2021). 'Why do you ask?' The nature and impacts of attitudes towards public opinion surveys in the Arab World. British Journal of Political Science, 51(1), 115-136.
Notes: data/conjoint/gengler_2021.R. Built from the authors' wide respondent file (attitudes-replication-anon), not their long conjoint file (which pre-reverses the outcome and repeats 10 caseids). Rating stored raw: 1 = very likely ... 4 = very unlikely (authors reverse it). Timing levels are nested in mode (60/30 min in person, 10/20 min by phone). Sponsor and mode text from the questionnaire's programming note (code order, matching the authors' R recode). cov_survey_weight = wgt. Don't know/refused omitted.

Description: Spanish pre-service elementary teachers (education students at 20 sampled universities, 2023, n = 1,717) each assessed one fictional 6th-grader from a full 2^7 factorial: student name (gender x Spanish/Moroccan origin), father's email (notary vs painter), subjects failed, behaviour, essay quality and an essay sentence signalling cultural capital; outcomes are the essay grade, grade-retention recommendation, academic-track expectations and perceived parental support.
Reference: Gil-Hernández, C. J., Pañeda-Fernández, I., Salazar, L., & Castaño Muñoz, J. (2024). Teacher bias in assessments by student ascribed status: A factorial experiment on discrimination in education. Sociological Science, 11, 743-776.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/gilhernandez_2024.R. One vignette per respondent (task 1, profile 1). Name and father's email are the displayed stimulus text (fictional; they carry gender, origin and SES); behaviour and subjects-failed levels are the article's English descriptions; the cultural-capital level is the Spanish essay sentence from the manipulation-check labels. Retention rating: higher = should repeat. Same data also in the JRC data catalogue (CC BY 4.0).

Description: German Bilendi panel respondents (April 2025, n = 3,864 in the deposit) chose between 3 pairs of hypothetical coalition agreements varying the coalition, economic policy, protectionism (tariffs, green tariffs or EU-contribution cuts), migration, women's quotas, LGBT funding and social-media regulation; outcomes are the preferred agreement and a 1-5 likelihood rating of each.
Reference: Grahn, M., Lawall, K., Mainz, S., Nordbrandt, M., & Turnbull-Dugarte, S. J. (2025). A game of tariffs: Is there demand for tariffs in Europe? Journal of European Public Policy.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/grahn_2025.R (Study 1). Level text = German text as displayed (emoji included) from the deposit's wide Qualtrics columns. Article reports 3,994 respondents, deposit 3,864. Outcome wording not deposited (paraphrase). The survey also held a video experiment whose assignment is not in the deposit.

Description: British Prolific respondents (May 2025, n = 1,500) chose between 5 pairs of hypothetical candidates of their own preferred party, varying name, age, job, photo, immigration position and motivation, social-media regulation, economic policy (including general and retaliatory tariffs) and position on the UK Supreme Court gender ruling; outcomes are the preferred candidate and a 1-5 likelihood of ever supporting each.
Reference: Grahn, M., Lawall, K., Mainz, S., Nordbrandt, M., & Turnbull-Dugarte, S. J. (2025). A game of tariffs: Is there demand for tariffs in Europe? Journal of European Public Policy.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/grahn_2025.R (Study 2). Level text as displayed (emoji included) from the deposit's wide Qualtrics columns. attr_photo is the Qualtrics graphic id of the candidate photo (images not deposited); the authors' candidate category (A-D) behind photos/names is undocumented and not stored. Both candidates run for the respondent's preferred party (trial_candidate_party).

Description: Urban residents of the USA, UK and South Africa (Qualtrics panels, n = 1,192) each read one vignette from a 2 x 2 x 3 factorial about a tourist trophy hunt in sub-Saharan Africa varying the animal (elephant/zebra), use of the meat and use of the revenue, and rated how acceptable the hunt would be (7-point).
Reference: Hare, D., Dickman, A. J., Johnson, P. J., Rono, B. J., Mutinhima, Y., Sutherland, C., Kulunge, S., Sibanda, L., Mandoloma, L., & Kimaili, D. (2024). Public perceptions of trophy hunting are pragmatic, not dogmatic. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences, 291, 20231638.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hare_2024.R. One vignette per respondent (task 1, profile 1). Level text is the article's description of the manipulated vignette language (vignette text itself is in supplement S3, not read). Rating numbered 1-7 from the deposited answer text (higher = more acceptable); 'I don't know' answers were removed by the authors. No respondent id in the deposit (row = respondent).

Description: US MTurk respondents (Aug 2014, n=2,217) rated on a 1-9 oppose-support scale each of two hypothetical US foreign-aid packages in 4 tasks; packages varied extra benefits to the US, cost, a potential issue in the recipient (none, placebo, aid theft, rigged elections, torture, media crackdown) and remedial aid (amount and channel).
Reference: Heinrich, T., & Kobayashi, Y. (2020). How do people evaluate foreign aid to "nasty" regimes? British Journal of Political Science, 50(1), 103-127.
Notes: data/conjoint/heinrich_2020.R. Authors' 2 test rows dropped; the authors' further exclusion (>=4 screener failures or conjoint page time outside 40-800 s; 124 respondents, leaving 2,093) is NOT applied but reproducible from cov_screener_failures and cov_duration_sec. Remedy display wording not deposited: amount stored as codebook value in million USD/year, target as codebook text; '(not shown)' when the amount is 0 (inferred from screenshot + authors' code). IP addresses and ZIP codes in the deposit dropped.

Description: World Bank staff (mostly task team leaders; elite online survey, 2022, n=178) rated 7 pairs of hypothetical development policy loans with eight binary features (prior-action conditions, amount, environmental/social and macroeconomic risk, gender-disaggregated targets, recipient CPIA score, past US opposition, income status) on the likelihood of board approval and of positive development impact (1-10 each).
Reference: Heinzel, M., Weaver, C., & Jorgensen, S. (2025). Bureaucratic representation and gender mainstreaming in international organizations: Evidence from the World Bank. American Political Science Review, 119(1), 332-348.
Notes: data/conjoint/heinzel_2024.R. Attribute 0/1 dummies mapped to the level text of Appendix Table A2 (direction from the variable labels). Two ratings per profile (rating_approval, rating_impact). cov_survey_weight = the preregistered region x sector post-stratification weight (weights_final). cov_women is 1 woman / 0 not (questionnaire also offered non-binary and prefer not to say). Region/sector kept as unlabelled codes; discipline and nationality codes dropped (no key). Published online 2024 (APSR 119(1), 2025).

Description: YouGov respondents in Kenya, Argentina and Pakistan (April 2023, n = 2,643) rated two hypothetical IMF loans whose eight conditions (foreign investment, import taxes, debt, corruption, anti-poverty, privatization, climate, gender equality) were each Yes/No; outcomes are support for the loan and willingness to pay more taxes or endure spending cuts (1-6).
Reference: Heinzel, M., Kern, A., Metinsoy, S., & Reinsberg, B. (2025). Public support for green, inclusive, and resilient growth conditionality in International Monetary Fund bailouts. International Studies Quarterly, 69(2), sqaf018.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/heinzel_2025.R. One task, two profiles, ratings only. Attribute wording from the article (English; Argentina saw Spanish). File has 2,643 respondents vs 2,694 in the article. Deposit also re-hosts WVS_TimeSeries_4_0.dta (not used). natgroup_Pak dropped (labels are a Gulf-states template).

Description: Swiss residents (IPSOS online quota sample, December 2017, n = 2,034) saw 5 pairs of proposals (initiative vs counter-proposal) to cut car emissions, each a policy instrument (7) with an implementation year (2025-2045) under an EV or emission-reduction frame; outcomes are support/reject of each proposal and the choice between them.
Reference: Huber, R. A., Wicki, M. L., & Bernauer, T. (2020). Public support for environmental policy depends on beliefs concerning effectiveness, intrusiveness, and fairness. Environmental Politics, 29(4), 649-673.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/huber_2020.R. First conjoint of the survey whose second conjoint is wicki_2020_vehicle_emissions (same respondents, separate experiment). Levels = appendix Table A4 English names (each shown with a frame-dependent description; display in de/fr/it). Wording paraphrased from the appendix example. Dataverse record cites the wrong article DOI (…1628872).

Description: Paired conjoint on Japan-China relations: 3,639 Chinese online respondents chose between two hypothetical bilateral policy packages in 3 tasks varying Yasukuni visits, One Belt One Road cooperation, tariffs in each direction, Japan's constitutional amendment and Diaoyu/Senkaku sovereignty and resource development.
Reference: Incerti, T., Mattingly, D., Rosenbluth, F., Tanaka, S., & Yue, J. (2021). Hawkish partisans: How political parties shape nationalist conflicts in China and Japan. British Journal of Political Science, 51(4), 1494-1515.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/incerti_2021.R (builds the China and Japan tables). Levels are the Chinese text as displayed (English in Online Appendix Table A.1). Per-profile 'score' (0-7, wording not deposited) and 'which country does this favour' items left out. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Panel ids dropped.

Description: Paired conjoint on Japan-China relations: 3,331 Japanese online respondents chose between two hypothetical bilateral policy packages in 3 tasks varying Yasukuni visits, One Belt One Road cooperation, tariffs in each direction, Japan's constitutional amendment and Diaoyu/Senkaku sovereignty and resource development.
Reference: Incerti, T., Mattingly, D., Rosenbluth, F., Tanaka, S., & Yue, J. (2021). Hawkish partisans: How political parties shape nationalist conflicts in China and Japan. British Journal of Political Science, 51(4), 1494-1515.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/incerti_2021.R (builds the China and Japan tables). Levels are the Japanese text as displayed (English in Online Appendix Table A.1). Per-profile 'score' (0-7, wording not deposited) and 'which country does this favour' items left out. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Panel ids dropped.

Description: Factorial vignette survey: 440 French education stakeholders (teachers, trainers, decision makers, researchers; online, 2022) each rated 8 text vignettes about a teacher accessing research, varying 6 binary factors (audience fit, teacher involvement, conceptual and instrumental utility, collaboration, institutional support), on how likely the teacher is to use the research (-5 to 5).
Reference: Jeune, N., Juhel, J., Dessus, P., & Atal, I. (2024). Six factors facilitating teachers' use of research: An experimental factorial survey of educational stakeholders' perspectives. Frontiers in Education, 9, 1368565.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/jeune_2024.R. Fixed D-efficient design: 16 of 64 vignettes in 2 blocks of 8. Vignette display order was randomized but not recorded: task = questionnaire position (trial_vignette = letter). Includes the 100 pilot respondents (cov_pilot = 1) the authors exclude from their main study (340).

Description: Paired candidate conjoint (Study 2): 1,043 US adults (Qualtrics panels, May 2017; Black, Latinx and white respondents oversampled to about one third each) saw 6 pairs of potential congressional candidates varying race, gender, policy priority, party, ideology and parental status; outcomes are vote choice with an 'I would not vote' option, which candidate addresses the respondent's concerns, and 1-4 ratings of likelihood of contacting, likelihood of donating and trustworthiness.
Reference: Joo, M., Lemi, D. C., Merolla, J. L., & Sellers, A. H. (2026). Only for some women: Experimental evidence on descriptive representation and political engagement. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/joo_2026.R. Levels are the .dta value labels. Ideology varies by profile and is in the authors' models but is not listed among the attributes in the article. Rating wording, anchors and direction undocumented (stored raw). Study 1 (6-arm single-vignette experiment, text not deposited) not built; the public Study 1 file contains zip codes, street numbers and GPS coordinates.

Description: Japanese adults (Research Now online panel, 2015, n = 1,611) chose between pairs of hypothetical House of Representatives candidates in 3 tasks varying gender, party, consumption-tax stance, policy priority, age, experience, education, children and marital status, and rated each candidate 1-7.
Reference: Kage, R., Rosenbluth, F. M., & Tanaka, S. (2019). What explains low female political representation? Evidence from survey experiments in Japan. Politics & Gender, 15(2), 285-309.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kage_2019.R. Levels are the authors' English labels (Japanese display). The 1-7 evaluation's wording/anchors are undocumented (stored raw; higher = more favourable by its association with choice). Attribute order randomized per task, not recorded. Survey 2 memo experiment and Studies 3-4 not built.

Description: Japanese adults (Research Now online panel, 2015, n = 1,611) chose which of two hypothetical politicians they would prefer to see promoted to LDP leader in 3 tasks varying gender, age, electoral experience, education, children and marital status, and rated each 1-7.
Reference: Kage, R., Rosenbluth, F. M., & Tanaka, S. (2019). What explains low female political representation? Evidence from survey experiments in Japan. Politics & Gender, 15(2), 285-309.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kage_2019.R. Levels are the authors' English labels (Japanese display). The 1-7 evaluation's wording/anchors are undocumented (stored raw; higher = more favourable by its association with choice). Attribute order randomized per task, not recorded. Survey 2 memo experiment and Studies 3-4 not built.

Description: Paired conjoint on recidivism-forecasting algorithms: 1,750 US online respondents (MTurk March 2018; Lucid March and April 2019) compared 5 pairs of algorithms varying 8 features (developer, accuracy, data size, human involvement, factor weights, data location, number of factors, error), choosing one and rating each 1-7 on willingness to use.
Reference: Kennedy, R. P., Waggoner, P. D., & Ward, M. M. (2022). Trust in public policy algorithms. The Journal of Politics, 84(2), 1132-1148.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kennedy_2022.R. Three fieldings pooled as in the authors' main analysis (cov_sample). Outcome wording paraphrased from the codebook (question stems not deposited). Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Covariate option lists differ between the MTurk and Lucid files. Qualtrics ResponseIds dropped.

Description: UK respondents (Prolific online sample, February 2022, n=975) chose between two hypothetical MPs from their party in 3 tasks, varying gender, age, education, former occupation (working-class vs white-collar) and years in politics; 15 forced-choice questions per pair (support, relatability, which better represents five groups, which better advocates on seven issues and on the respondent's top issue).
Reference: Kim, J. H., & Kweon, Y. (2024). Double penalty? How candidate class and gender influence voter evaluations. Research & Politics, 11(1).
Notes: data/conjoint/kim_2024_class_gender.R. UK table; companion kim_2024_class_gender_us. Represent items coded 1/4 in the export (4 = MP 2, verified against advocate items). Separate tables because separate samples analysed separately. Authors analyse only choice and choice_top_issue; the other 13 picks are kept. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Covariates mostly unlabelled codes (_code). Deposit is a raw Qualtrics export with IPs, GPS, Prolific IDs (all dropped).

Description: US respondents (Lucid online sample, October 2021, n=865) chose between two hypothetical candidates in their party's congressional primary in 3 tasks, varying gender, age, education, former occupation (working-class vs white-collar) and years in politics; 15 forced-choice questions per pair (support, relatability, which better represents five groups, which better advocates on seven issues and on the respondent's top issue).
Reference: Kim, J. H., & Kweon, Y. (2024). Double penalty? How candidate class and gender influence voter evaluations. Research & Politics, 11(1).
Notes: data/conjoint/kim_2024_class_gender.R. US table; companion kim_2024_class_gender_uk. trial_primary = Democratic/Republican primary block (by respondent's party). Separate tables because separate samples analysed separately. Authors analyse only choice and choice_top_issue; the other 13 picks are kept. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Covariates mostly unlabelled codes (_code). Deposit is a raw Qualtrics export with IPs, GPS, Lucid ids and ZIP codes (all dropped).

Description: MTurk (TurkPrime) participants in 2018 (n = 306) evaluated 12 fixed pairs of versions of a bank technology tracking card purchases, varying outcome favourability for the respondent, data sharing (none or one of two partners) and data protection; outcomes: choice of version A, B or neither, and 0-100 moral acceptability of each version. One of six technology tables from the same study; each respondent did two technologies.
Reference: Kodapanakkal, R. I., Brandt, M. J., Kogler, C., & van Beest, I. (2020). Self-interest and data protection drive the adoption and moral acceptability of big data technologies: A conjoint analysis approach. Computers in Human Behavior, 108, 106303.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kodapanakkal_2020.R. Licence: the DataverseNL record has no licence field; its terms of use read only 'CC-BY'. Built from the authors' processed per-domain files, whose respondent ids restart in each domain, so the two technologies a person rated cannot be linked (six tables). task = pair number of the fixed 12-pair design, not display order (loop order randomized, not recorded). Level text from the authors' Qualtrics .qsf on OSF (osf.io/4m2rg). Tasks with ratings but no choice kept with choice NA.

Description: Paired conjoint on how a district allocates a public-goods project: 1,043 Ghanaian adults (Ipsos face-to-face, nationally representative, 2023) compared 2 pairs of decision processes (status quo, citizen-elite deliberation, participatory, mini-public) varying party endorsement and whether their community gets the project; choice plus 1-7 fairness and democratic ratings.
Reference: Kramon, E. (2025). Are democratic innovations legitimate to the broader public? Evidence from survey experiments in Ghana. British Journal of Political Science.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/kramon_2025.R. Levels are the author's short English labels from the replication code (displayed wording, in the article's Table 2 and in four Ghanaian languages, not deposited). Experiment 2 (one attribute) not built. Authors' rescaled age/education scores dropped.

Description: Colombian online respondents (October 2019; 1,589 in the deposit, 1,528 who answered at least one task) chose in 4 tasks between two hypothetical candidates who were former combatants accused of violence against civilians (age, gender, education, recruitment, reputation, military success, crime, victims, involvement, attitude) and rated each 1-5 on likelihood of voting for them.
Reference: Levy, G. (2022). Evaluations of violence at the polls: Civilian victimization and support for perpetrators after war. The Journal of Politics, 84(2), 783-797.
Notes: data/conjoint/levy_2022.R. Attribute levels stored in Spanish as shown to respondents (codebook table; the data file has shortened English translations); gendered forms kept as the codebook writes them ('obligado/a'). Unanswered tasks: choice NA (744 tasks) and rows with neither outcome omitted (61 respondents answered nothing). Choice rows (11,224) equal the author's analysis data.

Description: Online panel respondents in Australia, Belgium, Canada, France, Switzerland and the USA (Qualtrics, winter 2020/21, n = 7,599, minority language groups oversampled) chose between 4 pairs of COVID-19 decision-making scenarios varying the responsible level of government, the influence of scientists, citizens and stakeholders, and transparency; outcome is the preferred scenario.
Reference: Mueller, S., & Bundi, P. (2024). Multilingual federalism in times of crisis. Regional & Federal Studies, 35(4), 631-665.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mueller_2024.R. Task and profile inferred from row order (8 rows per respondent, one choice per consecutive pair). Level text is the article's Table 1 English wording with its country-specific terms (federal/national; State/province/community and region/canton/region; municipality/county or city), mapped from the authors' short labels; the survey ran in Dutch, English, French and German. One pooled table with cov_country and cov_mother_tongue.

Description: Respondents in 32 countries recruited via Facebook/Instagram ads (Dec 2022-May 2023; 35,292 with a choice, 36,261 with any answer) chose which of two hypothetical countries they would prefer to live in (5 pairs; 10 in Turkey), varying elections, executive constraints, free speech, economy, crime, gender pay equality and ethnic diversity; they also rated each country's democracy and quality of life (0-1).
Reference: Neundorf, A., Dahlum, S., Frederiksen, K. V. S., & Ozturk, A. (2026). Elections without constraints? The appeal of electoral autocracy across the world. British Journal of Political Science, 56, e1.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/neundorf_2026.R. Level text = deposit value labels of the authors' binary recodes (displayed sentences in the article's Table 1 image, not deposited). Ratings only as the authors' 0-1 rescale of 0-10 answers. Task/profile derived from the countryprofile index (_1/_2 = task 1). ResponseId and city dropped. cov_gender_code codes unlabelled (1/3).

Description: Japanese voters (Rakuten Insight online panel, July 2020, n=2,267) rated 20 hypothetical Diet candidates one at a time on an 8-point favorability scale, 10 for the House of Representatives and 10 for the House of Councillors (chamber order randomized; half primed on the lower house's power to elect the PM); 8 attributes with real-world level probabilities (gender, party, age, education, occupation, hometown, experience, dynasty).
Reference: Ono, Y., Kasuya, Y., & Miwa, H. (2025). Analyzing gender gaps in bicameral legislatures: How asymmetrical institutions affect the supply and demand for female candidates. Legislative Studies Quarterly, 50(3), e12493.
Notes: data/conjoint/ono_2025.R. Demand-side study only (supply-side study is a single-factor vignette, not built). Levels stored in the Japanese displayed text (English in RIETI DP 22-E-094 Table A1); hometown keeps the source's template 'X出身'/'X外出身' where X was the respondent's prefecture (cov_prefecture). trial_chamber HoR/HoC, trial_priming = PM-power information arm. Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Task order rebuilt from HOR_first as in the authors' code. Level probabilities deliberately nonuniform (female 0.187).

Description: Residents of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba (online, n = 2,606) rated the acceptability (-5 to +5) of 6 of 54 one-sentence forest-management scenarios varying the managing agency, forest area type, disturbance type (wildfire, insects/disease, harvest), size and severity.
Reference: Parkins, J., Andison, D., Sponarski, C., & Nock, C. (2025). Forest disturbance preferences in the western forest regions of Canada [Data set]. Borealis.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/parkins_2025.R. Factorial vignette (54 scenarios in 2 fold-over blocks; trial_scenario). Display order of the 6 scenarios not recorded: task numbers follow scenario number (inferred). Rating stored as source codes 1-11 (= -5..+5). Deposit publishes 37 email addresses and partial postal codes (dropped).

Description: German-speaking students (SoSci Survey, 2016, n = 529) made 7 choices between two Facebook-use situations varying place of use (at home / elsewhere) and motive (information seeking, companionship, escapism, entertainment); fixed design in 4 blocks of 7.
Reference: Pelzer, E. (2019). The potential of conjoint analysis for communication research. Communication Research Reports, 36(2), 136-147.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/pelzer_2019.R. Levels are the author's English dummy-column names (German display text and question wording not deposited); task = order of situation number within the respondent's block (display order not recorded). One respondent whose situations straddle two blocks dropped. The traditional (ranking) conjoint in the same deposit shows the same 8 profiles to everyone and is not built.

Description: Paired candidate conjoint: 857 US adults (Dynata) chose between two hypothetical presidential-primary candidates in their own party in 5 tasks, with diet (none/vegetarian/vegan), animal-rights support, pets, race, gender, age, marital status and political experience randomized; outcome is a forced vote choice.
Reference: Saha, S. (2023). Why don't politicians talk about meat? The political psychology of human-animal relations in elections. Frontiers in Psychology, 14, 1021013.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/saha_2023.R. Built from the authors' cleaned long file clean_dat.csv; levels as stored there. Study 1 (one-factor vignette) not built. Question wording from the article (no questionnaire deposited). Qualtrics/panel IDs, free text and four undocumented 0-10/Likert items dropped.

Description: Finnish adults (Qualtrics online panel, May-June 2020, n = 1,030) chose between 6 pairs of prospective prime ministers varying on condemning/inciting violence against the opposition, respect for judicial decisions, ideology, immigration policy, populist decision-making, gender and education; outcomes are the preferred leader and whether they would also vote for that leader.
Reference: Saikkonen, I. A.-L., & Christensen, H. S. (2023). Guardians of democracy or passive bystanders? A conjoint experiment on elite transgressions of democratic norms. Political Research Quarterly, 76(1), 127-142.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/saikkonen_2023.R. Level text is the article's English Table 1 (the Finnish wording shown is not deposited), mapped from the .dta value labels. The same experiment underlies the authors' 'Lure of populism' files in the same OSF project (merged for respondent gender, age band and region). The authors' related policy-issue conjoint (OSF jn5kz) is christensen_2023_backsliding_issues, a different experiment.

Description: Vietnamese adults in the 2022 PAPI face-to-face survey (n = 5,890 with a vote) chose which of two hypothetical National Assembly candidates they would vote for, varying age, sex, education, party membership, whom the candidate benefits and kinship, after a randomized control, honesty or clientelism prime.
Reference: Schuler, P. (2024). Gender and clientelism: Do expectations of patronage penalize women candidates in legislative elections? Comparative Political Studies, 57(14), 2348-2375.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/schuler_2024.R. Built from Replication3 (PAPI 2022) only; the 2020/2021 files are a single-trait experiment. Level text = the survey's Vietnamese NAME fields. The authors' do-file codes inclan = 1 for the level named 'outside the clan' (label/code conflict; text kept as named). Prime arm kept as trial_prime. No weight in the 2022 file.

Description: Paired conjoint on preferred democratic institutions in Chile: 2,385 online respondents (2,650 in the file) compared up to 5 pairs of hypothetical democratic systems varying who can vote, law creation, same-sex marriage, presidential power, voting rules, party system and electoral system (Spanish text); outcome is a forced choice.
Reference: Singh, S. P., & Williams, N. S. (2021). What type of democracy do Chileans want? Research & Politics, 8(3), 20531680211031045.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/singh_2021.R. Levels are the Spanish texts in the deposit (one voting-rule level truncated in the source). All respondents kept; the authors analyse only attention-check passers (cov_attention_pass = 1, 1,630 respondents here). Article not reachable (bot wall): question wording, provider and dates undocumented. Authors' raking weights are computed in code, not deposited.

Description: US adults (SSI online sample, August 2016, n=2,521) read about a hypothetical state bill requiring 35% renewable electricity by 2025 with up to five randomized statements (cost increase, jobs, air pollution, climate-change framing, partisan legislator support; each with a no-information control) and rated their support on a 4-point scale; one vignette per respondent.
Reference: Stokes, L. C., & Warshaw, C. (2017). Renewable energy policy design and framing influence public support in the United States. Nature Energy, 2(8), 17107.
Notes: data/conjoint/stokes_2017.R. Level text = the authors' short figure labels (variables.tab), not the displayed sentences (paraphrased in the Methods; full instrument not deposited); control conditions (no statement) = '(not shown)'. Code-to-label mapping from the authors' plotting code, confirmed by reproducing the paper's cost/jobs/air effects exactly; climate code order rests on that mapping alone. Rating direction (4 = strongly support) inferred from the authors' binary recode. cov_ideo7_code has no labels. Raking weight is computed in the authors' code, not deposited.

Description: British Election Study panel members surveyed by YouGov in October 2021 (n = 1,636) chose 5 times between a Conservative and a Labour parliamentary candidate whose whole profiles (age, sex, left-right, EU vote, council experience, birthplace, four policy positions) were drawn from the realistic 2017 candidate distribution; half the respondents also saw the party labels. Outcome: vote choice with not-sure/would-not-vote options.
Reference: Titelman, N., & Lauderdale, B. E. (2024). The effects of party labels on vote choice with realistic candidate differentiation. Political Science Research and Methods.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/titelman_2024.R. Whole profiles drawn jointly from party-specific candidate models (not independent attribute randomization). Party label arm per respondent (trial_party_label; attr_party '(not shown)' without labels). attr_left_right holds only the 0-10 number; the band word shown with it (e.g. 'Centre right (6)') has no documented cut points. Attribute order randomized per respondent within blocks but the recorded permutation's indices are unmapped (no attrpos_). Deposit's candidate_Party_ProfileB duplicates ProfileA; B is the other party.

Description: Danish adults (YouGov quota sample, Dec 2020-Jan 2021, n=1,234) read three vignettes about a rich person varying gender, income (DKK 50,000/130,000 a month), family background, work ethic, treatment of workers, tax-loophole use, charity and consumption, and said whether that person's income taxes should be reduced or increased (1-5); survey weight included.
Reference: Trump, K.-S. (2025). When is it fair to tax the rich? The importance of pro-social behavior. Comparative Political Studies, 58(11), 2401-2435.
Notes: data/conjoint/trump_2025.R. Study 3. Respondents saw Danish text; levels stored in the English master text of the codebook/value labels (Danish translation docx leaves a placeholder unresolved). Loophole and consumption levels include gendered pronouns. Paper's loophole (0.25) and unfair-workers (0.1) AMCEs reproduce. cov_survey_weight = YouGov weight.

Description: US Prolific respondents (pilot, July 2020, n=599) read three vignettes about a rich person varying gender, income ($150k/$250k/$500k with top-percentile), source of income, work ethic, treatment of workers, tax-loophole use, charity and consumption, and said whether that person's income taxes should be reduced or increased (1-5).
Reference: Trump, K.-S. (2025). When is it fair to tax the rich? The importance of pro-social behavior. Comparative Political Studies, 58(11), 2401-2435.
Notes: data/conjoint/trump_2025.R. Pilot experiment (Appendix A2), not in the main text. Level text = displayed slot text; gender stored as the pronoun he/she. Companion tables trump_2025_tax_rich_us / _dk use a revised attribute set.
