Soft-launch item-order correction applied as in the authors' code. Authors' raking weights are computed in code, not stored. IP, GPS, one e-mail and forsa panel ids in the source dropped.

Description: Guatemalan household-survey respondents (n = 9,365, 14 departments) saw 2 pairs of crime scenarios varying victim gender, crime type, perpetrator type, perpetrator's community and perpetrator gender, and chose the case where community rather than police punishment would be better and the case deserving more severe punishment.
Reference: Dow, D., Levy, G., Romero, D., & Tellez, J. (2023). State absence, vengeance, and the logic of vigilantism in Guatemala. Comparative Political Studies, 57(1), 147-181.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/dow_2023.R. Attribute levels are the authors' English labels (survey fielded in Spanish; Spanish attribute wording not deposited). Municipality/community dropped; derived indices dropped; indigenous_lang and vigilante_assault dropped (ambiguous coding).

Description: YouGov respondents in France, Germany, Italy and the UK (early 2020, n = 14,000) each read five vignettes about an MP voting on a bill (one per policy area), with vote outcome, pivotality, MP gender, government/opposition party, tenure and rebellion against the party leadership randomized and bill-direction/public-opinion information varied by arm; outcomes are feeling represented, 'every MP should be like this MP' (1-7) and traits chosen after the last vignette.
Reference: Duell, D., Kaftan, L., Proksch, S.-O., Slapin, J., & Wratil, C. (2024). The rhyme and reason of rebel support: Exploring European voters' attitudes toward dissident MPs. Political Science Research and Methods, 12(2), 301-317.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/duell_2023.R. Level text = authors' English labels (respondents saw FR/DE/IT/EN; full wording in the article appendix). Bill direction and public opinion shown only in some arms ('(not shown)' otherwise); when shown, direction was set relative to the respondent's own preference (cov_pref_*). Trait items asked once after vignette 5 and stored on task 5. Follow-up UK study (Ext files) not built.

Description: Armenian adults (face-to-face tablet survey, 2023, n = 1,497) compared 5 pairs of fictional corruption scenarios varying type of corruption, sector, official's rank and gender, amount, use of funds and sharing, choosing which harms their family, the economy, political trust most, which is more morally wrong and which is more frequent.
Reference: Erlich, A., Gans-Morse, J., Nichter, S., & Holverscheid, A. (2025). What corruption is most harmful? Unbundling citizen perceptions. World Development, 194, 107001.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/erlich_2025_corruption.R (erlich_2025.R is a different study). Armenian level text from the formr design file; outcome wording from the English SurveyInstrument.docx (SPSS labels of X1_S*.2-5 are stale). Restricted design (two corruption types only with personal use and keeping funds). Tasks whose recorded screen number did not match are dropped (61). 244 formr IDs reused across interviews (same profiles; kept as the authors do); id is one interview (row of AIP_FINAL.sav, distinct submission time), never the formr ID. Second (anti-corruption agency) conjoint in the deposit not built: unpublished and undocumented. Authors' analysis sample 1,495; table 1,497.

Description: 1,788 US MTurk respondents (2021) each rated 10 pairs of hypothetical gubernatorial candidates varying age, gender, background, party, two policy positions and a democratic or undemocratic statement (aggressive vs non-aggressive behaviours); each respondent rated one randomly assigned trait: dominance, warmth, competence or vote likelihood (7-point, stored rescaled 0-1).
Reference: Frederiksen, K. V. S., & Laustsen, L. (2025). Interstate conflict increases the appeal of undemocratic candidates. British Journal of Political Science.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/frederiksen_2025.R. Second of the two Study 1 conjoint experiments only; the first experiment (2,022 respondents) is held because its behaviour statements differ (Appendix Table A1) and the .dta carries only the second experiment's labels. Ratings are the authors' 0-1 rescaling of 7-point items. One outcome per respondent (four rating columns, three NA on each row).

Description: 300 UK adults each made 20 forced choices between two burgers (Option A/B) shown on image cards varying type (normal, plant-based, cell-cultured), price, healthiness and customer star rating, framed as a supermarket or a restaurant purchase (randomized between respondents). Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Gan, Y. S. (2026). Who chooses alternative meat and where? Understanding how foodscapes and individual variation shape plant-based meat and cell-cultured meat choices using a Discrete Choice Experiment [Data set]. OSF.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/gan_2026.R. Fixed 20-set idefix design joined from the deposited design file; level text read off the choice-card images (4 cards checked against the design). Restaurant prices = design + £10. Question wording not deposited. The authors' descriptives use n = 285; all 300 kept. No article found.

Description: US respondents (n = 2,003 with answers) each compared 8 pairs of hypothetical candidates in their party's primary (independents assigned to either), with race, gender, age, ideology, experience, personableness, speaking ability and two district features randomized, choosing which candidate is more electable and which they would vote for.
Reference: Hassell, H. J. G., & Visalvanich, N. (2023). Perceptions of electability: Candidate (and voter) ideology, race, and gender. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/hassell_2023.R. Questionnaire not deposited and article unreadable: level text as stored in the data (incl. typo 'Not ersonable'), numeric district levels (55/95 % white, incumbent won 51/68) and paraphrased outcome wording from the codebook. Primary scenario (trial_primary) follows respondent party; ideology levels depend on it. Skipped pairs NA (authors code 0). Qualtrics/panel ids dropped.

Description: UK YouGov omnibus respondents (2022, n=2,058) rated two hypothetical UK aid agencies side by side (Experiment 3) on 1-10 support for giving foreign aid through each; agencies varied in Yes/No on seven reforms (expanded transparency, anti-corruption, aid to political allies, to the poorest countries, to countries respecting human rights, for climate change, donor coordination).
Reference: Heinzel, M., Reinsberg, B., & Swedlund, H. (2024). Transparency and citizen support for public agencies: The case of foreign aid. Governance, 38(2), e12863.
Notes: data/conjoint/heinzel_2024_aid.R. Article Experiment 3; one task of two profiles per respondent; same respondents and ids as heinzel_2024_aid_transparency. Attribute levels are the displayed Yes/No; statement wording in the script header (Stata labels vs article Table 4 differ slightly, e.g. 'focuses on' vs 'focuses more on'). YouGov weight kept; monadic FCDO experiment arm and outcome kept as covariates.

Description: UK YouGov omnibus respondents (2022, n=2,058) rated two hypothetical UK aid agencies side by side (Experiment 2) on 1-10 support for giving foreign aid through each; agencies varied in Yes/No on six types of information the agency discloses (aid strategy, decision-making, organisational structure, operational costs, staff, project details).
Reference: Heinzel, M., Reinsberg, B., & Swedlund, H. (2024). Transparency and citizen support for public agencies: The case of foreign aid. Governance, 38(2), e12863.
Notes: data/conjoint/heinzel_2024_aid.R. Article Experiment 2; one task of two profiles per respondent; same respondents and ids as heinzel_2024_aid_reforms. Attribute levels are the displayed Yes/No; statement wording in the script header (Stata labels truncated at 80 characters and worded slightly differently from the article tables). YouGov weight kept; monadic FCDO experiment arm and outcome kept as covariates. Article Table 3 reproduced exactly.

Description: Staff of six UN organizations (elite survey recruited by email and LinkedIn, n = 280) compared 7 pairs of hypothetical voluntary contributions varying earmarking (own area of work, country, sector, project), spending period and donor type; outcomes are a forced choice and, per contribution, the minimum worthwhile amount, the overhead to charge, and rejection.
Reference: Heinzel, M., Reinsberg, B., & Siauwijaya, C. (2025). Understanding resourcing trade-offs in international organizations: Evidence from an elite survey experiment. The Journal of Politics, 88(3), 1231-1244.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/heinzel_2025_earmarking.R. Amount and overhead were open-text answers; the table stores the authors' numeric cleaning (amount_clean, overhead_clean) and their refusal flag, not the raw text. Forced-choice wording not reported. cov_survey_weight is the authors' post-stratification weight to UN staff composition (robustness only).

Description: Participants in 15 Deliberative Monetary Valuation workshops in Poland, Italy, the Basque Country (Spain), Germany and France (2023-24, n = 172) chose among two marine-policy scenarios and business as usual on 16 fixed cards varying climate regulation, algal/jellyfish blooms, plankton stability, marine protected area status and an annual tax.
Reference: Jean-Louis, G. (2025). Europe-wide public preferences for plankton-based ecosystem services and marine biodiversity from a series of Deliberative Monetary Valuation workshops [Data set]. Zenodo.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/jeanlouis_2025.R. Card text parsed from the English questionnaire and checked against the Ngene design (all 32 designed alternatives match). The business-as-usual column shows attributes and is profile 3. Countries pooled (cov_country); levels stored in English, respondents saw translations. CS answer codes 1-3 inferred from the three columns (not in the codebook). Postcodes dropped. No linked article.

Description: COP29 participants (151 state representatives and non-state observers) chose between 2 UNFCCC reform proposals in each of 6 tasks, proposals varying presidency selection, decision-making, implementation focus, representation, role of observers and transparency.
Reference: Koliev, F., Nasiritousi, N., Buylova, A., & Linnér, B.-O. (2026). Reform preferences of key actors in the UNFCCC process. Nature Climate Change, 16(8), 915-921.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/koliev_2026.R. ' (SQ)' status-quo suffix stripped from levels (not shown to respondents per pre-registration and instrument). Qualtrics ResponseId and 'other group' free text dropped. Elite sample: only actor group, region and COP experience collected.

Description: US respondents in the UC Riverside module of the 2020 CCES (n = 1,000) each rated one hypothetical congressional candidate whose PAC-contribution policy (accepts/doesn't), prior elected experience (none/councilmember/mayor) and gender were randomized; candidate party matched the respondent's party. Outcomes: likelihood of voting for, donating to, and trustworthiness of the candidate (7-point).
Reference: Landgrave, M., Jenkins, N. R., & Hardesty, A. J. (2025). Do congressional candidates benefit from rejecting PAC contributions? Evidence from a pre-registered candidate evaluation survey experiment. Research & Politics, 12(3).
Notes: Script data/conjoint/landgrave_2025.R. Ratings stored raw: 1 = Very likely/trustworthy, 7 = Very unlikely/untrustworthy (authors reverse them). Vignette text and question wording not deposited (level text = value labels; wording paraphrased from codebook). Candidate party equals the respondent's party for partisans and is kept as trial_candidate_party. Zip codes and CCES ids dropped.

Description: Paired conjoint on Danish social-assistance reform: 1,287 Danish online respondents (May 2022) chose between 2 reform proposals in each of 4 tasks; proposals varied the proposing bloc, work and residence requirements, benefit rates for non-citizens, disabled people and parents, sanctions, job-offer and job-training requirements and tax cost. Outcome is a forced choice.
Reference: Larsen, M. H. (2025). Politics of welfare exclusion: Open and concealed welfare chauvinism and public support for social assistance reform. Acta Sociologica.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/larsen_2025.R. Levels are the author's English recode labels from the replication Rmd (respondents saw Danish; displayed text not deposited). Question wording paraphrased (not deposited; article not reachable). Attribute order randomized per respondent (attrpos_). Survey weight kept.

Description: Researchers in an online survey (2018-19, n = 224, mostly economists and social scientists) ranked 20 fixed sets of 3 fictitious publications described only by six metrics (citations, tweets, Mendeley readers, downloads, journal impact factor, h-index); outcomes are the first pick and the full rank.
Reference: Lemke, S., Mazarakis, A., & Peters, I. (2021). Conjoint analysis of researchers' hidden preferences for bibliometrics, altmetrics, and usage metrics. Journal of the Association for Information Science and Technology, 72(6), 777-792.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lemke_2021.R. Fixed chained design of 20 sets; two-step ranking (best, then second) stored as choice and rating_rank (1 = best). No codebook or questionnaire deposited and the article was not retrievable: attribute names from column abbreviations and the deposit/related descriptions; levels are the numbers shown. Screen position not recorded (profiles ordered by publication id). Sets 1-2 missing for many respondents; one task where the two deposit files disagree dropped.

Description: Swiss Mobility Panel wave 4 respondents (registry sample, online, winter 2022-23, n = 7,442) each read one public-transport policy proposal from a 3 x 3 x 3 x 2 factorial (connections per day, peripheral-region coverage, ticket prices, public funding), voted for or against it and rated support on a 7-point scale.
Reference: Lichtin, F. M., Smith, E. K., Axhausen, K. W., & Bernauer, T. (2024). How much should public transport services be expanded, and who should pay? Experimental evidence from Switzerland. Transport Policy, 158, 64-74.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/lichtin_2024.R. Level text = the pre-registration's English instrument sentences mapped from the deposit's short labels (respondents saw DE/FR/IT/EN). No respondent id in the deposit: one row = one respondent. All 54 designs kept; the article's n = 1,634 is the authors' 12 'plausible' designs (reproduced). Info arm (full/short instructions) in trial_info_arm. Data are an extract of the Swiss Mobility Panel (full data later on SWISSUbase).

Description: Taiwanese respondents (Study 1, n=2,078 with an answer) compared 5 pairs of ballot designs drawn from 7 (Chinese only, or Chinese with Paiwan and/or Vietnamese, stacked or in separate columns) and picked which ballot of each pair was more fair, more democratic and more efficient.
Reference: Liu, A. H., Selsky, S., Xu, M., & Yew, J. (2026). When bilingual ballot designs promote or undermine inclusivity: Evidence from three studies. Public Opinion Quarterly.
Notes: data/conjoint/liu_2026.R. Study 1 (Taiwan) only; Studies 2 (Texas, fixed 3 ballots best/worst) and 3 (Georgia, one-factor between-subjects) are not conjoints. Profiles are 7 fixed ballot images; attribute levels are the authors' English descriptions (Rmd), monolingual ballot has arrangement '(not shown)'. Outcome wording not deposited (paraphrased from variable names). Demographic codes have no codebook and are dropped except gender and region. Article closed access; N not checked.

Description: Israeli (Jewish) online respondents (n = 1,345) chose between two policy packages varying West Bank territorial control, rocket and terror attacks, the economy and the security/health/education budgets (one task), and rated each package 1-7.
Reference: Manekin, D. S., Grossman, G., & Mitts, T. (2019). Contested ground: Disentangling material and symbolic attachment to disputed territory. Political Science Research and Methods, 7(4), 679-697.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/manekin_2019.R. One task; profile inferred from row order (verified against Q8_conjoint_choice). Levels are the authors' English (survey in Hebrew). rank_policy (rating, 1-7) has no documented wording or direction. Three randomization restrictions (authors' cjoint design). Phase-2 conjoint in the deposit not built (numeric codes, only plot-axis labels).

Description: US state and local officials and staff (CivicPulse elite survey, Feb-Apr 2017, n = 745) rated 3 pairs of hypothetical state-legislative election scenarios varying salary, fundraising required, and the opponent's experience, advertising and ideology; outcomes are interest in running (1-5) and perceived chance of winning (1-5).
Reference: Marble, W., Lee, N., & Bram, C. (2025). Stepping up the political ladder: How the burden of fundraising limits candidate entry. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/marble_2025.R. Built from Clean.RDS (not the authors' reshaped file, which collapses opponent levels). Opponent ideology restricted to the side opposed to the respondent's own (moderates saw all). Ratings coded 1-5 from option text (authors use -2..2 and 5/25/50/75/95). 745 respondents vs 734 responses in the preanalysis plan. Jurisdiction population/expenditure fields dropped as identifying.

Description: Irish general practitioners (n = 150) read 6 vignettes of a 5-year-old with fever and cough varying repeat presentation, time and day, parental request for referral, parental capacity to cope and access to a rapid paediatric clinic, and decided whether to refer the child to the emergency department.
Reference: McDonnell, T., Nicholson, E., & McAuliffe, E. (2022). The role of contextual factors in decision-making by General Practitioners on paediatric referral to the Emergency Department: A Discrete Choice Experiment [Data set]. Zenodo.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/mcdonnell_2022.R. Fixed blocked design (blocks 1 and 3 of 4; blocks 2/4 belong to a separate study, not deposited). Levels coded from the instrument's scenario texts (trivial wording variants normalised); task order inferred from the instrument. 150 GPs answered vs n = 142 in the record. Free-text comments dropped.

Description: 458 parents of children under 16 in Ireland (Qualtrics panels, February 2021) each made 12 forced choices between two unscheduled healthcare services (discrete choice experiment, 24 sets in 2 blocks) varying wait, appointment system, telephone advice, who they would see and cost. Outcome: forced choice.
Reference: Nicholson, E., McDonnell, T., Conlon, C., De Brún, A., Doherty, E., & McAuliffe, E. (2023). Parent's preferences for unscheduled paediatric healthcare: A discrete choice experiment. Health Expectations, 26(5), 1931-1940.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/nicholson_2023.R. Built from the authors' long Stata file; appointment-level wording from the article's Table 1 (the deposited survey .docx and Ngene file are the pilot versions). All 458 respondents kept; the article analyses 450 (8 with impossible child age / visit counts, identifiable from covariates). The article's conditional logit (Table 3) reproduces exactly.

Description: 3,570 British adults (Deltapoll online panel) each compared 8 pairs of hypothetical policy packages to fund the NHS, varying income-tax rates in five income brackets (non-decreasing schedules), the share of government spending on the NHS and whether immigrants are entitled to free health care. Outcomes: choice with a don't-know option and a 1-4 liking rating of each option.
Reference: Pardos-Prado, S., & Xena, C. (2026). Immigration, tax progressivity, and support for redistribution. Journal of European Public Policy.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/pardosprado_2026.R. Tax schedule drawn from the 126 non-decreasing schedules (bracket rates not independent). Rating stored raw: lower = more favourable. Article reports ~3,500 respondents / 56,000 observations; file has 3,570. Constituency and respondent IDs dropped. The deposit's separate YouGov 2x2 vignette experiment is not built.

Description: Swiss respondents (n = 1,000, German-language online survey) chose between two hypothetical male candidates varying name (Swiss or non-Swiss), profession, age, policy focus and number of children; in one arm a competence or political-office cue was added.
Reference: Portmann, L. (2022). What makes a successful candidate? Political experience and low-information cues in elections. The Journal of Politics, 84(4), 2049-2063.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/portmann_2022.R. Survey Experiment 2 only (Exp 1 and the quasi-experiment not built). Attributes from the slot-specific Qualtrics fields; the authors' policy_f copies candidate 1's policy onto candidate 2 (745 rows), so the paper's policy estimates will not reproduce from this table. Competence cue is '(not shown)' in arm 0.

Description: Residents of 223 slums in Bangalore, Jaipur and Patna (India; n = 6,174) chose between two hypothetical ward-leader candidates in each of 3 pairs, each candidate described by one party/identity/education trait and one benefit-provision trait.
Reference: Rains, E., & Wibbels, E. (2023). Informal work, risk, and clientelism: Evidence from 223 slums across India. British Journal of Political Science, 53(1), 1-24.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/rains_2023.R. Task inferred from consecutive row pairs (exactly one choice per pair verified); screen position not recorded. Level text and question are the codebook's English descriptions; survey wording and language not deposited. 1,704 of 7,878 respondents dropped because their candidates' traits were not saved.

Description: Pakistani adults (Gallup Pakistan phone survey, June 2023, n = 1,691) read a short text on Pakistan's IMF credit line with six independently randomized statements (reform costs, social protection, and government/industry/civil-society blame of the IMF), then rated approval of the program, government and IMF responsibility, and confidence in the IMF.
Reference: Reinsberg, B., Abouharb, M. R., & Seiferling, M. (2026). Unlocking public support: How communication about program design affects public perception of IMF interventions. Foreign Policy Analysis, 22(2), orag003.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/reinsberg_2026.R. Factorial vignette, one per respondent; each statement attribute is its text or '(not shown)'. Statements T4-T6 and outcomes q1-q2 are analysed in Abouharb, Reinsberg & Heinkelmann-Wild (2026, Global Studies Quarterly, ksag010), whose text supplies T4-T6 (cut at 80 characters in the .dta). Authors' models use the 1,514 who answered the IMF-knowledge item correctly (cov_imf_knowledge). Articles report 1,600 respondents; deposit has 1,691.

Description: US adults on Prolific (May 2017, n = 1,577) rated, for 5 pairs of hypothetical countries, how fair the effects of redistributive policies would be (0-10), with the policies' effects on national wealth, the wealthiest, the poorest, social mobility and the origin of wealth randomized.
Reference: Rodon, T., & Sanjaume-Calvet, M. (2020). How fair is it? An experimental study of perceived fairness of distributive policies. The Journal of Politics, 82(1), 384-391.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/rodon_2020.R. Built from the raw Qualtrics export; ratings kept as exported codes 1-11 (= 0-10). Table 4 used different row labels and mobility wording (trial_label_set). Attribute order randomized per table (attrpos_). IP addresses, Prolific IDs and free text dropped. 1,577 respondents vs 1,567 in the article (10 lack a Prolific profile row); the authors' under-5-minute exclusion not applied (cov_duration_sec).

Description: UK Prolific adults (n=210) each read one vignette (Study 3) describing an online-dating matchmaking offer from a human expert and from an algorithm, with each agent's benefit (match accuracy 75% or 95%) and decisional control (decision made for you vs final say) randomized in a 2x2x2x2 between-subjects design; outcomes are a 1-7 relative preference (expert to algorithm) and a binary expert/algorithm pick.
Reference: Schaap, G., Bosse, T., & Hendriks Vettehen, P. (2022). How much for your agency? Users trade off decisional control and optimal outcomes in choosing between AI and human decision-makers [Conference paper]. 72nd Annual Conference of the International Communication Association, Paris, France.
Notes: data/conjoint/schaap_2022.R. Study 3 of the deposit (Study 2 not deposited). One vignette per respondent (task 1, profile 1); four factors = benefit and control of the expert and of the algorithm. Both outcomes stored raw (rating 1 = definitely the expert .. 7 = definitely the algorithm; rating_agent 1 = expert, 2 = algorithm). Manipulation-check answers in trial_mc_*; failers were replaced by the authors. Conference paper, no DOI.

Description: UK Prolific adults (n=211) each read one vignette (Study 1) describing a stock-investment assistance offer from a human expert and from an algorithm, with each agent's benefit (estimated profit 3% or 21% return) and decisional control (decision made for you vs final say) randomized in a 2x2x2x2 between-subjects design; outcomes are a 1-7 relative preference (expert to algorithm) and a binary expert/algorithm pick.
Reference: Schaap, G., Bosse, T., & Hendriks Vettehen, P. (2022). How much for your agency? Users trade off decisional control and optimal outcomes in choosing between AI and human decision-makers [Conference paper]. 72nd Annual Conference of the International Communication Association, Paris, France.
Notes: data/conjoint/schaap_2022.R. Study 1 of the deposit (Study 2 not deposited). One vignette per respondent (task 1, profile 1); four factors = benefit and control of the expert and of the algorithm. Both outcomes stored raw (rating 1 = definitely the expert .. 7 = definitely the algorithm; rating_agent 1 = expert, 2 = algorithm). Manipulation-check answers in trial_mc_*; failers were replaced by the authors. Conference paper, no DOI.

Description: UK Prolific adults (n=210, June 2023) each read one incentivized vignette offering to invest a real GBP 1 through a human expert or an algorithm, with each agent's estimated profit (3% or 21%) and decisional control (automatic vs final say) randomized in a 2x2x2x2 between-subjects design; outcomes are the expert/algorithm pick, a 1-7 relative preference, and a buy/abort decision for those who picked an agent offering control.
Reference: Schaap, G., Bosse, T., & Hendriks Vettehen, P. (2023). How users trade off agency and benefits in accepting AI vs human decision-makers. Part 2: Direct choice - incentivized interaction [Data set]. OSF.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/schaap_2023.R. Data file from OSF component 7ft2s (also in parent nwqgs). Not the 4-condition Study 2 of the ICA 2022 paper: a separate incentivized 16-cell study, no publication found. Companion of schaap_2022_ai_agency_stocks/_dating (same project, same representation: one profile per respondent, four factors). rating_invest keeps source codes 1 = BUY, 8 = ABORT. Prolific IDs in the deposited .sav dropped; two full dates of birth reduced to year.

Description: Arabic-speaking refugees and migrants in Germany (online Qualtrics survey in Arabic, August 2024, n = 735) chose in up to 5 tasks which of two cities they would prefer to move to, cities varying in jobs, number of refugees, local institutional benefits, local population and mayor hostility, and family ties.
Reference: Secen, S., Ozturk, S., & Ozturk, A. (2026). Fearing not belonging: How local attitudes and policies shape refugees' destination preferences. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/secen_2026.R (builds the Germany and Turkey tables; authors analyse each country separately). Built from the raw Qualtrics exports; level text in Arabic as displayed; attribute order drawn once per respondent (attrpos_). identical to the authors' reshaped Germany file (735 IDs, 7,024 rows). Article paywalled: wording from the export, respondent count not checked against the paper. trial_factor1/2 are undocumented embedded-data arms. Free-text fields dropped.

Description: Arabic-speaking refugees and migrants in Turkey (online Qualtrics survey in Arabic, August 2024, n = 4,322) chose in up to 5 tasks which of two cities they would prefer to move to, cities varying in jobs, number of refugees, local institutional benefits, local population and mayor hostility, and family ties.
Reference: Secen, S., Ozturk, S., & Ozturk, A. (2026). Fearing not belonging: How local attitudes and policies shape refugees' destination preferences. Political Behavior.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/secen_2026.R (builds the Germany and Turkey tables; authors analyse each country separately). Built from the raw Qualtrics exports; level text in Arabic as displayed; attribute order drawn once per respondent (attrpos_). 3,717 completed all 5 tasks. Article paywalled: wording from the export, respondent count not checked against the paper. trial_factor1/2 are undocumented embedded-data arms. Free-text fields dropped.

Description: US adults in the NORC AmeriSpeak panel (July-August 2021, Study One; n = 962) each rated one hypothetical state trial-court judge whose name/gender, race, tenure, party, sentencing record, selection method and vote share were randomized; outcomes are support for the judge (1-5) and perceived fairness (1-5).
Reference: Stone, A. R., & Olson, M. P. (2025). Elections improve support for state trial court judges in the United States. Journal of Law and Courts.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/stone_2025.R (both fieldings). One profile per respondent; level text from article Table 1, codes from README. Attribute order was randomized but not recorded. Question wordings not deposited (paraphrased from README). State-court legitimacy items not kept (about courts, deposited reversed/rescaled). No survey weight in deposit.

Description: US adults in the NORC AmeriSpeak panel (July 2023, Study Two; n = 1172) each rated one hypothetical state trial-court judge whose name/gender, race, tenure, party, sentencing record, selection method and vote share were randomized; outcomes are support for the judge (1-5).
Reference: Stone, A. R., & Olson, M. P. (2025). Elections improve support for state trial court judges in the United States. Journal of Law and Courts.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/stone_2025.R (both fieldings). One profile per respondent; level text from article Table 1, codes from README. Attribute order was randomized but not recorded. Question wordings not deposited (paraphrased from README). State-court legitimacy items not kept (about courts, deposited reversed/rescaled). No survey weight in deposit.

Description: 798 EPADE panel respondents in Chile (online panel, wave 3, 2026) chose between and rated 7 pairs of hypothetical presidential candidates varying age, education and seven democratic-versus-authoritarian positions. Outcomes: forced choice and 1-10 favourability.
Reference: Torcal, M. (2026). Elections, Affective Polarization and Democratic Erosion in 10 Democracies (EPADE) [Data set]. OSF.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/torcal_2026_epade.R. Kept apart from the EU table: Chile is outside the EU pre-analysis plan, the tax level is worded differently and favourability is stored 1-10 although the English questionnaire prints 1-7. No article yet.

Description: EPADE panel respondents in Germany (995), Portugal (956) and the Netherlands (811) (online panel, wave 3, 2025-2026) chose between and rated 7 pairs of hypothetical candidates for head of government varying age, education and seven democratic-versus-authoritarian positions (law and order, cultural values, decision style, tax, institutional checks, civil society and media, crisis management). Outcomes: forced choice and 1-7 favourability.
Reference: Torcal, M. (2026). Elections, Affective Polarization and Democratic Erosion in 10 Democracies (EPADE) [Data set]. OSF.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/torcal_2026_epade.R. Three countries pooled per the conjoint pre-analysis plan (osf.io/fwn9a); attribute text is the master English wording, not the translated text respondents saw (the Dutch file's back-translated labels differ). No article yet. Chile is a separate table.

Description: Labelled discrete choice experiment on agri-environmental schemes: 107 English farmers (online, 2021-22) chose in 6 cards among four schemes (flower strips, cover crops, maintaining permanent grassland, converting arable land to grassland) or no scheme, with contract duration, free advisory support, administrative effort and yearly payment per hectare varied; outcomes are the choice and the share of land the respondent would enrol in the chosen scheme.
Reference: Tyllianakis, E., Will, M., Václavík, T., & Ziv, G. (2025). Drivers and preferences of European farmers for agri-environmental public goods schemes: A two-stage analysis. Journal for Nature Conservation, 86, 126912.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/tyllianakis_2025.R. English case study only; the German (74) and Czech (69) samples of the deposit are under 100 each and use different (German/Czech, EUR) cards. Card contents transcribed from the survey PDF's card images (every payment checked against the article's UK payment list). No scheme = opt-out. IP addresses, coordinates, postcodes and panel IDs in the deposit dropped.

Description: Residents of 162 Swiss urban municipalities (registry sample, online, Jan-Mar 2023, n = 3,500) compared 4 pairs of housing-development proposals varying usage, developer, densification, cost-rent share, green space, climate measures and final decision-maker, choosing the preferred proposal and saying whether they would accept each.
Reference: Wehr, M., Wicki, M. L., Wittwer, S., & Kaufmann, D. (2026). Beyond NIMBY-ism: Rethinking acceptance of housing densification in a direct democratic renters society. Journal of Public Policy, 46(1), 21-49.
Notes: Script data/conjoint/wehr_2026.R. English level text (= the article's Figure 1 English screen) stored for all; respondents answered in DE/FR/IT/EN (cov_survey_language). rating_accept = per-proposal Yes (1) / No (0), wording paraphrased. Densification = % increase in residents, cost rent = % of units at cost rent (article Table 1). Postal codes/municipality numbers dropped. N 3,500 vs article 3,497.
